papers.title: AGR: Agentic Generative Retrieval with Tool-Augmented Search
papers.authors: Ming Yang, Yaqi Yin, Zhibo Wang, Xiaoze Jiang, Jingwei Zhuo, Chao Zhang, Quanzhi Zhu, Weiguo Zheng, Liang Zeng, Yunfeng ...
papers.summary: Generative retrieval need not encode every available feature up front. AGR requests intent, location, or behavioral evidence while decoding item identifiers, then resumes generation with a compact observation. A Kuaishou online experiment reports a 0.205% increase in requests with strongly relevant top-four results.
papers.key_insight: Feature value depends on the current identifier prefix. Learning when to request evidence can reduce redundant history encoding, although tool use still costs more than the feature-free baseline.

deep_reading.content_html:
AGR lets a generative retriever request features when they become useful instead of reading every available signal on every request. The model generates an item identifier, pauses to acquire intent or behavioral evidence, and continues along a better-informed branch. The Kuaishou and Fudan team evaluates this interface in production search as well as public benchmarks.

1. Why more features are not always better

Generative retrieval replaces direct item scoring with prediction of a short semantic identifier. Related items share parts of that identifier, so decoding progressively narrows the catalog. Industrial search, however, relies on more than the query: user history, location, intent, and freshness can all matter.

Encoding every feature up front creates two problems. Some signals are redundant or irrelevant for the current request. Others become useful only at a particular point in the identifier tree. Intent may distinguish a movie from a game early in decoding, while behavioral history may distinguish individual games later. Static injection does not explicitly make that distinction.

AGR treats feature acquisition as a decoding decision. Its contribution concerns when and where existing evidence enters the retriever, rather than the discovery of a new feature source.

2. How feature tools enter decoding

The output vocabulary includes tool-call tokens alongside item-code tokens. At each step the model can extend the identifier or request a feature. A request executes an external function whose result becomes a compact observation embedding. The call token triggers the action; the returned observation, rather than the call token itself, enters the next-step context.

Categorical features such as intent and location map to learned observation embeddings. Observations have a distinct positional representation and do not advance the item-identifier depth. The final retrieved output remains an ordinary identifier, with tool tokens removed.

Behavioral tools compress a sequence of historical interactions into evidence relevant to the current prefix. The default voting implementation retains historical items with matching identifier prefixes and returns their most frequent next code. The attention implementation retrieves nearby histories in embedding space and aggregates their successor information, allowing approximate rather than exact prefix matches.

The voting tool asks a narrower question than a full user-history encoder: given the branch reached so far, which continuation has this user preferred? That narrower interface explains why it can avoid repeatedly encoding a long sequence.

Training first teaches ordinary identifier generation, then introduces tool-augmented trajectories. Rule-based construction checks that a request-side feature agrees with the positive item and is not already explicit in the query. Placement reflects the depth at which the observation most sharply narrows the candidate set. Tool-token losses receive dynamic scaling because newly introduced tokens would otherwise dominate the already-learned identifier objective.

The reported backbone is an encoder–decoder model with roughly 574 million parameters. This is supervised tool learning from constructed demonstrations, rather than a reinforcement-learning policy discovered through online interaction. At inference, each beam has its own call budget. Valid identifier transitions and length-normalized comparisons keep tool use compatible with catalog-constrained search.

3. What the contribution amounts to

The central change is moving feature selection inside retrieval. A fixed user vector supplies the same representation throughout decoding; a prefix-conditioned tool can return different evidence at different branches.

The paper also supplies the training and serving machinery needed to make that idea concrete. Tool decisions, external observations, and item codes have distinct roles. Constructed trajectories supervise placement, while call budgets constrain inference. These details matter because adding an intent feature alone would not demonstrate adaptive acquisition.

The relevant comparison therefore holds the feature set constant and varies injection strategy. Otherwise a gain could come entirely from additional information rather than from the decision about when to read it.

4. Read quality and cost together

The industrial history-encoding comparison reports the following values. Cost figures are comparable within that experiment’s matched configuration.

Industrial configurationRecall@50Training seconds/stepServing GPUs/1K requests
Feature-free baseline0.28631.1632.38
Direct long-history encoding0.324110.7948.33
AGR with history tool only0.32371.9694.76
Full AGR0.3264——

The history tool nearly matches direct long-history encoding while reducing its serving cost by about 42.9%. This is a comparison between two ways of using history. The feature-free baseline remains cheaper than either of them.

A separate ablation holds the feature set constant. Static injection reaches Recall@50 of 0.3159, while adaptive injection reaches 0.3264; fixed-position tool calls fall between them. This supports a benefit from placement beyond the benefit of simply supplying more information.

The online experiment uses an initial A/A check followed by an A/B traffic split. The paper reports average serving latency of 35 ms and a 0.205% improvement in its relevance measure: the fraction of requests whose top-four results are strongly relevant. That is neither nDCG nor CTR. Offline comparisons use a generative-retrieval baseline, while the online comparison uses the production system, so their gains should retain their original baselines and metric definitions.

5. Remaining limitations

The authors identify rule-constructed demonstrations, a limited tool ecosystem, and training along correct identifier prefixes as key limitations. The last creates a concrete deployment gap: a tool that helps on the correct branch may not help the model recover after it has already generated an incorrect prefix.

Evaluation under model-generated prefixes would test that gap more directly. A successful production deployment also does not establish a fixed benefit for other businesses. Sparse histories, slow tools, or different relevance objectives can change the trade-off.

6. Practical experiments for search

Start with one existing feature source, such as query intent or recent clicks. Keep the catalog and identifier scheme fixed, then compare feature-free retrieval, fixed injection, and adaptive injection while measuring both relevance and request latency. This separates feature quality from acquisition policy.

A prefix-conditioned voting tool offers a relatively small history experiment. Break results down by history length and query ambiguity to check whether gains concentrate on requests that need additional evidence.

Finally, record call counts, tool latency, and ranking changes after each call. The useful design principle is to make established features available at the moment they distinguish candidates, with enough instrumentation to see whether the extra computation pays for itself.

papers.title: Evolving Semantic Indexes for Generative Retrieval
papers.authors: Jinming Nian, Jyun-Yu Jiang, Henry Tsai, Yi Fang, Zhirong Liang
papers.summary: An LLM evolves executable semantic-index programs while a tiny retriever screens them. With the target training recipe fixed, NQ320K Recall@100 rises from 85.82% to 90.57%.
papers.key_insight: Index construction and collision handling are coupled. A cheap proxy can rank index changes well, yet become misleading when the search also changes the generator objective.

deep_reading.content_html:
A small retriever can cheaply evaluate semantic-index programs proposed by an LLM, making it practical to search for better identifiers for generative retrieval. The paper holds the final generator and its training recipe fixed. It asks whether changing what the generator must learn can improve retrieval. Its most useful result is a boundary: proxy-selected index changes transfer, while proxy-selected training objectives can make the target model worse.

1. Problem and motivation: identifiers shape the search

Generative retrieval predicts a document identifier from a query, one token at a time. A semantic ID is a short code derived from document content. Documents with the same prefix share early decoding decisions; pruning that prefix removes every document beneath it.

A typical index quantizes document embeddings in stages and appends a token to distinguish documents that receive identical codes. Index construction and collision handling are coupled: changing the partition also changes which documents need disambiguation. Reconstruction error, balanced code usage and low collision rates are imperfect substitutes for downstream retrieval quality. Random codes can look balanced without being useful.

Training the target generator for every candidate index is expensive. The paper instead uses a tiny generator to rank candidates, then trains the target only for selected programs.

2. Method: mutate code and evaluate executable indexes

The outer loop maintains a population of programs, selects parents and asks a locally served open-weight LLM for edits. The inner loop executes each proposal, checks its output and collision rate, and trains a proxy only after the program passes those gates. Failed proposals receive execution diagnostics for revision.

The program interface stays fixed: document embeddings, query embeddings and training relevance pairs go in; aligned integer document IDs come out. The implementation can change quantization, clustering or initialization. The final generator receives query text and learns to predict the resulting codes.

The proxy has about one million non-embedding parameters. Original training relevance pairs are split between proxy training and search feedback. The split is by query–document pair, so different answers to the same query can occur on both sides. Held-out test queries remain inaccessible to search.

After selection, the winning program is rebuilt with all original training pairs and a 1B target generator is trained. Final public-dataset training additionally uses synthetic queries; the proxy–target calibration experiment does not. Their absolute scores therefore should not be compared as if they came from the same recipe.

A proxy evaluation takes roughly twenty minutes, versus five hours for a target run. That comparison excludes mutation, index construction and failed executions; it is not an end-to-end pipeline speedup.

3. Contribution: coordinate semantic codes and collision suffixes

The strongest NQ program retains residual quantization. It chooses codes by direction, using cosine similarity, while subtracting unnormalized code vectors so that magnitude still affects the next residual. It also increases codebook capacity and introduces several training stabilizers. The gain cannot be assigned to a single change.

Query supervision makes the reconstructed document embedding align with the mean embedding of its relevant training queries. The index therefore reflects how people look for a document, rather than preserving only its original content representation.

Collision suffixes gain a shared meaning. Non-colliding documents receive zero. Within a collision group, documents are ordered by similarity to the group's centroid. Smaller suffixes then consistently indicate more central documents, rather than arbitrary database order.

4. Results: useful index search, unreliable broader search

The table reports target-model Recall@100 on NQ320K. Changes are absolute percentage points.

Search scopeTarget R@100Change from seed
Seed85.82%—
SID only87.40%+1.58
Joint SID and collision handling90.57%+4.75
Generator objective84.46%−1.36
Full pipeline76.12%−9.70

Joint index search adds 4.75 points of recall on NQ. MSMARCO and the private multilingual commerce dataset also improve, although early-rank commerce gains are within one standard deviation. The paper does not establish that generative retrieval dominates dense or lexical retrieval: BM25 remains stronger on several MSMARCO metrics.

Across twenty-one calibrated index programs, proxy and target recall have a Spearman rank correlation of 0.90. Accurate absolute prediction is unnecessary if candidate preferences transfer.

Changing the training objective breaks that logic. Objectives affect how a model learns and interact with architecture, pretraining and optimization. An objective tuned to a tiny model can harm a larger pretrained model. Five observed objective or full-pipeline programs improved proxy fitness while reducing target recall. That small sample illustrates a failure mode rather than establishing a broad statistical law.

5. Limitations

Search scopes use different starting points, budgets and gates. Joint search beating sequential search is therefore not a controlled intervention on coordination alone. Several index changes occur together, limiting attribution to individual mechanisms.

The private commerce evaluation withholds absolute scores and provides no online A/B result. Purchases are also different labels from answer relevance or community-content satisfaction. The public collections are reduced subsets, not evidence of unrestricted web-scale deployment.

Proxy evaluation still requires final target-model checks. Mutation failures and index rebuilding add cost. The experiments also leave incremental document insertion and migration of existing identifiers unresolved.

6. Practical implications

A team with a generative retriever can freeze its encoder, generator and data, then compare alternative index programs. Measure agreement between proxy and target rankings on the same programs, rather than relying only on collision rate or code balance.

For short community text, a concrete experiment is to construct codes using query–clicked-document pairs alongside content. This transfers the paper's query-aware indexing idea; click bias and noisy short text remain separate data problems. The paper does not report UGC production results.

Collision suffixes are another inspectable component. If they encode database order, the generator learns arbitrary distinctions. Giving suffixes a consistent geometric interpretation may make that final token easier to learn. Keep automated search focused on shared index structure and verify the selected result with the real target retriever.

papers.title: UniRec: A Unified Expressive-Aligned Generative Recommendation Framework for E-commerce
papers.authors: Ziliang Wang, Gaoyun Lin, Xuesi Wang, Shaoqiang Liang, Yili Huang, Weijie Bian, Li Zhang, Mingchen Cai, Jian Dong, Guanx...
papers.summary: The Shopee authors measured three-level semantic IDs (SIDs) built by standard RQ-KMeans: the top 10% most-exposed full codes took 89.62% of exposure, so a generative recommender's probability mass concentrates on a few popular codes. UniRec has the model first generate the item's level-2 and level-3 category tokens and only then the three SID levels, and when building SIDs it gives every code an exposure-weighted capacity limit. ==Once the category is generated, each later SID level only has to choose within that category==. Offline HR@50 is 22.6% higher (relative) than OneRec-V2; online, against the old multi-stage pipeline, orders rose 4.76% and GMV 5.60%.

deep_reading.content_html:
Generative recommendation encodes each product as a few layers of discrete semantic IDs (SIDs), and the model generates these IDs layer by layer to perform retrieval and ranking. This Shopee paper points out one gap between it and discriminative ranking models: when a discriminative model scores a candidate it sees the product's category, shop and brand directly and crosses them with user features, while a generative model has seen no product-side information at all before it generates the first SID layer. UniRec's core technique is Chain-of-Attribute (CoA): the model first generates the product's category and then generates the SID conditioned on that category, which puts back into the decoding path the product features a discriminative model can use. Alongside it come an SID construction that caps codebook load by exposure, CDC that injects scenario and combination features into decoding, and business alignment via RFT plus DPO. Offline HR@50 is 22.6% higher (relative) than the strongest baseline OneRec-V2; launched on Shopee's main feed and landing pages, orders rose 4.76% and GMV 5.60%, with 110ms end-to-end latency versus 266ms for the original multi-stage pipeline.

The paper's arXiv title is "UniRec: Bridging the Expressive Gap between Generative and Discriminative Recommendation via Chain-of-Attribute"; this write-up is based on the arXiv full text.

1. Where generative recommendation falls short

A discriminative ranker estimates p(y∣f,u), the probability that user u engages (y) given product features f, with all product features visible at scoring time. A generative model generates the SID layer by layer as ∏l​p(sl​∣s<l​,u), and when generating the first layer it sees only the user, no product features.

The authors use Bayes' rule to show where the gap comes from:
p(y∣f,u)∝p(f∣y,u)p(y∣u),p(f∣y,u)=k=1∏n​p(fk​∣f<k​,y,u)
p(y∣u) does not vary across products, so ranking by the discriminative score is equivalent to ranking by p(f∣y,u), and the latter, expanded by the chain rule, is exactly generating product features one by one. The conclusion: if a generative model generated all of a product's features one by one, its ranking ability would equal the discriminative model's. Real systems cannot generate all features one by one because latency would be too high, so they compress product semantics into a few SID layers. Structured attributes such as category, shop and brand, which discriminative models cross directly, are folded into the SID during compression and no longer appear explicitly at decoding time, and that is where the gap comes from.

2. Method

2.1 Chain-of-Attribute: generate the category first, then the SID

CoA prepends m attribute tokens a to the SID sequence, so generation goes attributes first, SID second:
p(s∣u)=p(a∣u)⋅l=0∏L−1​p(sl​∣a,s<l​,u)
In the production configuration the attributes are the product's second- and third-level categories (categories have three levels L1, L2, L3, getting finer going down), so a product's decoding path is "L2 category → L3 category → s0​ → s1​ → s2​", two steps longer than before.

Why generating the category first helps: products in the same category sit close together in SID space, so once the category is known, the candidate range for the next SID layer shrinks. The authors write this as the reduction in conditional entropy ΔHl​=H(sl​∣s<l​,u)−H(sl​∣a,s<l​,u), which equals the conditional mutual information between the attributes and that SID layer and is greater than 0 whenever the two are correlated. With a lower error probability at each layer, the probability of getting the whole path right goes up, and beam search becomes more stable.

2.2 Capacity-constrained SID: balance the codebook by exposure, not product count

Existing balanced quantization (such as the RQ-KMeans used in OneRec) gives each codeword a similar number of products, but product popularity is long-tailed, and an even product count does not mean even exposure. The authors measured on Shopee production data: ranked by exposure, the top 10% of first-layer codewords take 33.24% of exposure; the top 10% of (s0​,s1​) combinations take 87.90%; the top 10% of three-layer combinations take 89.62%.

High-exposure token paths appear often in the training data, so the model keeps generating those few paths during beam search; the authors call this a Matthew effect inherited layer by layer. Capacity-constrained SID adds one constraint to the residual clustering at each layer: the sum of exposure weights Vk​ of the products in each cluster may not exceed τ times the average load.
{zi​},{μk​}min​i=1∑N​∥xi​−μzi​​∥22​s.t.Vk​=i:zi​=k∑​wi​≤τCcap​
xi​ is product i's residual vector at the current layer, zi​ the cluster it is assigned to, μk​ a cluster center, wi​ its historical impression count, Ccap​ total exposure divided by the number of clusters, and τ=1.05 in production. Solving this exactly is NP-hard, so a two-step greedy procedure is used: assign each product to its nearest cluster, then move products from overloaded clusters to the nearest cluster that is not full, repeating until reconstruction error stops changing.

2.3 CDC: tell the model which task it is on, then add combination features

One generative model has to serve objectives such as click, purchase, add-to-cart and cross-border, and scenarios such as main feed, search, similar items and flash sale. Task-Conditioned BOS replaces the fixed start token with a learnable vector looked up by "objective × scenario", steering decoding toward that scenario's distribution from the first step.

Content Summary deals with the combined meaning of tokens: the same s1​ following different categories may stand for completely different products. Giving every token pair its own embedding would mean about 16 million combinations for two layers with 4,000-token vocabularies. CDC instead uses 3 hash functions ($x+y$, x⋅y, p1​x+p2​y, with p1​, p2​ primes) to map combinations such as (L2 category, s0​), (L3 category, s1​) and (s0​, s1​) into one shared hash embedding table, concatenated into each step's combination feature ct​.

2.4 Decoder and business alignment

The decoding-side sequence [BOS, attribute tokens, SID tokens] is Q; the item vectors of the user's latest 200 clicks, followed by 100 multimodal vectors fused from multi-layer SID embeddings, together form K and V, passing through 3 layers of cross-attention with a learnable gating coefficient and an MMoE-FFN. Each step has its own Rank Head, which concatenates the attention output, the embedding of the prefix generated so far, ct​ and the aggregated user representation, and outputs that step's token distribution through SENet and MaskNet.

Next-token prediction only fits the impression distribution and does not optimize GMV directly. RFT computes a business reward for each sample, subtracts the batch mean, divides by the root mean square and clips to get A~i​, and multiplies the sample's loss weight by (1+λA~i​). DPO builds preference pairs from items impressed under the same request, with purchase > click > impression only, and back-propagates only through the last SID layer while the predictions of earlier layers are left unchanged, so alignment does not disturb the prefix. The two are trained together:
L=LRFT​+λDPO​LDPO​
In production the RFT to DPO loss weight ratio is 20:3, and DPO's β=0.1.

3. Experiments

3.1 Main results

This experiment is meant to show that UniRec's retrieval quality is higher than existing generative and discriminative methods. The data is 9 consecutive days of Shopee main-feed production logs, billions of interactions. HR@K generates the top K candidates with beam search and checks whether the target product is among them; "order samples" counts only samples that ended in a purchase. Baselines: SASRec, a self-attention sequential recommender that does nearest-neighbor retrieval over the SID codebook with its learned representation; TIGER, generative retrieval with an encoder-decoder architecture; OneRec-V2, decoder-only generative retrieval with cross-attention. All three generative models have 0.05B parameters.

On all samples UniRec is 9.5 to 10.1 points above OneRec-V2; on order samples it is 9.0 to 11.5 points higher. The authors attribute the gain on order samples to Task-Conditioned BOS separating click and purchase objectives and to RFT weighting samples by GMV.

3.2 Which attribute chain to use

This experiment answers which category level is best to put in front of the SID. It compares no attributes against different category combinations, looking at both each step's token Top-3 hit rate and the final HR.

Without attributes the first SID layer's Top-3 hit rate is only 0.314; with the L2 and L3 categories added it rises to 0.682. The improvement is concentrated in the first layer because the first SID layer originally had no product-side condition at all, so adding category information shrinks its choices the most. The finer the category, the higher the first-layer hit rate; generating L2 → L3 in sequence works best.

3.3 Component ablations

This experiment is meant to quantify the contribution of capacity-constrained SID, Task-Conditioned BOS and Content Summary; each time one component is removed and compared with the full model.

Removing any one of the three components drops HR@50 by 4 to 6 points. After switching back to RQ-KMeans, the authors also compared the exposure concentration of the two SIDs: on three-layer combinations, the top 1% of tokens take 57.33% of exposure under RQ-KMeans and 26.04% with the capacity constraint.

Task-Conditioned BOS also got a multi-scenario experiment: trained on mixed samples from three production scenarios, HR@100 is 0.470 with a separate model per scenario, 0.486 for mixed training without scenario prompts, and 0.510 with the scenario BOS. Mixed training helps by itself, and adding the scenario condition improves all three cutoffs a bit more.

Increasing model width dmodel​ from 64 to 512 raises HR@50 from 0.397 to 0.557, without saturating.

3.4 Online A/B

Online experiments ran on the main feed and landing pages, with the original discriminative multi-stage recommender as control and 20% of user traffic per bucket.

4. Limitations

The paper has no separate limitations discussion. Two points stand out from the experimental setup. First, all offline comparisons are on Shopee's internal data, with baselines also limited to 0.05B parameters, and there are no results on public datasets. Second, the online control is the entire discriminative multi-stage system, so the A/B gain includes the combined effect of the generative architecture, CoA, capacity-constrained SID, CDC and alignment; the paper gives no per-component online contribution.

5. Practical implications

  • If the first-layer SID hit rate of your generative retrieval is low, try CoA first: put one or two category levels in front of the SID, at the cost of only two extra decoding steps; in Table 2 the first layer's Top-3 hit rate rose from 0.314 to 0.682.
  • When building SIDs, check exposure concentration, not just whether product counts are even. A codebook balanced by product count can still let a few popular combinations take nearly 90% of exposure, and beam search will keep walking those few paths; adding an exposure-based capacity constraint only changes the clustering assignment step, so the cost is low.

papers.title: OneLatent: Latent Reasoning for Efficient Foundation Recommendation Models
papers.authors: Hao Jiang, Peiru Du, Pengfei Yao, Mengting Li, Siyuan Lou, Kuo Cai, Sheng Yu, Qiang Luo, Jian Liang, Ruiming Tang, Fei P...
papers.summary: When an LLM serves as a recommendation foundation model, generating a natural-language reasoning trace (CoT) before outputting the item's semantic ID (SID) makes the output long and cuts throughput. Kuaishou's OneLatent inserts 3 learnable special tokens between the user context and the target SID: training first makes the model reproduce a teacher LLM's reasoning text after these 3 tokens, then switches to predicting the SID directly after them; at serving time only these 3 tokens are fed and no reasoning text is generated. The teacher writes reasoning from three angles: inferring intent, scoring the clicked item, and explaining why it was clicked. On the industrial dataset, SID@64 is 17.44% higher than OneReason-CoT's reason-then-answer mode; but against the strongest baseline trained on the same teacher reasoning and answering directly, the gain is only 1.58%, so most of the improvement comes from the teacher reasoning data. ==The reasoning slots are fixed at 3, so decoding does not grow with reasoning length==, and throughput is 17.49x that of explicit reasoning. A local-services advertising A/B test estimates a 9.6% revenue lift.

deep_reading.content_html:
When a large language model serves as a recommendation foundation model, one approach is to have the model first write a natural-language reasoning trace (CoT) and then output the semantic ID (SID, an identifier that maps an item to a three-level discrete code) of the next item. The reasoning text is far longer than a three-level SID, so it holds back both decoding time and throughput; moreover, earlier work on OneReason already reported that reasoning first and then answering does not consistently beat answering directly with the same model. Kuaishou's OneLatent appends 3 fixed special tokens after the user context and trains in several steps: first the model learns to reproduce a teacher LLM's reasoning text after these 3 tokens, then it is switched to outputting the target SID directly after them; at serving time only these 3 tokens are appended and no reasoning text is generated. On Kuaishou's local-services industrial data, OneLatent reaches SID@64 of 0.1993, 17.44% higher than OneReason-CoT in reason-then-answer mode, and its inference throughput is 17.49 times that of explicit reasoning, essentially the same as direct prediction without reasoning. Against the strongest baseline trained on the same teacher reasoning data and answering directly, the 3 latent tokens add only 1.58% on the industrial data, which shows that most of the gain comes from the teacher reasoning data itself. An online A/B test on 5% of traffic estimates a 9.6% revenue lift, and the model is now serving all traffic.

1. Why explicit reasoning works poorly in recommendation

The input of a foundation recommendation model (FRM) is the user profile Pu​, the chronologically ordered interaction history Hu​ and the request-time context Cu​ (time, location, search terms and so on); the output is the SID of the next item the user interacts with. Making the model write reasoning first causes two problems. One is cost: every request must decode the whole reasoning text token by token. The other is that accuracy does not necessarily rise: an extra generation path sits between the reasoning text and the SID, and if the reasoning goes off by one step, the SID that follows goes off with it. In the paper's Table 2, OneReason-CoT in reason-first mode reaches SID@64 of 0.1697 on the industrial data, below the 0.1823 of the same checkpoint answering directly.

The authors' idea is to use the teacher's reasoning only as a training signal and keep the reasoning process in the model's internal hidden states, with no text output at inference.

2. Method

2.1 What the latent tokens are

The authors add 3 special tokens ⟨L1​⟩⟨L2​⟩⟨L3​⟩ to the vocabulary, and all samples share this same set of token IDs. When the Transformer reaches these 3 positions it produces hidden states that vary with the context, and the SID tokens that follow read those hidden states through ordinary causal attention. There is no extra encoder, projection layer or decoder; the only added compute at inference is the fixed 3 tokens. The authors also state explicitly that later tokens can still see the raw context directly, so there is no guarantee that all the reasoning information is compressed into these 3 positions.

2.2 Teacher reasoning: three views, length adjusted to difficulty

The teacher model is Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507, which writes reasoning for each sample from three views:

  • Exploration: given only the user profile and history, the teacher infers the user's likely consumption intents and outputs reasoning plus a list of intents.
  • Evaluation: additionally told the item the user actually interacted with, the teacher judges how well that item matches the user's evidence and outputs reasoning plus a score from 1 to 5.
  • Attribution: told that this item is a positive sample, the teacher explains which historical signals led to the interaction.

The evaluation and attribution views use the true item, but this information goes only to the teacher and never enters the student model's input, so the answer does not leak. The prompt also asks the teacher to first judge how complex the evidence is: samples with a clear signal converge quickly, and samples with conflicting signals get a multi-dimensional comparison. The resulting reasoning drops to 65% of its original average length (taking the non-adaptive average length as 100), and on the longest tenth of samples the semantic similarity between the two kinds of reasoning is about 0.92.

2.3 Three-stage alignment and post-training

The student model is initialized from Qwen3.5-0.8B and first pretrained on the recommendation domain so that SIDs and item text descriptions can generate each other:
Lsem​=−logpϕ​(Sv​∣Cv​)−logpϕ​(Cv​∣Sv​)
Here Sv​ is the three-level SID of item v and Cv​ is its text description. The latent tokens are then trained in three stages:

  • Stage I: the input is "profile, history, view marker, 3 latent tokens", and the target is to reproduce one view's teacher reasoning.
  • Stage II: the same input, with the target changed to all of that sample's view reasonings. The loss of each reasoning is averaged over its tokens, so that long reasoning does not take a larger share of the loss.
  • Stage III: the request context is added to the input, and the target changes from reasoning text to the SID of the next item.

Post-training first runs curriculum fine-tuning from high-activity to low-activity users, then trains on a 1:1 mix of "append latent tokens, then predict the SID" and "predict the SID directly without latent tokens", so that both modes remain usable.

3. Experiments

3.1 Main results

This experiment compares OneLatent with three groups of baselines: item-ID-based sequential recommenders (GRU4Rec, BERT4Rec, HSTU), SID-based generative recommenders (TIGER, OneRec), and reasoning-enhanced models based on OneReason. There are two datasets: 7 days of industrial logs from Kuaishou local services (test set of 20,393 instances), and Kuaishou's public LLM-Rec benchmark (test set of 10,000). The metric Hit@64 indicates whether the correct item appears among the top 64 results the model generates. The table below is taken from the paper's Table 2; NoThink and Think are the direct-answer and reason-first modes of the same checkpoint, and the parentheses give the reasoning data used for training:

MethodPublic SID@64Public ID@64Industrial SID@64Industrial ID@64
TIGER0.00780.01560.14320.0859
OneRec0.00820.01770.14680.0900
OneReason0.00810.02720.16580.4941
OneReason-CoT NoThink (original CoT)0.01040.03340.18230.4936
OneReason-CoT NoThink (evaluation view)0.02130.06230.19620.5065
OneReason-CoT Think (original CoT)0.00890.03050.16970.4759
OneReason-CoT Think (three views merged)0.00910.03030.15050.4567
OneLatent (three views merged)0.02390.07420.19930.5088

OneLatent is highest on every metric. But the source of the gain must be read from two separate comparisons. Against Think mode, industrial SID@64 is 17.44% higher; and when trained on the same three-view data, Think mode reaches only 0.1505 while OneLatent reaches 0.1993, which shows that for the same reasoning data, having the model write it out token by token before answering actually lowers accuracy, because the SID is generated only after the reasoning is finished and any error in the reasoning carries over to the SID. Against the strongest non-OneLatent result in each column, industrial SID@64 is only 1.58% higher and ID@64 only 0.45% higher; on the public data the gains are 12.21% and 19.10%. The strongest baseline on the industrial data is the model trained on evaluation-view reasoning that answers directly, and it already captures most of the gain.

On the 9B backbone, OneLatent reaches SID@64 of 0.2008, 8.13% above the best same-size non-latent result of 0.1857 (paper Table 3).

3.2 Inference efficiency

This experiment checks the inference overhead of the latent tokens. The authors compare three inference modes on 872 test instances (paper Table 7):

MethodTotal time (s)QPS
Direct prediction (no reasoning)3.17274.56
Explicit reasoning55.5915.68
OneLatent3.17274.29

OneLatent's throughput is 17.49 times that of explicit reasoning and nearly identical to direct prediction, because each request processes only 3 extra fixed tokens and does not need to decode reasoning text token by token. The paper's conclusion says "more than 10 times", which disagrees with the 17.49 times in the body; the number in the table is used here.

3.3 Quality and role of the teacher reasoning

This experiment checks whether the three-view reasoning is better than the original reasoning. The authors have GPT-5.5 score 100 samples of each kind of reasoning from 1 to 5 on nine dimensions (factuality, evidence use, causal logic and so on): OneReason's original reasoning averages 3.14, the adaptive-length reasoning 3.54, and the exploration, evaluation and attribution views 4.16, 4.33 and 4.03 (paper Table 4). Training OneLatent on different reasoning data raises public SID@64 from 0.0092 with the original reasoning to 0.0239 with the three views merged, and the evaluation view alone reaches 0.0233 (paper Table 5).

As the number of latent tokens goes from 1 to 3, the hit rates of all three SID levels rise; with 4 or 5 tokens they no longer improve consistently, so 3 are used in the end.

To see what is stored in the latent tokens, the authors feed the profile, view marker and 3 latent tokens to the trained model, deliberately leaving out the interaction history, have it generate reasoning text, and compare its semantic similarity with the teacher's reasoning; the cosine similarities of the three views are between 0.79 and 0.80 (paper Table 8). The authors themselves note that the profile is still visible, so this similarity only shows an association and cannot prove that the reasoning information is all stored in the latent tokens.

3.4 Deployment and A/B test

Even without reasoning text, calling the foundation model synchronously for every request still exceeds the latency and throughput budget. OneLatent is therefore deployed as a separate retrieval channel: new user behavior triggers asynchronous inference, refresh priority is set by user value and behavior strength, the generated candidates are written to Redis, and online requests take candidates from the cache, where they compete with the existing retrieval results in fine ranking. The A/B test ran in a sub-scenario of Kuaishou's local-services advertising, with 5% of traffic each for the treatment and control groups, from September 3 to 10, 2026. The treatment group's impressions rose 2.566%, ad spend rose 5.157%, and the posterior estimate of revenue rose 9.6%.

4. Limitations

The paper has no separate limitations section; in the body the authors acknowledge two points: the latent tokens are not a strict information bottleneck, and the reasoning information may be spread across the whole model; and the gain in Table 6 comes from the complete training pipeline and cannot be attributed to the latent tokens alone.

Two further points deserve attention. First, on the industrial data OneLatent is only 1.58% above the direct-answer model trained on the same teacher data, and the paper reports no variance across runs, so it is impossible to judge whether this gap is stable. Second, the online deployment uses an asynchronous cache, with candidates generated after the user's last behavior; the paper does not separate how much of the A/B gain comes from latent reasoning and how much from adding one more retrieval channel.

5. Practical implications

First, to give a recommendation model reasoning ability, the teacher's reasoning can first be used as training data rather than requiring the model to generate reasoning online. In the paper, the same three-view reasoning data reaches industrial SID@64 of 0.1993 when used as a training signal, but only 0.1505 when the model must write it out before answering.

Second, when evaluating "latent reasoning" methods, include a direct-answer model trained on the same teacher data as a baseline. On the industrial data in this paper, most of the gain already appears in that baseline, and comparing only against explicit reasoning overstates the effect of the latent tokens themselves.

papers.title: Controllable Generative Recommendation via Guided Token Refinement
papers.authors: Haichao Zhang, Zhixuan Liang, Chong Zhang, Zixi Chen, Wen Wang, Jia Wang
papers.summary: Generative recommenders emit item-ID tokens left to right, so temporary diversity at inference ==can only rewrite one position mid-decode and often produces IDs that do not exist in the catalog==. ReGen uses a bidirectional Transformer to predict all 4 ID tokens at once, subtracts a score only on the coarsest positions for token values common in the user history, remasks low-confidence positions and repredicts, and uses a prefix tree of all legal IDs to drop token values that cannot complete a real item—without changing model parameters. On Amazon Instruments, top-10 category coverage rises from 0.41 to 0.59 while Recall@10 falls only from 0.0427 to 0.0394 (TIGER-MMR falls from 0.0433 to 0.0319 in the same range); without the prefix tree only 27.63% of IDs map to real items.

deep_reading.content_html:
Generative recommenders first encode each item as a discrete token string (Semantic ID), then generate the next item's tokens from the user history one by one. Businesses often need temporary controls—for example mid-sale, covering more categories—when retraining is too slow, and forcibly rewriting a token during left-to-right decoding often produces IDs that do not exist in the catalog. Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool's ReGen changes the decoding style: the model predicts all 4 tokens of an item ID at once; at inference it adds a "bias toward categories the user has not seen" score only on the coarsest few tokens, remasks low-confidence tokens and repredicts, and uses a prefix tree of all legal catalog IDs to drop tokens that cannot complete a real item. Control never changes model parameters. On Amazon 2023 Instruments and Scientific, raising top-10 category coverage (Diversity@10) from 0.41 to 0.59 drops Instruments Recall@10 only from 0.0427 to 0.0394, while TIGER-MMR falls from 0.0433 to 0.0319. Pure accuracy is not best: without a diversity requirement, Recall@10 trails Paragon, and on Video Games it also trails SASRec, RPG, and LLaDA-Rec.

1. Why left-to-right generation is hard to control at inference

Items are encoded with RQ-VAE: Sentence-T5 embeds title and text metadata, then 4 residual codebooks of 256 codes each quantize them into tokens (c1​,c2​,c3​,c4​). Residual quantization makes position 1 set the coarse direction and later positions fill detail, so the first few tokens roughly correspond to category-level semantics.

TIGER-style models generate c1​→c2​→c3​→c4​; once position 1 is chosen, every later token must continue under it. The authors call this decision locking: to raise diversity one can only rewrite a mid-generation token, but later tokens were trained conditioned on the original prefix and often form catalog-missing combinations. The other two existing families also have issues: baking the control objective into parameters at training (e.g. Paragon) requires retraining when the objective changes; post-generation reranking (e.g. MMR) can only pick among already generated candidates and fails when the candidate set itself lacks diversity.

2. Method: three changes

2.1 Predict all tokens at once

ReGen uses a BERT-style bidirectional Transformer encoder. Input is the user's history of semantic IDs plus a 4-position ID to fill, with some positions known and the rest [MASK]. The model outputs a 256-d score vector at each [MASK], softmaxed into per-code probabilities. Bidirectional attention lets predicting c3​ see c1​, c2​, and c4​ together.

Training masks coarse positions less often (α1​<⋯<αL​), so the model more often sees "coarse known, fine to fill"—matching inference where control fixes the coarse positions and the model fills the rest.

2.2 Control scores only on coarse tokens

For diversity, the goal is to land recommendations in categories rare in the user history. Count how often each code appears in the user's history on the first K coarse positions, give frequent codes a negative score sy(l)​, and at inference add λsy(l)​ to the model scores on those first K positions while leaving later positions untouched:
Z~(l)=Z(l)+λsy(l)​ (l≤K),Z~(l)=Z(l) (l>K)
Larger λ pushes toward large categories the user rarely saw. Fine positions get no bias and are left for the model to refill under the new coarse class.

2.3 Low-confidence reprediction + prefix-tree constraint

After coarse positions are pushed to a new class, previously filled fine tokens may no longer match. Each round takes every position's max softmax probability as confidence; positions below a threshold are remasked and repredicted, while high-confidence positions stay as known context. Default $T=4$ rounds.

Parallel prediction also risks selecting four individually top codes that form no real item. The authors build a prefix tree of all catalog IDs and allow at each position only codes that can complete at least one full legal path with already fixed positions; other codes get score −∞.

Inference keeps a beam of 50 candidates with 100 legal expansions per step. Candidate IDs are mapped back to items, deduplicated, and items already in the user history removed; top-10 is built greedily by picking the item that maximizes "controlled generation score + μ × newly covered categories."

3. Experiments

Data: Amazon 2023 Instruments (57,439 users, 24,587 items), Scientific (50,985 / 25,848), Video Games (94,762 / 25,612); leave-one-out; last interaction for test. Encoder: 4 layers on Instruments/Scientific, 6 on Video Games; embedding dim 256; trained from scratch.

3.1 Accuracy without control

This checks whether parallel fill-in decoding loses basic recommendation quality. ReGen's config is chosen by validation accuracy and compared to 9 baselines on Recall and NDCG. Recall@10 only:

ReGen ranks second on the first two categories; Paragon is clearly higher; on Video Games it trails SASRec, RPG, and LLaDA-Rec. The authors' own conclusion: this structure provides a usable accuracy floor but is not designed for pure accuracy.

3.2 At matched diversity, whose accuracy drops less

This is the main experiment for inference-time control. Each method tunes its own diversity knob (ReGen tunes λ) and plots Diversity@10 against Recall@10 / NDCG@10—upper-right is better.

Format is Recall@10 / NDCG@10. On Instruments, raising diversity from 0.41 to 0.59 drops ReGen Recall@10 from 0.0427 to 0.0394 and NDCG@10 from 0.0205 to 0.0188; TIGER-MMR in the same range drops Recall@10 from 0.0433 to 0.0319. ReGen is almost flat on this segment. On Scientific near diversity 0.59, ReGen still has the highest Recall@10 at 0.0296.

3.3 What each of the three parts does

Ablations under a shared "bias toward diversity" inference setting, removing one part at a time:

Three rows make three points. Dropping the control score slightly raises accuracy and lowers diversity—diversity mainly comes from the control score. Dropping reprediction pushes diversity to 0.73 but drops Instruments Recall@10 from 0.0339 to 0.0130: after coarse positions move to a new class, fine positions are not adjusted, so the system surfaces category-diverse but user-irrelevant items—what the authors call "fake diversity." Dropping the prefix tree leaves under 30% of generated IDs mapping to real items—most of the 4-token combination space is empty.

3.4 Parameters and speed

λ is stable between 4 and 12; past 20, reprediction cannot recover and accuracy falls sharply. Reprediction rounds T converge near 4; more rounds barely help while eval time keeps rising—on Instruments, T from 1 to 8 grows full-eval time from 41 to 114 minutes. Only full-eval wall time is reported, not per-request latency.

4. Limitations

Only category diversity is tested as a control objective; fairness, freshness, and exposure balance are left to future work. Diversity is top-10 category coverage—the paper itself calls it a simplified proxy. Control depends on RQ-VAE's first positions truly corresponding to category; a poorly learned codebook may not turn coarse-position scores into category change. All three datasets have only ~20K items; prefix-tree and 50-beam cost at tens of millions of items is unmeasured.

5. Takeaways

If you already use semantic IDs for generative recall, this offers a no-retrain way to add operational objectives: put control scores only on the first few ID positions, let the model refill the rest, and use a prefix tree for legality. Remember the ablation row where dropping reprediction raises diversity but collapses recall—diversity alone can mislead. Before shipping, measure per-request latency (4 reprediction rounds + 50 beams) and verify that coarse positions align with category on your own codebook.

papers.title: GenPage: Towards End-to-End Generative Homepage Construction at Netflix
papers.authors: Lequn Wang, Jiangwei Pan, Linas Baltrunas
papers.summary: The Netflix homepage consists of rows, each with a theme and a set of titles, and it used to be assembled by several stages such as a row model and an entity model. GenPage encodes the user's viewing history, device, time of day and so on as tokens forming a prompt, and a ~200M-parameter decoder-only Transformer generates row and title tokens one by one, left to right and top to bottom. ==Every row and every title is a single token, so business rules can be written directly as a candidate mask at each step==. In an online A/B test the core metric used for launch decisions rose 0.24% and end-to-end latency fell 20%; offline, enriching the prompt reduced the loss more than scaling the model from 120M to 900M parameters.

deep_reading.content_html:
The Netflix homepage is made of rows, each row a theme (such as "Korean TV Dramas"), with several titles laid out horizontally in each row. The old homepage was assembled by a multi-stage recommender: first retrieve candidate rows and candidate titles, rank them separately, and finally build the page. GenPage uses one decoder-only Transformer to generate the whole page directly: user history, account attributes and request information are encoded as a prompt, and the model generates row tokens and title tokens one by one, left to right and top to bottom, with each row and each title taking just one token. Training copies the large-language-model recipe: first pretrain with next-token prediction on homepages that received positive feedback online, then post-train with weighted binary classification (WBC) or reinforcement learning. The roughly 200M-parameter WBC version raised the core engagement metric Netflix uses for launch decisions by 0.24% in a 14-day A/B test and cut end-to-end latency by 20%; the reinforcement learning version has not launched yet.

1. Why generate the whole page

In a multi-stage system, retrieval, ranking and page construction each have their own models and objectives, and feature engineering is scattered across the stages. Whole-page generation aims to solve three things. First, one model goes from raw inputs straight to a page, so fewer models need maintaining, and the problem of inconsistent objectives across stages goes away. Second, a page generated token by token can be optimized with reinforcement learning on a whole-page reward, accounting for interactions between rows: for example, when the "Continue Watching" row is at the top, users mostly resume a show they have already started and stop browsing further down; the paper calls this ability to hold attention and make users stop browsing stopping power. Third, model quality can keep improving by adding data and parameters, without repeatedly changing the system structure.

Going online brings four constraints: the homepage must be generated in real time, so latency comes first; the catalog gets new titles every day, so cold start must be handled; user interests and trends change, so the model must stay fresh; and the page must satisfy a large number of business rules.

2. How data becomes tokens

Each training example corresponds to one homepage impression and has three parts: context (user history, account attributes, request information), page (rows and titles in layout order), and feedback (plays, thumbs-up, abandonment, etc.). Only context and page are tokenized as the model's input and output; feedback is turned into a supervision signal by the reward system.

The team did not use an off-the-shelf text tokenizer but designed custom tokens for homepage data. The fact "the user watched Orange Is the New Black for 50 minutes 30 days ago" takes 16 tokens with GPT-5's tokenizer and only 4 with GenPage: title ID, action type, action-time bucket, watch-duration bucket. Each title and each row corresponds to one token, so sequences are shorter, inference is cheaper, and business rules can be written directly as masks on certain tokens. The row and title vocabularies are updated daily.

The homepage is usually generated over several requests, a few rows each time. Before each page-down, the rows already generated and the user's latest actions on those rows are appended to the prompt, so the next batch of recommendations can use both long-term preferences and in-session behavior.

3. Reward and model

The reward comes from Netflix's existing reward system, which has been tuned through online A/B tests and aligned with users' long-term satisfaction. The system gives each impressed title on the page a scalar reward: a show binged in one night gets a high reward, a movie watched for only 10 minutes a low one, and a title the user abandons after impression a negative one. The whole-page reward is the sum of all impressed titles' rewards.

The model is a standard decoder-only Transformer with one change: input embeddings and the output projection do not share weights. Pretraining optimizes a softmax over the whole vocabulary, while WBC post-training optimizes a separate sigmoid for each token; the two need very different logit ranges, and untying the weights lets the model adapt to both objectives. The online A/B used a model of about 200M parameters, to stay within the latency budget.

4. Training

4.1 Pretraining: imitate the production system

Pretraining uses homepage impressions that received positive feedback online: given the context and the first few page tokens already generated, predict the next page token. The model is trained from scratch, not initialized from an existing large model. This step teaches the model to generate pages similar to the production system's, but it only imitates and does not directly optimize the size of the reward; after GenPage launches, repeatedly retraining on its own generated pages also risks degrading the model.

4.2 WBC post-training: turn generation into per-token valuation

WBC has the model estimate, given the context and the generated prefix, the value of generating each candidate row or title. Each impressed title's label is the sign of its reward (1 for positive engagement, 0 for abandonment), its weight is the absolute value of the reward, and a row's reward is aggregated from the rewards of the titles in it. Following the paper's description, the loss is written as:
LWBC​=−t∑​∣rt​∣[yt​logσ(zt​)+(1−yt​)log(1−σ(zt​))],yt​=1[rt​>0]
t is one impressed row or title on the page, rt​ its reward, zt​ the logit the model gives this token at that position, and σ the sigmoid. Besides each impressed target, some tokens are randomly sampled as negatives. Rarely impressed titles are drawn as random negatives far more often than they appear as positives, so the model naturally values long-tail titles lower; this acts as a popularity prior and keeps the model from ranking long-tail titles very high because of a few noisy examples.

At generation time, the model computes logits over all candidate tokens at each step, greedily picks the largest, appends it to the prefix, and generates the next. On the standard offline evaluation set for the production ranker, the WBC model beat the production ranker on title-level metrics such as weighted AUC.

4.3 Reinforcement learning post-training: optimize for the whole-page reward

WBC optimizes individual titles; reinforcement learning optimizes the whole page. The approach follows RLHF for large models: first train a reward model that takes any generated page and predicts its whole-page reward (the supervision target is the sum of title rewards given by the reward system), then optimize the generation policy with Dr. GRPO (a variant of GRPO that corrects an objective bias), with verl as the training framework and vLLM as the inference engine. The policy, reference model and reward model are all initialized from the pretrained checkpoint. The reward model's training data comes from the production policy and is only reliable on pages similar to production ones, so the policy is kept near the reference model with a KL penalty, to stop the policy from generating pages the reward model would wrongly score high. There are also rule-based rewards, for example that the page must have a row-by-row structure and that business-critical rows must not be placed too far down.

5. Engineering problems to solve for launch

Cold start has two remedies. One is to write the metadata of new titles or time-sensitive content such as live events directly into the context tokens. The other is semantic embedding fusion: each title's input embedding fuses an ID embedding with a content embedding built from the synopsis, cast, subtitles, genre and video content, so a new title has a usable representation even with few interactions.

Freshness relies on multi-cadence incremental training: every so often, a full pretraining and post-training pass over a longer history window; between those passes, post-training continues daily from the previous day's checkpoint on the most recent day of data plus a sample of historical data, keeping up with new titles and trends without forgetting old knowledge. New rows and new titles are first initialized with the fallback token of their type, and during training a small fraction of known tokens is randomly replaced with fallback tokens, so the model learns to handle tokens it has never seen.

Business rules are guaranteed by constrained decoding: at each step a mask of allowed tokens is computed from the applicable rules and multiplied onto the output logits, so only compliant tokens can be generated. For example, to pin the "Popular Games" row to row 2, all other row tokens are masked at the row-2 position. Rules vary by request, so the masks must be built dynamically per request and per position, and the team modified the inference engine for this.

Each row autoregressively generates only its first few titles, because those draw the most attention and most determine the impression the row makes; the remaining positions are filled with one forward pass conditioned on that prefix, taking the highest-logit compliant titles. This is called hybrid row decoding and is used to reduce decoding steps.

6. Experiments

6.1 Does pretraining help

This experiment is meant to show that pretraining gives WBC post-training a better starting point. It compares pretraining followed by WBC against doing WBC directly.

MetricWith pretrainingWithout pretraining
Loss (weighted BCE)0.3210.333
Row AUC0.8840.879
Entity AUC0.9200.910

Entity AUC going from 0.91 to 0.92 looks small, so the authors restate it: ignoring example weights, if you randomly draw a pair of impressed titles (one positive, one negative), the probability the model orders them wrongly drops from 9% to 8%. On a mature production system, a single change rarely brings an improvement this large.

6.2 Add parameters or add context

This experiment compares the gains from two ways of improving: scaling the model from about 120M to 900M parameters, versus keeping the model size fixed and progressively enriching the prompt's content and tokenization.

Scaling the model about 7.5x lowers WBC loss by only about 1.3%; enriching the context lowers it by about 6.9% cumulatively, and several single context improvements each gained more than the whole parameter scale-up. The authors' judgment is that at the current stage, personalization quality is limited first by the information available to the model and how it is represented, and only then by capacity. The two experiments use different axes, and each context step is measured as an improvement over the previous step on a different data snapshot and then multiplied together, so only relative comparisons are possible.

6.3 Is reinforcement learning optimizing the whole page

This experiment is meant to show that reinforcement learning learns a page-level policy rather than greedy token-by-token choices. The reward rises steadily during training, but it is computed by the same reward model the policy is optimizing, so it only counts as a sanity check. More convincing is diversity: measured by pairwise embedding distance between titles on the page, it is not part of the training objective, yet it also rises during training.

6.4 Online A/B

The online control is the existing multi-stage homepage recommender, and the treatment is the roughly 200M-parameter WBC model. To keep business rules such as eligibility checks, GenPage decodes within the candidate row and title sets produced by the existing system. There are 5 treatment arms, differing in the number of random negatives and which online impressions are included in training.

ResultValue
Core engagement metric (5 treatment arms)All significantly up, p<0.001
Best treatment arm+0.24%, 95% confidence interval [0.17%, 0.30%]
End-to-end latency-20%

The 5 configurations gained similar amounts, showing that the gain does not depend on one particular training-data setup. The authors call it one of the largest algorithm-driven gains in recent years. Latency dropped because one Transformer consumes tokenized raw inputs directly, replacing several ranking stages and a lot of feature computation, while custom tokens and hybrid row decoding reduce decoding steps, and the available optimizations are not yet exhausted.

Two more things were observed after launch. First, the latest in-session actions quickly influence later recommendations and fall back to long-term preferences after a day or two, showing the model really uses action timestamps, which the old system needed many hand-crafted features to do. Second, the composition of impressed content changed unexpectedly: for example, the ratios of new to old titles, series to movies, and high-quality to low-quality engagement all shifted. The authors speculate this is because GenPage's personalization is more precise, exposing that components inherited from the old system, such as the reward system, are not yet aligned with the generative paradigm, and they will tune these components next.

7. Limitations

The authors list three unfinished parts: reinforcement learning post-training has not launched; long context still relies on hand-designed summaries; and text, multimodal and reasoning capabilities have not been brought in. Reinforcement learning also has two open problems: offline evaluation depends on the reward model the policy is optimizing, so the conclusions are circular; and WBC decomposes fully by title while whole-page reinforcement learning does not decompose at all, and how to exploit partial structure between the two remains unanswered.

In addition, the online experiment decodes within the candidate sets from the old system and does not replace the retrieval stage, so this A/B validates ranking and page construction, not fully end-to-end generation.

8. Practical implications

  • If you work on generative recommendation, check your tokenization first: one item or one layout unit per token keeps sequences short, and business rules can be written directly as logit masks, without maintaining complex constraints over a multi-token text vocabulary.
  • Enrich the context before scaling the model. In Netflix's data, the cumulative loss reduction from context improvements is about 5 times that from a 7.5x parameter scale-up.

papers.title: Gryphon-v2: One Model in Place of a Cascade - Generate-and-Rank Recommender with Rollout Distillation
papers.authors: Lipkina, Anna, Tikhonovich, Daria, Yanush, Viktor, Ulianova, Mariia, Sorokin, Oleg, Dodonov, Vladislav, Murzin, Ilya, Bu...
papers.summary: Gryphon-v2 encodes user history once, generates semantic item IDs, and ranks the resolved items with a small shared-state head. A larger teacher supplies training targets but stays out of serving. Replacing the Yandex Music cascade increased active users by 1.41% in an online experiment.
papers.key_insight: Distill on candidates the generator actually produces as well as logged impressions. This teaches the ranking head its serving distribution while retaining exposure-based supervision; sharing the history encoder then removes redundant online work.

deep_reading.content_html:
Gryphon-v2 combines generative candidate retrieval with a small ranking head, then trains that head to imitate a larger offline teacher. The aim is to preserve broad candidate generation while learning the finer preferences needed to order actual items. In a Yandex Music experiment, one served model replaces the existing recommendation cascade.

1. Generating an item is not the same as ranking it

A production cascade often has separate candidate generators, a pre-ranker, and a final ranker. Each stage adds infrastructure and may repeat work on the same user history. Semantic-ID generation offers a shorter path: predict a compact item code from the user's interactions, then resolve it into catalogue items.

The probability of a code is an imperfect final ranking score. A code can be easy to predict without identifying the most valuable song, and several items can share a code. Candidate coverage and ordering quality therefore need separate evaluation.

Gryphon-v2 retains the shared-encoder architecture of Gryphon. A history encoder runs once; both the decoder and a lightweight item-level ranking module reuse its states. The main change is supervision: the ranking module learns a stronger teacher's scores instead of relying only on next-item feedback. The teacher is absent from serving.

2. Why training needs two candidate pools

At serving time, catalogue-trie-constrained beam search generates valid semantic IDs. The system resolves them into items, expands collisions, and applies a candidate budget. Each candidate then attends to the already encoded history. Task-specific heads produce scores, whose fixed weighted combination sets the final order.

This is a small ranking module inside a shared model, rather than a separate production ranker appended to the generator. The served model has approximately 0.5 billion parameters and processes up to 2,048 history events. The teacher can use a longer history because its cost is paid during training.

Next-token prediction continues to train the generative path. Distillation trains the ranking module on two distributions. First, the current decoder produces its own candidates at every training step without checkpoint lag. These rollouts resemble the candidates that the module will receive online. A training beam of 32 keeps generation and teacher scoring affordable.

Second, logged impressions from the corresponding request provide complementary coverage. A generator has blind spots; training only on what it already generates would not expose the ranking head to the full range of items present in production logs.

The two pools receive separately normalized mean absolute error losses, added with equal coefficients. Rollouts account for more than 90% of distinct distillation candidates, but this is not a 90% loss weight. Separate normalization prevents pool size from setting the relative importance of each source.

Generation loss updates the decoder and shared encoder. Distillation updates the ranking head and shared encoder. No gradient passes through beam search, and the teacher supplies targets only. This is supervised distillation, not a policy-gradient method that directly rewards the decoder.

3. The important change is the training distribution

The earlier Gryphon already has the same ranking-module architecture. Its comparison with Gryphon-v2 isolates the value of teacher supervision more cleanly than a comparison against a generator with no ranking head.

The teacher can score an arbitrary history-item pair without requiring prior exposure. That enables supervision on the generator's own unexposed candidates, closing part of the gap between training on production logs and ranking a newly generated pool.

The ranking module still cannot recover an item that never enters the pool. Joint training lets both paths influence the history representation, but the decoder is not directly optimized as a teacher-reward policy. A high-recall proposal model with a shared-state student ranker is the more precise description.

4. What the experiments establish

Matched offline generative baselines use the same tokenizer, history features, and backbone with chronological data splitting. The table separates candidate recall, teacher top-10 agreement, and weighted pair accuracy on logged impressions.

ModelRecall@1000TeacherRecall@10Weighted pair accuracy
Generative retrieval0.86430.03820.5429
Gryphon0.85930.03920.5528
Gryphon-v2, beam order0.86150.03810.5478
Gryphon-v2, complete0.86150.56540.5892

The clearest change is ordering. The complete model recovers more than half of the teacher's top-ten selections; bypassing its ranking module removes that gain. Candidate recall remains essentially unchanged.

Candidate-source ablations support the distribution argument. Teacher top-10 agreement rises from 0.2983 with impressions alone to 0.5654 with mixed pools. Rollout-only training preserves teacher agreement but has lower logged-impression pair accuracy, showing that the pools provide different information.

The online test supplies the end-to-end result. The control uses the full cascade; treatment uses only Gryphon-v2. Active users increase by 1.41%, where an active user listens for at least seven minutes per day. This estimates the combined system change, not the isolated effect of distillation.

End-to-end latency is described as comparable to the production cascade; the paper does not provide a reusable absolute millisecond value. Its roughly fourfold throughput comparison is against the same generative backbone followed by the teacher online. That comparator is different from the production cascade.

5. Limits of the evidence

The authors acknowledge that generation, ranking, and online updates change together, preventing isolation of their marginal effects. The experiment covers one music recommendation surface, with each arm containing 8% of eligible users. It does not establish long-term or full-population effects.

Long-tail catalogue coverage, artist diversity, novelty, and exposure concentration were not evaluated. Reducing the candidate pool while improving engagement leaves these exploration questions open.

TeacherRecall measures agreement with the training teacher. Weighted pair accuracy uses impressions exposed by the old cascade, rather than independently judging everything the new model surfaces. The teacher and production ranker also use longer training histories than the offline student, so those reference results are not matched baselines.

Finally, the paper provides no controlled comparison against reinforcement-learning post-training. It establishes a viable distillation route, without resolving relative quality, stability, or compute efficiency between the approaches.

6. Practical experiments for search and recommendation

The first useful experiment is candidate-distribution alignment. With an existing generative retriever, train a small ranking head on impressions, generated candidates, and their mixture. Track retrieval coverage, teacher agreement, and independently labeled relevance separately to distinguish missing candidates from poor ordering.

A second opportunity is shared history encoding. Measure feature preparation, network transfer, inference, and candidate resolution together. Trie constraints, ID collision expansion, and candidate budgets remain operational components even when the learned serving model is unified.

Community short-text search adds explicit query intent and content freshness. A teacher trained for a music feed does not automatically measure query relevance. A transfer experiment should retain query relevance labels and check whether fresh and long-tail posts still reach the candidate pool.

papers.title: From Habits to Discovery: Deploying LLMs for Personalized Generative Recommendations at Spotify
papers.summary: Spotify wants the home feed to surface podcasts the user has not yet formed a habit around (under 10 minutes on a show in the past 28 days). GLIDE, based on Llama 3.2 1B, first learns to translate between episode semantic IDs and text, then reads recent episode semantic IDs, region and other text fields, ==a soft-prompt token projected from a collaborative-filtering user vector==, and an instruction to push familiar versus unseen content, and directly generates 30 episode candidates.
