papers.title: Coarse-to-Fine Long-term Interest Modeling for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Shiteng Cao, Junda She, Ji Liu, Bin Zeng, Chengcheng Guo, Kuo Cai, Qiang Luo, Ruiming Tang, Han Li, Kun Gai, Zhiheng Li,...
papers.summary: Because attention cost grows with the square of sequence length, generative recommenders usually consume only short behavior sequences. GLASS, from Kuaishou and Tsinghua, uses the long-term history in two places: before generating the first SID level, it computes the cosine similarity between every long-term history item and the center of each first-level code, counts the items per similarity tier, and compresses this into one interest token fed to the encoder; after the first SID level is generated, it uses that code to pull long-term history items sharing the same first-level code and fuses them through a gate to help generate the remaining two levels. ==The first-level code fixes the broad category, and the later two levels must tell items apart within it, so what they need is same-category history==. In a two-week Kuaishou short-video A/B test, app usage time per user rose 0.052%.

deep_reading.content_html:
Generative recommendation encodes each item as a few levels of semantic IDs (SIDs) and uses a Transformer to generate the next item one code at a time. Attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, so these models usually take only the most recent few dozen behaviors. In the paper's two datasets, the average user history length is 987 (TAOBAO-MM) and 884 (KuaiRec), yet the model input keeps only the last 50. The authors also observe a pattern: in plain generative retrieval, after the first-level code is generated, the true item's rank in the beam gets worse rather than better, with the average rank dropping by 1.25 at the second level. GLASS uses the long-term history differently for each SID level: before generating the first-level code, it compresses the whole long-term history into one interest token fed to the encoder; after the first-level code is generated, it uses that code as a retrieval key to pull items of the same broad category from the long-term history, which help generate the last two codes. On TAOBAO-MM, R@1 is 21.57% higher than the strongest baseline, DualGR; in a two-week A/B test on a short-video platform, app usage time per user rose 0.052% and recall rose 3 percentage points in absolute terms.

1. The problem: getting long histories into generative retrieval

The ranking stage has a mature recipe for long sequences, SIM's two-stage design: a GSU (General Search Unit) first uses the target item to retrieve a relevant sub-sequence from the long history, then an ESU (Exact Search Unit) runs fine-grained target attention over it. The retrieval stage has no target item, so the GSU has nothing to search with. OneRec and OneSearch use a Q-Former to compress long-term behavior into fixed-length vectors, which stops at the granularity of interest clusters. DualGR already uses SIDs as retrieval keys in generative retrieval, but it treats codes at every level the same way.

The authors start from the structure of SIDs themselves. The first-level code decides which broad category an item belongs to, and the last two codes locate the specific item inside that category. When the first-level code is generated there is no path yet, so the model needs the user's overall preference across categories; when the last two codes are generated the category is fixed, so the model needs what the user actually engaged with inside that category. The two levels need long-term information at different granularity, so it is injected in two places.

2. Overall structure

The backbone is a TIGER-style encoder-decoder. Each item's multimodal vector is quantized by RQ-VAE into three levels of codes; on the public datasets the codebook sizes are [64,128,128], the embedding dimension is 96, and the encoder and decoder each have 4 layers. The user history is sorted by time and split in two: the most recent 50 behaviors are the short-term sequence, and everything earlier is the long-term sequence.

3. First-level code: SID-Tier compresses the long-term history into one token

This step addresses the fact that the first-level code is generated with no clue at all. Running attention directly over the long-term history is too expensive, so the authors exploit the small size of the first-level codebook: there are only tens to a little over a hundred first-level codes, so cross features between the user history and every code can all be computed.

Each first-level code k first gets a prototype vector h~k​, the mean of the vectors of all items whose first-level code is k. The cosine-similarity range $[-1,1]$ is then split evenly into N bins, and for each first-level code the model counts how many long-term history items fall into each bin:
tk​[j]=v∈Hlongid​∑​I(bin(Cos(h~k​,hv​))=j)
hv​ is the multimodal vector of history item v, bin(⋅) maps a similarity to its bin, and I is the indicator function. Intuitively, tk​ describes how many items in the user's history are very similar to category k, how many are somewhat similar, and how many are not. The histograms of all first-level codes are concatenated into a vector of length K0​⋅N, compressed by an MLP (hidden size 256) into one d-dimensional vector etier​, and appended after the short-term sequence embedding before entering the encoder.

This token depends only on the user history and the codebook, not on the item being generated, so it can be precomputed offline. It is really the familiar "user's historical preference statistics per category" feature from ranking models, computed over first-level SID codes instead.

4. The last two codes: retrieve from the long-term history with the generated first-level code

After the first-level code c^0​ is generated, the model takes every item in the long-term history with the same first-level code:
Hret​={c(vi​)∣vi​∈Hlongid​, c0​(vi​)=c^0​(vn+1​)}
This is SIM's hard search with the key changed from "the target item's category" to "the first-level code just generated". Each decoder layer runs self-attention and then two cross-attention paths in parallel: one with the encoder output as key/value, giving Zshort​; one with the retrieved item embeddings as key/value, giving Zret​. A gate merges the two:
g=σ([Zshort​;Zret​]Wg​),Zcontext​=(1−g)⊙Zshort​+g⊙Zret​
Wg​ is a 2d×d projection and σ is the sigmoid. A large g tilts the result toward the retrieved long-term items; a small g tilts it toward the short-term sequence. The training objective is the standard autoregressive cross-entropy over the three codes.

5. What if too few items come back

Hard search has an obvious problem. In the paper's example, with a history of 1000 and a first-level codebook of 128, each first-level code retrieves only about 7.8 items on average: too little information, with a high share of noise. The authors offer two fixes:

  • Semantic neighbor augmentation: precompute cosine similarities between first-level codes and record each code's top-k nearest neighbors. When fewer items than a threshold τ come back, the history items under the neighbor codes are merged in as well.
  • Shrinking the first-level codebook: make the first-level codebook smaller during training so that each first-level code covers more items. The first level is responsible for volume, the last two for precision.

6. Experiments

Main results. The goal is to show that GLASS beats both ID-based sequential models and SID-based generative models. Both datasets keep only positive feedback: TAOBAO-MM keeps clicks, uniformly samples 10,000 items and keeps those that appear at least 5 times in the training set; KuaiRec keeps samples whose play time exceeds the video length. The table below takes, from the paper's Table 2, the strongest ID model HSTU and two SID baselines: TIGER is standard generative retrieval, and DualGR uses separate long- and short-term branches with routing.

DatasetModelR@1R@5R@10N@10
TAOBAO-MMHSTU0.02740.05120.07840.0495
TAOBAO-MMTIGER0.02800.07560.10760.0627

On KuaiRec the gain is only 3.81%–4.94%. The authors attribute this to KuaiRec's multimodal vectors coming from a simple text encoding, which gives poorer SIDs, whereas TAOBAO-MM uses multimodal features trained with contrastive learning.

Which level each module helps. This ablation shows that SID-Tier mainly helps the first-level code and semantic search mainly helps the second. The authors track two quantities: acci​, the training accuracy of the level-i code under teacher forcing, and Pi​, the probability that the level-i code is also correct under top-1 beam search given all earlier levels are correct. Adding SID-Tier raises acc1​ from 0.2410 to 0.2485, P1​ from 0.1470 to 0.1587, and Recall@5 from 0.0702 to 0.0842. Adding semantic search on top mainly lifts acc2​ and P2​.

Why the rank drops. The authors define Conditional Rank Progression (CRP): over samples whose first $d-1$ codes all stayed in the beam, the average rank of the correct level-d code among the top-K candidates; closer to 1 is better. With beam size 20, the plain generative model's rank worsens by 1.25 on average at the second level, and only by 0.98 with semantic search; at the third level the worsening falls from 0.19 to 0.13. The cause is that when a plain model generates the last two codes, its conditioning context is still the original one, with no new information to widen the probability gap between the right answer and the distractors.

Does the gate matter. A fixed weight of 0.5 helps when the first-level codebook is small but hurts once the codebook gets finer, because retrieved-sequence length varies a lot, and when it is too short the noise flows straight into beam search's cumulative probabilities. The learned gate value rises overall with retrieval length: the more items are retrieved, the more weight the model puts on the long-term branch.

Sparsity fixes. Shrinking the first-level codebook gave the best Recall@10. Semantic neighbor augmentation helps only without codebook shrinking; adding neighbors on top of a shrunken codebook lowers the metrics slightly, which the authors attribute to neighbor items blurring the boundaries between different interests.

Online. A two-week A/B test on a short-video platform, with 3% of users (about 12 million) in each of the treatment and control groups. At 95% confidence, total app usage time rose 0.056%, app usage time per user rose 0.052%, and recall rose 3 percentage points in absolute terms.

7. Limitations and what to try

The paper has no separate limitations discussion; two facts are worth keeping in mind. The public datasets are small: KuaiRec has only 3790 users and TAOBAO-MM's items are sampled down to 10,000, far from industrial codebook scale. Results are sensitive to SID quality: on TAOBAO-MM each metric improves 14.03%–29.91% over the strongest baseline, on KuaiRec only 3.81%–4.94%.

If you work on generative retrieval and have long behavior sequences, two things are worth trying directly:

  • Append the "user's historical preference histogram over first-level codes" as an extra token to the encoder input; it can be computed offline and adds almost no online cost.
  • Before doing hard search with the generated first-level code, measure how many items each first-level code retrieves from user histories on average; if too few, try shrinking the first-level codebook first and neighbor augmentation second.

papers.title: Progressive Learning from Content to Relevance to Personalization for CTR Prediction
papers.authors: Zhiguang Yang, Yulin Yang, Fuyu Lv, Dan Ou
papers.summary: Taobao search CTR models mainly remember historical clicks through item IDs, so ==the same item with a different main image is almost indistinguishable to the model==. FineSID turns each item image into 30 discrete codes across four VAR tokenizer scales from 1×1 to 4×4, tokenizes titles and OCR text by field, and looks them all up like ordinary ID features; the shared network is first trained on query–item relevance labels from a Qwen3.5 teacher, then fine-tuned with a click head on click logs. Offline AUC is 0.25 points above the HiFormer baseline and 0.38 points higher on cold items; a seven-day Taobao main-search A/B test raised GMV by 0.85%.

deep_reading.content_html:
Taobao search's fine-ranking CTR models mainly remember historical clicks through user, query, and item ID features. The same item with a different main image or a rewritten title keeps the same item ID, so the model's score barely changes; newly listed, rarely clicked items have learned little from the ID itself. Alibaba's FineSID splits item images and text into fine-grained discrete codes and looks them up together with ordinary ID features into the same ranking network: images become 30 position-aware codes across four VAR tokenizer scales from 1×1 to 4×4; titles and OCR text are tokenized per field. Training has two stages: first train the whole network on LLM-labeled query–item relevance, then swap in a click head and fine-tune all parameters on click logs. Offline AUC is 0.25 points above the HiFormer baseline and 0.38 points higher on cold items; a seven-day Taobao main-search A/B test shows click +0.21% and GMV +0.85%.

The overall structure has three stages: offline, turn content into discrete codes; pretrain the shared network on relevance labels; fine-tune for personalization on click labels. Stages two and three share one network and only swap the output head.

1. Problem: how content enters an ID model

Industrial CTR models are mainly ID embeddings plus a feature-crossing network. Multimodal content usually enters in one of three ways. First, jointly train an image encoder end to end—too expensive. Second, concatenate continuous vectors from a pretrained model, for example the LEARN-style baseline that concatenates Qwen3.5 content vectors; continuous vectors and sparse IDs have different distributions and often only fuse in late layers. Third, semantic IDs (SID): quantize a whole item's content vector into a few discrete codes and look them up like IDs—RQ-VAE SID is representative.

The authors agree with the third direction but say the granularity is too coarse. RQ-VAE compresses a whole image into a few codes and loses spatial detail such as "is there a promo badge in the top-left" or "what color is the model wearing"; two main images of the same item can get the same codes. FineSID wants to keep those details without running an image model online.

2. Method

2.1 Content → discrete codes

Images use VAR's pretrained tokenizer. VAR generates images scale by scale; its tokenizer is trained for reconstruction and encodes an image into multi-scale code maps. FineSID takes scales 1×1, 2×2, 3×3, and 4×4—1+4+9+16 = 30 codes per image. Coarse scales capture overall style; fine scales capture local regions.

Codes are computed offline and stored; online serving only adds 30 table lookups and does not run an image model. The ranking network's embedding tables for these codes are randomly initialized and trained with the task, independent of VAR's reconstruction codebook. Flattening keeps a fixed "which scale, which cell" order, so the same position always enters the same input slot.

For text, query, title, and OCR each use their own BPE and n-gram vocabularies; each field stays an independent token sequence rather than being collapsed into one summary vector.

2.2 Shared prediction network

The three input types meet as follows. Text fields first do cross-attention: query embeddings as queries, title and OCR token embeddings as keys/values, yielding text representations weighted by the current query. Then ordered fusion concatenates, in a fixed order, the original ID-feature embeddings, the 30 visual-code embeddings, and each field's text representation.

The long vector is projected to 768-d, then through two HiFormer layers. HiFormer is Google's feature-crossing structure; here its latent-slot attention maps inputs onto a small fixed set of slots to avoid quadratic self-attention over thousands of tokens. An MLP 768→256→64 yields a 64-d shared representation h for the output head.

2.3 Relevance first, then clicks

Stage 2 pretrains on relevance. Each impression gets a four-way soft relevance distribution from a Qwen3.5 model fine-tuned on millions of human labels; the network fits soft-label cross-entropy:
Lrel​=−Ex​k=1∑4​tk​(x)logπθ,ψrel​,k​(x)
tk​(x) is the teacher's probability for tier k, π the network's prediction, θ shared-network parameters, ψrel​ the relevance head. The intent is for SID embeddings and crossing layers to learn "does this image and title match this query" first—clicks alone learn that slowly because clicks mix price and brand preference.

Stage 3 drops the relevance head, attaches a randomly initialized click head, and fine-tunes all parameters—including SID embeddings, ID embeddings, crossing layers, and normalization stats—with binary cross-entropy on click logs. The authors stress this is full-parameter transfer, unlike migrating only embeddings and discarding upper layers.

3. Experiments

Data are real Taobao search impressions: seven days Aug 25–31 for training (~51.2B impressions, 251M users, 418M items); one day Sep 1 for eval (453M impressions). Metrics are AUC, query-grouped GAUC, and the same two on the cold-item subset with under 1,000 views that day. Taobao numbers are absolute differences versus the HiFormer baseline, in percentage points.

Main results versus other content-injection methods. This shows fine-grained codes beat whole-image vectors and coarse SIDs. Controls all add content on the same HiFormer backbone: Visual ID quantizes visual vectors into discrete IDs; COINS aligns SID content with collaborative signals for cold start; PRECTR and Joint relevance + CTR are two ways to bring relevance supervision into CTR.

FineSID leads every column; cold-subset gains exceed full-set gains, matching "content codes fill in when ID signal is scarce." LEARN-style continuous concatenation only gains +0.05 AUC; Joint relevance + CTR is below the baseline on the cold subset.

Same-item creative discrimination. This rules out "the model only memorized item IDs." Item ID is fixed; only creatives (main image, title) differ. Metric is NSCTR: for each impression, the model picks the highest-scoring creative among that item's candidates; a match with the logged creative counts, and matching impressions' CTR is weighted by the item's original impression count. Candidates share the exact same ID, so score gaps can only come from content. FineSID's relative NSCTR gain is 0.75%; COINS is 0.27%.

Ablations: what each stage contributes.

Dropping SID nearly zeros the gain and slightly hurts cold AUC—most of the lift is the content codes themselves. Relevance pretraining adds another 0.05 AUC and matters more for NSCTR (0.51% → 0.75%). Mean pooling cuts more than half of the AUC gain, so keeping position and field identity helps.

Public MMCTR. MMCTR has no relevance labels, so only the version without stage 2 is tested. HiFormer baseline AUC 0.9767; FineSID reaches 0.9844 (+0.77 points), above COINS 0.9825 and LEARN-style 0.9823.

Online A/B. Seven days on Taobao main search versus the production model: click +0.21%, GMV +0.85%, both significant. The authors report no significant fine-rank latency increase because the 30 visual codes are extracted offline and online only adds lookups and a wider first projection.

4. Limitations

The authors list three: the VAR tokenizer is trained for reconstruction and frozen in stage 2, so codes are not optimized for search semantics; relevance pretraining is only shown transferring to CTR, not to retrieval or conversion; 30 codes widen the concatenated vector and need more work for million-candidate retrieval.

One more: MMCTR only tests the version without relevance pretraining, so the full three-stage pipeline has evidence from only one Taobao data source; online GMV +0.85% with click only +0.21% is not broken down by which item types drive the GMV lift.

5. Takeaways for fine-ranking teams

If your fine-ranker already has a content-vector feature with little gain, try FineSID's idea: replace images with multi-scale, position-aware discrete codes that share the same embedding lookup path as IDs; online cost is mainly storage and lookups.

If you already have relevance labels or a relevance model, pretrain the whole ranking network on it, then fully fine-tune on clicks. In the ablation this step helps same-item creative discrimination (NSCTR) the most—useful when you need multi-image, multi-title creative selection.

papers.title: ECHO: Efficient Cascade with Homogeneous Operators for Distillation-Guided 100K-Sequence Modeling
papers.authors: Wenhao Li, Qinglin Jia, Chenghou Jin, Zihong Xian, Jiezhou Ji, Yanzhi Liu, Zezheng Wang, Ruiming Tang, Chaoyi Ma, Zhaoji...
papers.summary: ECHO makes 100K-event histories affordable by retaining reusable original records before candidate-aware retrieval. A full-history teacher supervises selection, while retrieval and aggregation share relevance parameters. Kuaishou reports a 0.613% increase in app usage time in an online test.
papers.key_insight: Compression can preserve individually addressable events rather than only latent interest vectors. Reusable user-level selection moves work out of the request path and leaves candidate-specific matching to a smaller evidence set.

deep_reading.content_html:
ECHO (Kuaishou) is a three-stage funnel: 100K raw behaviors → a user-side learned top-K (candidate-agnostic, computed outside the request path and cached per user) keeps 10K → each candidate runs GSU-style retrieval for 100 → target attention aggregates them for the ranker. Because the user-side selector never sees the candidate, it is trained by knowledge distillation from a target-attention teacher that sees the full history and the candidate, plus a boundary loss that pushes "teacher-preferred but not in top-K" events over the cut. Retrieval and the final attention reuse the teacher's relevance parameters; that is the "Homogeneous Operators" in the title. By the paper's analytical estimate, sequence-branch FLOPs are ~160× lower than STCA; GAUC on KuaiRand Comment improves 1.520% relative to the strongest baseline, and a 7-day online A/B test shows +0.613% app usage time.

1. Architecture: what each funnel stage does

This section shows how 100K events shrink to a size the ranker can afford.

Four terms used throughout:

  • Target attention: attention with the candidate as query and history events as keys/values. It outputs a candidate-specific interest vector. DIN is the classic example.
  • GSU / ESU: SIM's two-stage design. The General Search Unit retrieves a few relevant events with a light scorer. The Exact Search Unit runs full target attention over them.
  • Top-K: keep the K highest-scoring positions.
  • Knowledge distillation (KD): train a student to match a teacher's output distribution.
StageModuleIn → outSees candidate?Runs whereTraining signal
① User-side compressionDistilled Selector (DS)100K → 10K raw recordsNoReal-time training, written to a storeKD + boundary loss
② Candidate retrievalTFR, TWIN-style GSU10K → 100 per candidateYesOnline requestRanking loss; scorer params from teacher
③ AggregationTWIN-style ESU100 → interest vectorYesOnline requestMulti-task ranking loss
TeacherFull-history target attentionFull history + training targetsYesTraining onlyIts own prediction loss

TFR stands for Target-aware Fine-grained Retriever, the stage-two retriever.

Two graphs train concurrently. The selector graph trains the teacher and DS; DS writes each user's top-K records to an intermediate store. The ranking graph reads those records and trains TFR, aggregation and the ranker.

Online requests only read the store. They never run DS or touch the 100K history.

DS keeps original records: item ID, timestamp, side features. C-Former and SequenceO1 compress history into latent tokens; each ECHO record stays individually matchable.

2. Walk-through: one request through three stages (illustrative numbers)

This section ties the table together with one example. All numbers here are illustrative, not from the paper.

User A has 80,000 events. During real-time training overnight, DS scores all 80,000 and stores the top 10,000. One of them is a fishing video A finished eight months ago.

At 9 a.m. A opens the feed. The ranker must score 500 candidates, one of which is a new fishing-gear video.

Stage one is already done. The ranker reads A's 10,000 records once; all 500 candidates share them.

Stage two: TFR uses the fishing-gear video as query, scores the 10,000 records and keeps the top 100. The eight-month-old fishing video scores high and is retrieved.

Stage three: target attention weights those 100 records. Fishing-related events get large weights, the interest vector goes into the ranking tower, which predicts click, like, comment and so on.

Had DS dropped that fishing record, stage two could never find it. That is why DS needs teacher supervision.

3. Title keywords mapped to modules

Cascade: the 100K → 10K → 100 → attention budgets. 10K bounds interest coverage; 100 bounds per-candidate compute.

Homogeneous Operators: TWIN shares relevance parameters between GSU and ESU. ECHO goes one step further: the teacher's learned query/key relevance parameters Θrel​ are exported to both TFR and the final target attention. All three use one scoring operator, so coarse retrieval and fine aggregation agree on what "relevant" means.

Distillation-Guided: DS is trained from the teacher (Section 4).

100K-Sequence Modeling: online raw history is capped at 100K events.

4. Training DS: scoring, distillation, boundary loss

This section solves stage one's core problem: DS cannot see the candidate but must pre-select events useful for candidates.

4.1 DS scoring

Symbols: sjS​ is the student's (DS) score for event j; e is a user vector built only from profile features; zjS​ encodes event j (features plus timestamp); WQ,hS​, WK,hS​ are head-h query/key projections; Hs​ is the number of heads.

Intuition: attention scoring with the user as query. No candidate is involved, so one set of scores serves every candidate and can be cached. DS keeps the top K positions, IK; in production K=10,000.

4.2 Teacher scoring

sv,jT​=Ht​1​h=1∑Ht​​⟨WQ,hT​fT​(c,xv​),WK,hT​zjT​⟩
Symbols: sv,jT​ is the teacher's score for event j given candidate v; fT​(c,xv​) encodes context c and candidate features xv​ into a query; zjT​ is the teacher's own event encoding (not shared with DS).

Intuition: a standard full-history target attention. It knows the candidate, so its scores say which history truly matters for that candidate.

4.3 Distillation loss

LKD​=−∣B∣T2​b∈B∑​j=1∑Lb​​sg[pb,jT​]logpb,jS​
Symbols: B is a batch and b one user–candidate sample; Lb​ is that user's history length; pb,jT​, pb,jS​ are teacher and student softmax probabilities over history positions at temperature T; sg is stop-gradient, so the student loss never updates the teacher.

Intuition: soft-label cross-entropy. A user has several training candidates, each with its own teacher distribution, but the student has one score vector, so it fits what those distributions share. It learns to rank events useful for most candidates first.

4.4 Boundary loss

Even after distribution matching, a few teacher-preferred events can sit outside the student's top-K. The boundary loss targets them.

Three steps. Compute a sharper teacher distribution p~​T with temperature Tm​<T. Outside the top-K, take the n positions with the highest teacher probability, j+ (missed positives); inside it, take the n lowest, j− (placeholder negatives). Pair them by rank:
ωb,i​=sg[max(p~​b,jb,i+​T​−p~​b,jb,i−​T​,0)]Laux​=∑b​∑i​ωb,i​+ϵ∑b​∑i​ωb,i​softplus((sb,jb,i−​S​−sb,jb,i+​S​+δ)/Trank​)​
Symbols: i indexes pairs; ωb,i​ is the pair weight, the teacher's preference gap (clipped at 0); sS is the student score; δ is the desired margin; Trank​ scales the loss; ϵ avoids division by zero.

Intuition: a weighted pairwise ranking loss acting only at the top-K boundary. It pushes "should be in" events up and "taking a slot without mattering" events down, harder when the teacher's preference gap is larger. Pairs and weights are detached, so no gradient flows through the discrete top-K.

4.5 Full objective

Lsel​=αLpred​+βLKD​+γLaux​
Symbols: Lpred​ is the teacher's multi-task prediction loss; α, β, γ are weights.

Intuition: Lpred​ updates only the teacher, keeping it current on what is relevant; LKD​ and Laux​ update only DS. Both train live in the same stream; the teacher is not frozen. The ranking graph uses its own Lrank​.

5. Deployment: three engineering optimizations

Common-feature sharing. Samples of one user in a batch load the long history into GPU memory once.

Compact record encoding. Eight int64 fields cost 64 bytes per record, 640 KB at 10K records. ECHO packs each field into a fixed width sized to its value range.

Move the key projection to the query side. Standard target attention projects every history event into a key, so online cost or key-cache size grows with history length. ECHO uses:
⟨qWQ​,hWK​⟩=⟨(qWQ​)WK⊤​,h⟩
Symbols: q is the candidate-side query vector; h is one history event vector; WQ​, WK​ are the projection matrices.

Intuition: multiply WK​ into the query once per request; history vectors enter the dot product directly, with no per-event projection and no key cache.

6. Experiments

Baselines. DIN: target attention over the latest 100 events. SIM: GSU/ESU retrieval. TWIN: SIM with shared GSU/ESU parameters. STCA: end-to-end stacked target-aware cross-attention (trained at ~2K, extrapolated to 10K). TWIN V2: clusters the latest 50K events into ~10K units. SequenceO1: a fixed 100-token sketch. GAUC is per-user AUC, weighted-averaged.

7. Limitations

The 100K → 10K cut is hard. Events DS drops cannot be recovered by TFR; the authors note extremely long-tail candidates may suffer.

DS updates with real-time training and store refresh, so new interests enter after a delay.

Retention quality for new users, interest shifts and new candidate types is not evaluated separately. The industrial data is not public.

8. Practical takeaways

Add a user-side top-K before the GSU and compare it with recency and random at the same storage budget.

Monitor retention quality offline with teacher top-100 recall and attention-mass coverage.

Reuse an existing model as teacher and export its query/key parameters to both GSU and ESU.

Use the key-projection identity on its own in any online target attention.

Define refresh metrics: delay for new events to enter top-K, model/store version compatibility, rollback.
