papers.title: A Framework for Value-Aligned Modeling and Robust Experimentation
papers.authors: Krishna Harsha Reddy Kothapalli, Angela Liu, Kamal Nayan Reddy Challa, Pavithra Seshadrivijayakrishnan, Yongpeng Yang, M...
papers.summary: Google's Discover Ads team found that the offline Poisson Loss of its conversion model (pConvs) correlated only 0.1 with online advertiser value (Delivered Value: conversions per click times the advertiser's target cost per acquisition, tCPA, summed over clicks), so models that improved offline often did not gain once launched. The authors weight each click in the loss by its tCPA, and pair every low-traffic experiment with a retrained production model serving at the same traffic as its control. ==With tCPA weighting, the offline loss measures exactly the conversions advertisers are willing to pay for==. Offline-to-online correlation rose to 0.65, and low-to-high-traffic experiment correlation rose from 0.53 to 0.93.

deep_reading.content_html:
The Google Discover ads team iterates on models in three steps: compare the loss of the new and old models offline, run a small-traffic A/B to see the value delivered to advertisers, and finally bundle the changes that pass into a large-traffic launch. The old problem was that these three steps did not line up: the correlation between the change in the conversion model's (pConvs) offline Poisson loss and online value was only 0.1, and many changes that looked better offline failed in the small-traffic stage; the correlation between small-traffic and large-traffic results was only 0.53. This paper (RecSys 2026 Best Industry Paper) fixes both ends: the offline loss is weighted by how much each click is worth to the advertiser, so that a loss decrease corresponds to a value increase; on the experimentation side, systematic biases and noise are removed one by one. After the changes, the offline-to-online correlation rose to 0.65 and small-to-large traffic to 0.93, switching two models to the new objective raised online value by 4.7% in total, and the authors estimate that R&D efficiency roughly doubled.

1. Three stages, three kinds of error

The auction ranking stage has two models: pCTR predicts the click after an impression, pConvs predicts the number of conversions after a click; together with the advertiser's bid they produce the auction score for a second-price auction. The business metric behind launch decisions is Delivered Value (DV):
DV=i∈Clicks∑​Ti​⋅Ci​
Ti​ is the target price per conversion the advertiser is willing to pay (tCPA), Ci​ is the number of conversions from the i-th click. A purchase of a 1,000-dollar mattress is worth more than a hundred visits to a merchant's website, yet an ordinary conversion prediction loss counts both as equal conversions.

The stages take O(X), O(Y) and O(Z) time respectively, with X much smaller than Y and Y much smaller than Z, so every wrong judgment in an earlier stage wastes the more expensive resources of later stages. The authors split measurement error into three kinds: objective misalignment (what an earlier stage measures does not predict the later stage's result), systematic error (bias introduced by the experimental setup), and random error (variance from system noise).

2. Aligning the offline loss with delivered value

2.1 pConvs: Poisson loss weighted by tCPA

pConvs originally did maximum likelihood under a Poisson distribution, with loss PL=∑i​Pi​−Ci​logPi​, where Pi​ is the predicted number of conversions for the i-th click. The authors changed the prediction target from "conversions after a click" to "delivered value after a click", and the loss becomes the weighted Poisson loss (WPL):
WPL=i∈Clicks∑​Ti​[Pi​−Ci​logPi​]
The paper gives a derivation for why the weighting is correct. Let the advertiser's true value be v=Ti​Ci​, the bid b=Ti​Pi​, and the second price (what the advertiser actually pays) s have density $f(s)$; the expected profit of one auction is the integral of "value minus cost" over winning outcomes, ∫0b​(v−s)f(s)ds. If f(s)∝1/s, the integral comes out as vlnb−b plus a constant, so maximizing profit is equivalent to minimizing b−vlnb; substituting b and v back and dropping parameter-independent constants gives WPL. Poisson regression works here not because conversion counts really follow a Poisson distribution, but because the 1/s cost distribution approximately holds.

2.2 pCTR: from "whether clicked" to "how many clicks"

pCTR originally predicted the probability that an impression is clicked at least once, trained with log loss and evaluated with AUCLoss (1 minus AUC). A carousel ad impression often gets several clicks, and each extra click has value, so the team changed the target to the expected number of clicks per impression, raising online DV by 1.2%.

This change is almost invisible offline:

Offline metricChange
Binary AUCLoss-0.10%
Multi-class AUCLoss-0.15%
LL+0.08%
PL_CTR-0.21%

Log loss even got worse; only the Poisson loss computed on click counts, PL_CTR, dropped clearly, matching the direction of the 1.2% online gain.

pCTR also needs to carry value, but using conversion value directly as the weight fails because too few clicks have conversions and the labels are an order of magnitude sparser. The authors instead use expected delivered value EDV=∑i​Ti​⋅pConvsi​ as a proxy, with each impression weighted by Tj​⋅pConvsj​, giving WPLCTR​=∑j​Tj​pConvsj​[Pj​−Yj​logPj​], where Yj​ is the number of clicks on the j-th impression. The appendix uses the assumption that the runner-up's effective cost-per-thousand-impressions bid follows a $1/r$ distribution to give a derivation of the same form as 2.1.

2.3 Results after switching objectives

This experiment is meant to show two things: WPL as an offline metric better predicts online value, and training on WPL directly raises value.

ModelPL changeWPL changeOnline DV
pConvs trained on WPL+0.1%-0.35%+3%
pCTR trained on WPL+0.03%-0.04%+0.5%

For both models PL got worse, WPL got better, and online DV went up, which shows that what PL measures points in a different direction from the business objective.

Correlation is measured as follows: over the same set of changes, compute the Pearson correlation between the change in the offline metric and the change in online DV (absolute values are reported below). For pConvs, over about 40 experiments with online data, PL's correlation is 0.1 and WPL's is 0.65 (p<0.01); over 25+ later new experiments it is close to 0.69. For pCTR, over 25 experiments in the "whether clicked" phase, the correlation with EDV is 0.16 for AUCLoss and 0.09 for log loss; over 20 experiments after switching to expected clicks, multi-class AUCLoss reaches 0.33 and WPLCTR​ 0.63. Computed directly against the noisier DV, the correlation rises from 0.26 to 0.44.

3. Offline stage: systematic and random error

All models are trained continuously online, each example passes through only once, and offline evaluation uses progressive validation: each example is first predicted and its loss recorded, then used for training.

Systematic error has two sources. The first is label maturity bias: conversion labels arrive with delay, the experiment model starts later than the control, and while catching up on historical data it sees more complete conversion labels, so its loss over the same time period looks better only because it has more information; the fix is to compare only over periods where the two models' training data have the same quality. The second is optimizer artifacts: with second-order optimizers and architectures like DLRM that group features for interaction, adding one constant feature can change the grouping and split important features that need to interact into different groups. After fixing these two, the offline difference between two equivalent models stays within 0.02%, where previously significant differences were often measured.

Random error is suppressed by standardizing the measurement method. The table below compares, over 25 pConvs experiments, the offline-online correlation and the AUC-ROC of using the offline result to judge whether the online result is good, when the offline metric is measured over different time windows. T is each experiment's launch time.

Offline measurement windowCorrelationAUC-ROC
[T−6 months, T−3 months]0.6500.760
[T−1 month, T]0.5770.690
[T−1 week, T]0.010.489
Same fixed 3 months for all experiments0.6400.755
[T, T+online experiment duration]0.6040.736

Looking only at the last week, the correlation is close to 0 and AUC-ROC is below 0.5, worse than random guessing; a 3-month window beats a 1-month one. WPL weights range from 0.01 dollars to 1,000 dollars and are very noisy; capping the weights at the same upper limit used for DV capping halves the confidence interval without introducing bias.

4. Online stage: the small-traffic control must be as small as the experiment

4.1 Systematic error comes from different traffic sizes

The common practice is to compare the small-traffic experiment model against the large-traffic production model, which is necessarily biased. There are three reasons: a small-traffic model sees little of its own traffic during continuous training and cannot correct its own prediction bias, which is the winner's curse; advertiser budgets are fixed, and under small traffic the budget constraint barely binds, so value is overestimated; under large traffic, feedback control pulls prediction bias back toward the target constraints, and small traffic lacks this correction.

The authors' approach is to set a standard small-traffic size and retrain a copy of the production model at that traffic size, as a shared control for all experiments of that size. When another traffic size is needed, a separate control of that size is trained. After the change, the DV difference between two identical retrained models is close to 0%, where it used to often exceed 1%.

This comparison uses 7 historical experiments (old setup) and 8 new experiments (new setup); the small-to-large traffic correlation rose from 0.53 to 0.93. The sample is small because large-traffic experiments are expensive, but each large-traffic experiment runs long with a lot of traffic, so each single measurement is itself precise. The two groups evaluate the same set of models and are correlated at about 0.75 with each other; the authors use a Williams t-test that accounts for this correlation and get p<0.05.

4.2 Random error: capping and expected values

DV depends on sparse conversions, so its confidence interval is wide. Capping large per-click values shrinks the confidence interval width by 40% with bias under 3%; replacing actual DV with expected DV (pConvs predictions in place of actual conversions) shrinks the width by another 70% with bias of about 5%. Combined, the width shrinks by about 82%, and a 2%-traffic experiment now reaches the precision of a former 30%-traffic experiment, so the same traffic can run more experiments in parallel.

5. Why correlation determines efficiency

The authors assume that offline and online results follow a correlated bivariate normal distribution; multiplying the probability that the offline judgment agrees in direction with the next stage by the probability that the small-traffic judgment agrees with large traffic gives the probability that both judgments are correct:
Pgood​=[21​+πarcsin(ρoff​)​]⋅[21​+πarcsin(ρon​)​]
ρoff​ is the offline-to-small-traffic correlation and ρon​ the small-to-large traffic correlation. Before the improvements they were 0.1 and 0.53, giving a probability of about 0.36; after, about 0.69 and 0.93, giving about 0.65.

The text gives the improved offline correlation as 0.65 while the figure marks 0.69; by the formula, 0.69 corresponds to a probability of about 0.65 and 0.65 to about 0.64. The paper's efficiency evidence is 100+ experimental changes over 3 years: the number of successful changes included in each bundled pConvs launch, and the number of changes per contributor, both kept rising; the authors estimate overall efficiency roughly doubled, with exact numbers withheld for confidentiality.

6. Limitations

The authors acknowledge that all evidence comes from a single continuously trained online environment, Google Discover ads. The WPL derivation relies on costs following a $1/s$ distribution; the authors note in the appendix that the actual runner-up bid distribution decays faster with a lighter tail, and leave cost distributions closer to reality for future work.

In addition, DV itself is a simplified metric the paper uses to illustrate the problem; real launches look at several interdependent metrics, and the small-to-large traffic correlation is based on only 7 and 8 experiments.

7. Practical implications

  • If your model serves an auction ranked by bids, try multiplying the offline evaluation loss by each example's business value and check whether its correlation with online results improves; without changing training, this tells you whether your current offline metric is measuring the wrong thing.
  • A small-traffic experiment's control should be the same size and retrained the same way as the experiment arm. Comparing a small-traffic experiment arm against the large-traffic production model mixes winner's curse, budget and feedback-control biases into the measured difference, and an A/A experiment can catch this first.

papers.title: KuaFu: Compressing Long User Behavior into Understanding at Billion Scale
papers.authors: Jiahao Hui, Lin Zhu, Ben Tan, Yishen Hu, Jingdong Shu, Zetai Jiang, Xining Ran, Yeshou Cai, Gong Chen, Haijie Gu
papers.summary: KuaFu avoids repeatedly encoding the same content across users and profiling tasks. It caches compact item representations, assembles them chronologically and uses staged training to preserve evidence. Tencent reports a 1.37% overall GMV increase against a long-term holdout.
papers.key_insight: Make items the unit of reuse. Encode shared content once, while preserving actions and sequence order on the user side. The cache then scales with item inventory, supporting more frequent multi-task profile refreshes.

deep_reading.content_html:
KuaFu compresses an item once and reuses that representation wherever the item appears in user histories. Interest extraction and profiling tasks then read chronologically assembled compressed sequences. Tencent uses this separation to make long-history understanding cheaper and refresh profiles more frequently at billion-user scale.

1. Motivation: repeated encoding across users and tasks

Separate profiling tasks often reread the same behavior history. Content interests, shopping interests and occupation inference may each invoke a model over overlapping item text. That duplicates work both across tasks and across users who consumed the same content.

Compressing an entire user history has its own costs. New interactions may require rebuilding the summary, while aggressive compression can lose rare interests or temporal relationships. The paper distinguishes fabrication, omission, date misattribution and broken reasoning, showing why final recommendation quality alone is insufficient to evaluate compression.

KuaFu shares item-side computation while retaining action and chronological structure when constructing the user input. It is an asynchronous understanding and profile-refresh system, rather than a requirement to call an LLM for every online ranking request.

2. Method: item compression, compact caching and chronological decoding

A compressor reads an item's text and appends learned memory tokens. Their hidden states carry the compressed information. These are continuous vectors, rather than discrete product identifiers.

A two-axis projector reduces both the number of vectors and their width. The paper's example reduces eight memory vectors to two and the width from 2,560 to 128. The cache stores only the compact core; a lightweight up-projection restores the width expected by the decoder.

A pooled residual stabilizes early training and decays away. This matters operationally: inference must not require the original wide states if the compact cache is to deliver its storage benefit.

The decoder consumes chronological item representations alongside ordinary instructions and action information. Sharing item representations does not imply identical user profiles. The consumed items, action types and sequence order still distinguish users.

Training proceeds through reconstruction, preference-understanding post-training, joint compression-generation training and hallucination-aware reinforcement learning. Reconstruction teaches the memory to preserve information with the decoder frozen. Question answering then focuses compression on evidence useful for understanding. Joint training adapts both ends of the interface.

The final stage freezes the compressor and projector while updating the decoder. Rewards penalize specific errors and reward completeness, discouraging a trivial strategy of saying less. Judgments compare outputs against original text, rather than relying only on the compressed input.

A curriculum gradually increases history difficulty. Ablations show optimization problems when all lengths are mixed immediately, and poorer generalization without inheriting earlier training stages. Compression and the ability to read its output need coordinated training.

3. Contribution: representation dependencies determine cache reuse

Reuse works because an item's cached representation does not depend on a particular user or downstream task. Updating a user's behavior mainly changes the assembled input, whereas changed item content requires an item-cache update. The representation bank therefore scales with inventory rather than a separate long-history state for every user-task combination.

KuaFu also evaluates representation fidelity directly. It asks whether compressed inputs preserve retrievable events, dates and grounded conclusions. Such intermediate checks can expose damage earlier than an expensive end-to-end production experiment.

Compression ratios require careful denominators. The projector example changes 8×2,560 elements into 2×128, an 80-fold reduction. Shortening the decoder's input relative to raw text is a different quantity. Neither is automatically the whole-service cost reduction.

4. Results: efficiency funds longer histories and faster refreshes

The table selects four production outcomes. Interest tasks use F1, while stable profile attributes use classification accuracy. They should not be interpreted as a single common metric.

TaskMetricPrevious online modelKuaFu
Content interestF185.986.5
E-commerce interestF195.796.1
OccupationAccuracy86.787.6
Life stageAccuracy76.078.0

Content-interest throughput rises from 40 to 180 requests per minute per GPU. That is a 350% increase, calculated as (180−40)/40, or 4.5 times the original throughput. The paper reports 190 decoder-side GPUs saved across independently provisioned tasks; the single-task multiplier should not be applied to all hardware.

On public recommendation evaluation, the compressed 4B model improves over its same-size backbone, supporting a representation effect beyond model scale. The CDs subset is an exception where compression underperforms. Public reading-comprehension and private profiling benchmarks also follow different protocols, so their gains should remain separate.

After hallucination-aware training, fabrication falls from 33.5% to 4.5% while overall completeness remains nearly unchanged. Independent model judging and human-agreement checks strengthen the evaluation, though they do not establish coverage of every production failure.

The online experiment randomizes by unique visitor and keeps the end-to-end resource budget equal. Treatment uses compression savings to cover a longer history and refresh profiles more often. Overall GMV increases by 1.37%, with a positive confidence interval. Because the control has a shorter history and slower refresh cadence, this supports the complete profile upgrade rather than isolating a projector or training-stage effect.

5. Limitations: shared representations encode shared trade-offs

The authors identify fixed task-family compression ratios as a limitation. Information-dense content may need more memory than short items, making adaptive compression a natural next step.

Industrial logs and training data cannot be released. External reproduction is limited to public benchmarks and disclosed implementation details. Some private evaluations also rely on model judges and inherit their biases.

Cache versioning is an additional engineering concern. Item edits, compressor upgrades or decoder-interface changes require a compatibility policy. Shared encoding reduces duplicate work, but an incorrect item representation can affect many users. This is an architectural implication, not a production incident reported by the paper.

6. Practical implications

Measure how often the same text is encoded across user histories and tasks. The economics of item-side caching depend on actual reuse, edit frequency and storage cost, not just a large user count.

Evaluate interest labels, temporal attribution and event recovery separately. A representation sufficient for occupation inference may be inadequate for explaining a recent click. Task-specific fidelity checks identify where shared compression is appropriate.

Keep representation, history coverage and refresh cadence distinguishable in experiments. Holding two fixed while changing the third helps explain how saved compute reaches business outcomes. KuaFu demonstrates one useful path from efficiency to better update capability.

Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2609.31045v2 . First submitted September 25, 2026; this run discovered the October revision. Calculations and deployment suggestions are editorial analysis.

papers.title: FLMNet: Self-Ensemble Distillation from Masks to Seeds for Single-Tower CTR Prediction
papers.authors: Yifan Wang, Yifei Du
papers.summary: CTR self-distillation can be replaced with a computable disagreement penalty. FLMNet keeps gates on clean inputs and distills independently trained towers into one serving model. The distilled model reaches 0.8169 AUC on Criteo.
papers.key_insight: Separate mask disagreement from seed disagreement: regularize the former within a run and distill the latter across runs. The moment formulas require gates that do not read masked intermediate activations.

deep_reading.content_html:
FLMNet replaces repeated masked predictions with a computable disagreement penalty, then distills the agreement of independently trained models into one serving tower. The paper separates two sources of variation: masks within a model and training seeds across models.

1. Problem and motivation

CTR models combine categorical user, item, and context features. Possible feature combinations greatly outnumber training examples, so the model must generalize beyond observed combinations. Dropout exposes it to incomplete views during training. Self-distillation additionally encourages these views to agree with an ensemble prediction.

The open question is what that extra objective buys. Is random sampling essential, or is it a noisy way of applying a useful regularizer? Repeated forward passes also make training more expensive, even when only one network is served.

2. Method

The derivation pools logits, the scores before conversion to click probabilities. Averaging logits and averaging probabilities are different operations. The exact result applies to the specified pooling objective, rather than every loss described as self-distillation.

As the number of masks tends to infinity, the objective decomposes into label loss at the mean logit and a penalty on disagreement. That penalty is a Jensen gap: the expected value of a convex function minus its value at the expected input. This is an identity about the objective, not a guarantee about optimization trajectories or test accuracy.

FLMNet makes the required moments tractable by keeping its gates off the masked path. Gates read clean input embeddings. If gates instead read masked intermediate representations, later factors inherit earlier randomness and independence assumptions fail.

Training still approximates the true disagreement gap. It replaces the mask distribution with a Gaussian of matching variance and uses three-point quadrature. Variance truncation is a separate approximation examined in the paper. One unmasked forward pass supplies the prediction and statistics; computing their gradients still costs work.

The second stage addresses seed disagreement. Independently initialized and trained towers remain different even after mask disagreement is regularized. Their pooled scores become a teacher for a single student. This saves serving cost but requires extra offline training runs.

3. Main contribution

The useful distinction is between within-run regularization and across-run distillation. Their gains largely add in the experiments. The architecture also exposes a concrete condition to audit: whether random masking reaches the gates that control feature interactions.

Single-pass training should not be confused with free training. Moment computation, differentiation, teacher training, and student fitting all belong in a cost comparison.

4. Results

The main comparison covers five benchmarks and seventeen established models. Selected advertising results are test-mean AUC values; higher is better.

ModelCriteo AUCAvazu AUC
FinalNet0.81510.7607
QNN, one head0.81530.7572
FLMNet-CF0.81620.7617
FLMNet-KD0.81690.7620

CF uses the closed-form penalty approximation; KD adds cross-seed distillation. On Criteo, each step contributes. Same-backbone regularizer comparisons help separate the loss effect from architecture changes.

The timing intervention is especially informative. Turning the penalty on slows the growth of the train–validation gap; turning it off accelerates overfitting. Applying it from the first epoch can also slow early learning.

That intervention uses one dataset and a constant learning rate. It supports the proposed mechanism without establishing a universal activation epoch.

5. Limitations

The authors identify three boundaries: moment formulas require the stated architectural conditions, training uses a Gaussian surrogate, and the recoverable cross-seed gain is known empirically rather than in closed form.

Evaluation details matter too. Avazu uses a disclosed re-splitting and retraining protocol. Some distilled students share teacher sets, so they are not independent replications. Public benchmark AUC gains do not establish an online CTR lift.

An additional engineering implication is refresh cost. A frequently updated service must budget for teacher runs, score caching, and student training, alongside its single-tower serving savings.

6. Practical implications

Audit the pooling rule and the gate inputs before adapting the formula to an existing CTR model. Hold the backbone, embedding sizes, and training budget fixed when comparing no penalty, sampling-based regularization, and the deterministic approximation.

Report paired-seed differences and train–validation curves. Evaluate cross-seed distillation as a separate budget decision, with calibration, latency, and refresh interval alongside AUC.

Sources: Sections 3–5, the conclusion, and Appendix B. All figures are original assets from the paper’s arXiv HTML.

papers.title: LSNR: Learned Sparse News Recommendations with Attentive User Modeling
papers.authors: David Vos, Andrew Yates, Maarten de Rijke
papers.summary: Encode articles separately, then learn which ones matter. LSNR combines weighted sparse article vectors with a user-level semantic expansion, improving MIND NDCG@10 by about 11% over STAR.
papers.key_insight: Article boundaries matter beyond context length. A lexical path preserves evidence from individual clicks, while a semantic path adds aggregate interests. Gains with a single history article show that truncation is only part of the problem.

deep_reading.content_html:
Encode each article separately, then learn how to combine a reader's interests. LSNR replaces a flattened history string with an explicit user encoder while retaining sparse, vocabulary-based retrieval. Its strongest diagnostic result comes from readers with just one history article: gains survive even when truncation is absent.

1. Motivation: a reading history is a collection

Concatenating news articles mixes distinct interests and forces a language model to infer which article matters. Long articles also exhaust the input window. STAR, the learned sparse baseline examined here, uses this concatenation approach.

Sparse representations assign weights to vocabulary terms, with most weights zero. They can use inverted indexes and can include learned expansion terms absent from the literal text. This makes them attractive for teams with established lexical retrieval infrastructure. The question is whether the user representation preserves enough information to make that infrastructure useful for recommendation.

LSNR separates article understanding from user aggregation. An article can be encoded once, independently of the reader. The user encoder then learns how to combine the articles that particular reader consumed.

2. Method: two paths into a sparse user vector

The shared article encoder produces a sparse vocabulary vector and an auxiliary dense vector. SPLADE-style projection, activation, and pooling form the sparse representation. The dense representation helps estimate the relevance of history articles to the overall user profile; candidate articles need only their cached sparse vectors at serving time.

A user-side transformer contextualizes the dense history vectors. Additive attention assigns a weight to each article. The model omits positional encodings because the authors' ablation finds no benefit from adding them on these news benchmarks.

The first user path takes an attention-weighted sum of article sparse vectors. Its active terms remain traceable to individual history articles. The second path pools dense interests and projects them back into vocabulary space, allowing aggregate interests to activate terms that no single article's expansion supplies. The paths share attention weights and the vocabulary projection rather than adding independent encoders.

Training separately regularizes document and user sparsity. At retrieval time, the default configuration retains the user's 30 highest-weight terms. Candidate scoring is a sparse inner product, so article encoding remains offline while online work consists mainly of aggregation, pruning, and retrieval.

3. Contribution: more than avoiding truncation

Independent article encoding removes the history-window bottleneck. Learned aggregation addresses a separate problem: how several reading interests should contribute to one profile. The single-history experiment helps distinguish those explanations.

With only one history article, STAR and LSNR receive the same content without history truncation. LSNR still improves. This supports the importance of its representation-learning and user-training design, rather than attributing every gain to access to more text.

The paper also separates ranking accuracy, index size, and latency. A compact index is useful, but compactness does not establish a speed advantage.

4. Evidence: stronger with short histories

The experiments use the small versions of English MIND and Danish EBNeRD. Because official test labels are unavailable, the authors evaluate on the official validation split and reserve part of training for tuning. These NDCG@10 results rank the candidates recorded in each impression, not the full article catalog.

MethodMIND, full historyEBNeRD, full historyEBNeRD, one article
STAR0.38150.47040.4656
NRMS0.42560.52900.4880
NAML0.42470.53120.4889
LSNR0.42340.52000.5022

LSNR improves MIND NDCG@10 by about 11% relative to STAR. Against dense recommenders, the conclusion is narrower: it is close to the strongest MIND models with full histories and trails them on EBNeRD. Its clear advantage is the short-history setting.

Ablations favor using both user paths. Learned attention also beats the tested pooling alternatives. These results support the aggregation mechanism rather than merely the choice of a sparse representation.

On EBNeRD, the reported index footprint falls from 31.84 MB for the dense baseline to 2.41 MB for LSNR. The dense baseline nevertheless has lower measured latency. The authors also identify a favorable dense-index recall–latency frontier, so footprint is the main efficiency advantage.

5. Limits: accuracy and retrieval use different scopes

The authors explicitly acknowledge that LSNR does not consistently beat strong dense models with full histories. Evidence is limited to two small news benchmarks and two languages. Community posts differ in length and interaction structure.

Accuracy is evaluated within impression candidate lists. Full-catalog retrieval is used for index and latency measurements, not the main accuracy tables. Those tables therefore do not establish full-catalog recall or an online CTR lift.

On MIND, initialization is not fully controlled: STAR starts from a retrieval-pretrained checkpoint while LSNR starts from ordinary BERT. This favors STAR directionally but remains a comparison limitation.

Vocabulary terms also require care as explanations. Inspectable dimensions do not guarantee that each expansion weight represents a reader's literal intent. The paper leaves direct evaluation of editable interest controls to future work.

6. Practical implications

An existing inverted-index platform could test LSNR as an additional personalized candidate source. Cache article representations offline and compare complementary recall against the dense source. For short community posts, interest aggregation may matter more than avoiding article truncation.

Evaluate by history length, including a one-article control. This distinguishes gains from improved user modeling from gains caused by retaining more text, and prevents active users from obscuring cold-history behavior in aggregate metrics.

Measure index storage, user-aggregation cost, and tail latency separately. Sweep user-vector pruning locally rather than assuming the paper's default is optimal. The useful trade-off depends on whether the platform needs smaller indexes, complementary candidates, or faster responses.

Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2610.23510v1 . Figures and experimental results come from the full paper; the implementation suggestions are editorial analysis.

papers.title: Predictable Scaling: Efficient Model Exploration via Scaling-Law Prediction
papers.authors: Aishwarya Wesanekar, Sheng-Tao Yang, Jiawei Zhang, Flavio Sales Truzzi, Chen Chen, Nader Beigiparast, Shengyuan Huang, R...
papers.summary: Predictable Scaling evaluates ranking-model changes with reduced-scale proxies and estimates their full-scale effects using historical learning curves. Training compute falls by 88% and 79% on two industrial ranking models.
papers.key_insight: A useful proxy preserves which changes are better, not merely a small average prediction error. Scaling must be chosen for each architecture: reducing embedding width alone can scramble the ordering of candidate changes.

deep_reading.content_html:
A smaller ranking model is useful for experimentation only if it still identifies which changes are better. Meta's Predictable Scaling makes that requirement explicit and tests it against known full-scale results. The compute savings concern model-development experiments, rather than a claim that a compressed production model preserves every business metric.

1. Motivation: experimentation becomes a bottleneck

Recommendation teams repeatedly change features, interaction layers, and data sampling. Each idea may require a costly full training run before its value becomes clear. This verification cost limits how many ideas a team can explore.

Reducing data or network size seems straightforward, but ranking models contain coupled embedding tables, interaction networks, history encoders, and task heads. Shrinking one component can change the bottleneck and reverse the relative value of two candidate changes.

The paper therefore predicts each candidate's improvement relative to its baseline rather than predicting absolute final loss. This matches the development decision: which changes deserve further compute?

2. Method: choose the proxy and test its distortions

Each candidate and baseline receive the same scaling treatment and are trained as a pair. Their relative metric gap is the proxy observation. Without that pairing, scaling effects could be confused with the candidate's actual contribution.

The main metric is normalized entropy, which scales prediction cross-entropy by the entropy of the overall positive rate. Lower is better; a negative relative gap means improvement. These gaps are not CTR percentage-point changes.

Scaling functions reduce samples, embedding-table rows, embedding width, input features, hidden dimensions, or layer depth. They may be composed, but their interactions can create more distortion than either component alone. Historical candidates with known full-scale outcomes provide a benchmark for selecting configurations.

The simplest predictor uses the proxy gap directly. Linear regression adjusts approximately affine relationships. An empirical Gaussian process learns the mean and covariance structure of historical learning curves and extrapolates a proxy's convergence behavior while estimating uncertainty.

This distinction matters: a flexible predictor cannot recover information destroyed by an unsuitable scaling rule. Predictions with excessive relative uncertainty are rejected rather than treated as dependable screening results.

The framework checks stable convergence, transferable gaps, and preservation of improvement direction. Under a compute budget, it evaluates feasible proxy configurations against historical results using cross-validation. Ranking fidelity and sign reversals complement average error when deciding which configuration can screen new hypotheses.

3. Contribution: evaluate proxies as decision tools

The framework connects proxy design, prediction accuracy, and development decisions. It replaces a universal shrink ratio with evidence that a particular configuration works for a particular architecture.

Repeated baseline training provides a noise floor. Differences below that scale may be indistinguishable from run-to-run variability. The paper separately measures ordering among actionable changes whose full-scale effects exceed the noise floor.

A low mean absolute error alone is insufficient. Predictions clustered near zero can have a small error while offering little information about which idea is better. Ordering matters when a team must decide which candidate receives the next expensive run.

4. Evidence: reduced experiment cost, with architecture dependence

The industrial evaluation includes a task-specific feed CTR/CVR model and a multi-task foundation model. Public Criteo experiments examine several common recommendation architectures to test behavior beyond the internal systems.

Evaluation headRaw-proxy MAEGP MAEInterpretation
Task-specific CTR0.8650.738About 15% lower error
Foundation CTR-12.1500.701About 67% lower error
Foundation CTR-21.7500.753About 57% lower error
Foundation CVR-10.9500.854Smaller improvement

Errors are expressed in units of the repeated-run noise scale. The task-specific improvement is indicative and has substantial standard error. Some foundation-model heads benefit more, consistent with a larger proxy-to-full-scale mismatch that curve fitting can address.

Reported training-compute reductions are 88% and 79% for the two industrial models. The accounting includes trainer count, processed samples, and throughput. Lower proxy throughput can coexist with lower total consumption when devices and samples decrease sufficiently.

Perfect ordering is reported for actionable industrial hypotheses above the noise floor. It does not apply to every candidate, architecture, or public experiment.

Public results expose the boundary. Different architectures prefer different scaling configurations. Embedding-width reduction alone performs poorly at preserving rankings, and the best DCN-v2 configuration still provides only moderate ranking correlation. Low prediction error and reliable candidate ordering can diverge.

5. Limits: fitting cannot repair lost structure

The authors discuss tightly coupled feature-interaction networks as a difficult case. Shrinking dimensions can remove the interactions responsible for a candidate's gain. A Gaussian process may correct predictable bias but cannot undo that structural loss.

Data subsampling also depends on the original scale. A fraction of a huge internal dataset may retain sufficient signal, while the same fraction of a smaller public dataset may not. There is no universal optimal reduction ratio.

The industrial target is primarily offline normalized entropy. Extending the framework to additional online metrics is future work. Development-compute savings cannot be converted into equivalent CTR or revenue gains from these experiments.

An operational implication is that the historical benchmark must remain representative. A new backbone or feature pipeline can invalidate an old proxy configuration. The fallback to full training should be enforced in the workflow whenever uncertainty or fidelity checks fail.

6. Practical implications

Maintain a paired-experiment ledger containing the baseline, candidate change, proxy configuration, final metrics, learning curves, and actual compute. Relative changes are more useful for this purpose than isolated final scores.

Replay screening against held-out historical changes. Measure missed useful candidates and incorrect improvement signs, rather than only average prediction error. For community-search ranking, separately examine how click-prediction effects relate to relevance metrics.

Allocate compute between exploration and confirmation. A validated proxy can cheaply explore many ideas; close calls, contradictory rankings, and uncertain predictions return to full-scale evaluation. The practical objective is more credible discoveries within a fixed experiment budget.

Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2610.23453v1 . Methods and numerical results come from the main paper and appendices. The workflow illustration and practical suggestions are editorial analysis.

papers.title: DuoLM: Fast and Effective Personalized Recommendation with Language Models
papers.authors: Jiang Wu, Yutong Song, Hongbo Wang, Guanghe Cao, Jeff Liang
papers.summary: DuoLM precomputes one vector per item and uses a personalized ranker with user history and feedback. Shared history computation and a specialized runtime reduce online work. Throughput reaches about 26,400 candidate scores per second on one H100.
papers.key_insight: Train reusable content representations and personalized judgments jointly. Compression pays off in end-to-end serving only when repeated history prefill, input transmission, and scheduling are reduced too.

deep_reading.content_html:
DuoLM reads item content offline and reserves online computation for deciding whether a particular user will like it. An encoder language model compresses each item, while a ranker uses those representations with user history and feedback. The system design turns that reuse into measured serving gains.

1. Problem and motivation

A full-text cross-encoder reads item descriptions together with user context. Its representations depend on the request and cannot simply be cached across users. Repeating this work for every candidate makes language-model recommendation expensive.

A compact item vector is cheaper, but a generic text embedding may discard details needed for personalized judgments. DuoLM trains content compression and personalized ranking together.

There is also overhead outside the model. Candidates in one request share a user history, yet input construction, transmission, and scheduling can repeat. Prefix caching does not necessarily remove those operations. As model execution gets faster, they become a larger share of total cost.

2. Method

The encoder reads templated item text and uses its final EOS hidden state as one item representation. A continuous interface normalizes and calibrates its scale against the ranker’s native token embeddings. Both history items and candidates use this interface; textual feedback remains beside the relevant history entries.

During training, ranking gradients flow through the interface into the encoder. Item vectors are recomputed while learning and cached only after training. A frozen full-text teacher supplies scores for the exact histories and candidate groups used by the student. The student learns both observed targets and the teacher’s relative preferences.

The paper compares feedback in the encoder with feedback in the ranker. The former caches an item–rating pair; the latter caches one representation per item. Their quality is close, and the latter provides a simpler reuse boundary.

At serving time, virtual token IDs reference a GPU-resident item-vector table. Requests carry IDs and feedback instead of transmitting complete vectors. These IDs are an access mechanism for continuous representations, rather than generated semantic item codes.

The multi-item scoring path prefills the user history once and shares its key–value cache across candidate branches. A tree-structured mask keeps branches independent. CUDA Graph replay further reduces launch and scheduling overhead. These changes save work at different points in the request path.

3. Main contribution

The central design boundary separates reusable content understanding from request-specific preference judgment. The representation is shared across users, the history computation is shared across candidates, and candidate scores remain independent.

The paper measures complete requests rather than treating lower model FLOPs as proof of faster serving. Runtime ablations help explain where the end-to-end improvement comes from.

4. Results

Recommendation quality is evaluated on Amazon Books and Video Games. NDCG@10 rewards relevant items appearing earlier in the ranking; absolute values should not be compared across datasets.

ModelBooksVideo Games
HLLM0.55080.5025
DuoLM0.55860.5298
Full-text teacher0.54400.5313

The student exceeds the teacher on Books and approaches it on Video Games. This demonstrates useful compression in these settings, not lossless compression for every domain.

On one H100, with 100 candidates per request, high-concurrency throughput reaches about 26,400 candidate scores per second. The unit is candidate scores, not user requests. Full-request p99 latency is about 537 ms at that concurrency.

The teacher comparison includes vLLM with automatic prefix caching. The gain combines a different model representation with a specialized serving path; it cannot all be attributed to switching inference engines.

Ablations also favor restraint: the simple EOS readout beats the tested learned readouts, stronger distillation does not keep improving quality, and extra hidden-state self-alignment hurts the reported setting.

5. Limitations

The evidence covers two product categories and specified hardware, without an online UGC search experiment. It does not establish behavior on rapidly edited posts, long comment threads, or breaking events.

Two engineering implications follow from the architecture. First, cached item vectors need versioning, incremental refresh, and memory budgeting. Moving encoding offline relocates its cost rather than eliminating it. Second, prefix reuse requires identical user history and context; candidate-isolation masks must remain correct.

Independent scoring also differs from list-level optimization for diversity or competition. Evaluation should preserve the paper’s candidate construction before expanding to a production recall pool. NDCG values from different candidate protocols are not interchangeable.

6. Practical implications

A content-rich ranking stage is a useful trial setting. Compare compressed and full-text scoring on long-tail items and narrow preference segments, where a single vector might hide important details.

Measure cache hits, history prefill, input preparation, and GPU execution separately. Report both candidate throughput and request throughput, plus tail latency. For UGC, include new and edited posts, recording the time until refreshed vectors become visible and the representation version used for ranking.

Sources: Sections 2–4 and Appendices A, C, and D. All figures are original assets from the paper’s arXiv HTML.

papers.title: EASformer: Environment-Action-State Alignment for Industrial Generative Ranking
papers.authors: Bohao Li, Dinglun Cao, Pengcheng Huang, Yingda Tang, Zhiting Zhao, Yi Cao, Jilei Fu, Miao Yan, Tianying Liu, Heng Chang,...
papers.summary: EASformer addresses a mismatch between historical tokens containing observed actions and candidates with no observed action. It separates environment, action and state before matching them. The larger of two reported online eCPM lifts is 3.94%.
papers.key_insight: Attention should compare semantically aligned representations. Separating environmental matching from action prediction also lets masked historical actions reuse the candidate-prediction pathway for self-supervision.

papers.title: SPAR: Stepwise Personalized Autoregressive Recommendation with Prefix-Balanced Semantic IDs
papers.authors: Chunrui Zhang, Gaoyun Lin, Chang Zhou, Zheng Hu, Qiran Song, Shimin Cai, Tao Zhou
papers.summary: SPAR reduces early branch errors in semantic-ID recommendation by retrieving user evidence at every decoding step and balancing traffic across sibling branches. A Youku online experiment reports a 3.95% increase in average watch time per user.
papers.key_insight: Personalization should change with the generated prefix. Inspect user-evidence retrieval and branch-load imbalance together to diagnose early decoding errors that prevent the right item from remaining reachable.

papers.title: The Fusion Tax: A Diagnostic Analysis of When Hybrid Retrieval Hurts
papers.authors: Aaditya Chauhan, Arun Agarwal
papers.summary: Hybrid retrieval fuses BM25 and dense retrieval into one ranking, and most search engine and RAG framework docs default to reciprocal rank fusion (RRF). The authors keep a per-query ledger on 7 BEIR datasets: the best fusion method, score interpolation with weight 0.7 on the dense score, beats dense-only retrieval on mean nDCG@10 on every dataset, yet still ranks 8–21% of queries worse than dense-only. These losses concentrate on queries where only one retriever finds a relevant document; ==the other retriever then contributes only noise, and fusion pushes relevant documents that were already ranked high back down==. Scaling the dense encoder from 22M to 596M parameters does not remove this loss. RRF beats dense-only only on datasets where the two retrievers are roughly equal, ==so the fusion method should be chosen from the measured gap between the two retrievers on the target corpus==.

deep_reading.content_html:
Hybrid retrieval fuses the results of term-matching sparse retrieval such as BM25 with those of dense vector retrieval into a single ranking. The documentation of Elasticsearch, Azure AI Search and LangChain all list reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) as the recommended or only fusion method, on the basis of gains in average metrics. This paper keeps the books differently: it compares nDCG@10 before and after fusion query by query, and treats "no fusion" as a legitimate option. The authors test on 7 BEIR datasets with standard Anserini BM25 and the BGE-small dense model. The best fusion method is score interpolation with a 0.7 weight on the dense score, which beats dense-only retrieval in mean nDCG@10 on every dataset, by 0.008 to 0.051; yet in the same setting 8–21% of queries rank worse than with dense-only retrieval, and 13–48% rank worse than the better of the two retrievers on that query. The authors call this per-query loss the "fusion tax". The losses concentrate on queries where only one retriever finds a relevant document, and the other retriever then contributes only noise. Switching to a larger dense encoder, replacing BM25 with SPLADE, or adding a cross-encoder reranker after fusion does not make this tax disappear.

1. The average went up, so why look query by query

A higher mean nDCG@10 only says that more queries were helped than hurt; it does not say that no query was hurt. For a RAG system the difference has practical consequences: if fusion pushes a query's relevant document out of the top 10, the context given to the generator no longer contains the answer, and the answer quality for that query drops directly, while the average does not show it.

The authors therefore keep two accounts for every query. The first uses the "per-query best" as reference: whichever of BM25 and dense retrieval does better on a given query is compared with the fused result. This reference is only known after the fact and measures whether fusion drags down the better retriever. The second uses "always dense-only" as reference, an alternative that can actually be deployed, and answers whether adding BM25 is worth it at all.

2. The accounting: one formula, four quadrants

The fusion tax of a single query is defined as the nDCG@10 of the better of the two retrievers minus the nDCG@10 after fusion:
τ(q)=max(NDCGs​(q),NDCGd​(q))−NDCGf​(q)
Here s is sparse retrieval (BM25), d is dense retrieval and f is the fused result. τ(q)>0 means fusion is worse than the better retriever on that query. The share of queries with τ>0 is called the "oracle tax"; the share of queries where fusion falls below dense-only retrieval is called the "deployable tax".

Three fusion methods are compared. RRF sums the reciprocals of the ranks, with the constant set to 60. Score interpolation first min-max normalizes the scores of each retriever's top 100, then adds them as sf​=αs~d​+(1−α)s~s​ with α=0.7. CombMNZ sums the normalized scores and multiplies by the number of retrievers that returned the document.

To find where the losses come from, the authors split queries into four quadrants by whether each retriever puts at least one relevant document in its top 10: both retrievers hit (Both-Win), only dense retrieval hits (Dense-Only), only BM25 hits (Sparse-Only), and neither hits (Both-Fail).

The sparse side uses BM25 with Anserini default parameters (k1=0.9, b=0.4, title and body indexed as separate fields), which the authors confirm reproduces the published BEIR results to 4 decimal places; this rules out the explanation that "BM25 drags fusion down because it was badly tuned". The main experiments use BGE-small (33M parameters) on the dense side, with MiniLM (22M), BGE-base (110M), BGE-large (335M) and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (596M) as alternatives, all searched exactly with FAISS. The 7 datasets are SciFact (scientific claim verification), FiQA (financial QA), NFCorpus (medical nutrition retrieval), TREC-COVID (COVID literature retrieval), ArguAna (finding counter-arguments), SciDocs (citation recommendation) and Quora (duplicate question retrieval), with query counts ranging from 50 for TREC-COVID to 10,000 for Quora.

3. Experiments

3.1 Averages: interpolation does win

This experiment first checks whether fusion is as effective on average metrics as is usually claimed. The authors compare nDCG@10 of each retriever alone and of the three fusion methods with BGE-small on the 7 datasets (paper Table V):

DatasetBM25Dense-onlyRRFInterpolation α=0.7CombMNZ
SciFact0.66470.72000.71520.73070.7230

Score interpolation beats dense-only retrieval on all 7 datasets. RRF beats dense-only retrieval only on NFCorpus and TREC-COVID, where BM25 and dense retrieval are at similar levels (0.656 vs 0.666 on TREC-COVID); on the other 5 datasets RRF is below dense-only retrieval. RRF looks only at ranks and not at scores, so even when dense retrieval is clearly stronger it treats BM25's ranks as equally trustworthy, which dilutes the dense side's advantage.

3.2 Per-query accounts: how many queries get worse behind the higher average

This experiment checks how many queries are hurt, and how badly, while the average rises. The authors compare interpolation and RRF query by query against dense-only retrieval and against the per-query best (paper Table VIII):

DatasetInterp. worse than denseMean loss when worseInterp. better than denseMean net changeInterp. below per-query bestRRF worse than dense
SciFact10.0%0.20514.7%+0.010720.0%15.3%

Take ArguAna: interpolation makes 19.1% of queries worse, the worsened queries drop by 0.213 on average, almost as much as the 0.221 average gain of the improved queries, and the mean net change is only +0.0077. The small rise in the average is the difference left after large gains and large losses across many queries cancel out.

One might suspect that the 0.7 weight was picked on the test data. The authors re-select the weight with leave-one-dataset-out cross-validation: choose α on the other 6 datasets and apply it to the 7th. The resulting deployable tax is 11–25%, slightly higher than with a fixed 0.7, which shows the tax is not caused by tuning on the test set. The risk-sensitive test TRisk, which weights the losses of worsened queries more heavily, judges interpolation riskier than dense-only retrieval on 6 of the 7 datasets.

3.3 Which quadrant the losses come from

This experiment checks which kind of query the losses come from. The authors split interpolation's per-query gains and losses by the four quadrants of Section 2 (paper Table VII). Result: Sparse-Only queries make up no more than 7% of the total, but 87–95% of them are hurt by fusion, with mean net losses of 0.14 to 0.37 within the quadrant. The reason is that dense retrieval has no relevant document in its top 10 on these queries, and the 0.7 dense weight pushes down the relevant documents BM25 found. Dense-Only queries are the mirror case: BM25 becomes the noise source and 38–65% are hurt. Among Both-Win queries, 10–48% are reordered, with help and harm nearly cancelling and a quadrant net change between −0.04 and +0.01; because this quadrant holds the most queries, it contributes 38–72% of the worsened queries.

The losses are mainly rank changes, not lost relevant documents: queries whose top-10 recall drops are only 1–7%, and most of the loss is relevant documents moving down within the top 10; across all datasets, 77 queries have all their relevant documents pushed out of the top 10.

3.4 A bigger encoder does not remove the tax

This experiment checks whether the fusion tax exists only because the dense model is weak. The authors step the dense encoder up from 22M to 596M, then redo the experiment with BM25 replaced by the learned sparse retriever SPLADE. Result: with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, interpolation still puts 14–43% of queries below the per-query best; with SPLADE it is 14–41% on 6 datasets and 60% on TREC-COVID. A stronger encoder only changes the balance between the two retrievers, and that balance decides which retriever becomes noise on each query, so the share of hurt queries does not decline as the encoder grows.

3.5 Can we tell in advance which queries should not be fused

If this could be predicted, queries could be routed: fuse where fusion helps and use dense-only retrieval elsewhere. This experiment checks whether that is feasible. The authors extract 17 features available at inference time for each query (query length, IDF statistics of its terms, the score gap between the first and second result of each retriever, the overlap of the two top-10 lists, and so on) and train gradient-boosted trees to predict whether fusion will fail. Result: AUC is 0.63 within a dataset, falls to 0.59 across datasets, and is as low as 0.49, close to random; 11 of the 17 features flip the direction of their association with failure across datasets. A router built on these features does not beat fixed interpolation on any dataset. A concrete example is the dense side's score lead: on datasets where dense retrieval is stronger it signals that fusion is safe, but on TREC-COVID it signals that fusion will fail.

3.6 Can reranking repair the damage

This experiment checks whether a cross-encoder reranker after fusion can repair the losses fusion causes. The authors rerank the top 30 with BGE-reranker-v2-m3. Result: the deployable tax falls by a third on SciFact and does not fall on FiQA or TREC-COVID. Reranking both repairs losses and creates new ones: on SciFact it repairs 27 of the 30 previously hurt queries and newly hurts 17; on FiQA it repairs 75 of 95 and newly hurts 81; on TREC-COVID it repairs 5 of 7 and newly hurts 9. After reranking, nDCG@10 differs by at most 0.011 whether the candidates come from interpolation or from dense-only retrieval. On cost, BM25 takes 1.1–4.3 ms per query on an Apple M5, while cross-encoder reranking of 30 candidates takes about 1.6 s.

4. Limitations

The authors list five limitations: only retrieval ranking is evaluated, not the final answer generation; only one reranker and one reranking depth are tried; TREC-COVID has only 50 queries, so its percentages fluctuate a lot; latency is measured on one machine only; and the prediction experiment uses only cheap features, without trying LLM judgments.

Two further points deserve attention. First, all 7 datasets are English BEIR datasets whose queries are mostly natural-language questions, and dense retrieval is stronger than BM25 on all 7 of them; in keyword-heavy settings such as e-commerce or code search, Sparse-Only queries may be far more than 7%, and both the quadrant shares and the recommended weight need to be re-measured. Second, Section 3.3 shows that most of the loss is relevant documents moving down within the top 10; if the downstream system feeds all 10 documents into the generator's context, this loss affects the answer much less, which is exactly the gap left by not evaluating generation.

5. Practical implications

First, before adopting hybrid retrieval, measure the nDCG@10 of each retriever on the target corpus. The authors' rule is: if dense retrieval leads by more than 0.04, use score interpolation with a dense weight of 0.6–0.7; if the two are close, use RRF, CombMNZ or interpolation with weight 0.5. Labeling 200–400 queries is enough to make this call, and transferring the 0.6–0.7 weight to another dataset costs at most 0.014.

Second, in online evaluation, report "the share of queries worse than dense-only retrieval" and "the mean loss when worse" alongside the average. These two numbers show directly whether a higher average comes from most queries gaining a little, or from some queries gaining a lot and cancelling out large losses on others.

papers.title: pplx-embed-v2-late Technical Report
papers.authors: Markus Krimmel, Louis Milliken, Ekaterina Glazkova, Maximilian Schall, Antoine Chaffin, Sedigheh Eslami, Jonas Golde, De...
papers.summary: Perplexity releases 0.6B and 9B multi-vector retrievers that encode text, images, and document screenshots: each document token stores a 128-d vector, and scoring sums MaxSim of each query vector against document vectors. Both models distill token-by-token from the same 18B teacher, ==so they share one vector space== and a 9B offline document index can be queried by a 0.6B online encoder. On 72 domain retrieval tasks the 9B model averages nDCG@10 81.3%, 1.6 points above nemotron-3-embed-8b; a 0.6B query with a 9B index scores 79.6%, above 78.0% when both ends use 0.6B. On BrowseComp+ the 9B model lets an agent answer 64.0% correctly with the fewest searches.

deep_reading.content_html:
Perplexity releases two multi-vector retrieval models, pplx-embed-v2-late at 0.6B and 9B, that encode text, images, and document page screenshots. They are late-interaction retrievers: every document token stores a 128-d vector, every query token gets a vector, and scoring sums MaxSim—each query vector takes its max inner product against document vectors. The two models are not trained separately with contrastive learning; they both distill token-by-token from the same 18B teacher's output vectors, so they live in one vector space: the corpus can be indexed offline with 9B and queried online with 0.6B. On the authors' 72 domain retrieval tasks, 9B averages nDCG@10 81.3%, 1.6 points above next-best nemotron-3-embed-8b; a 0.6B query with a 9B index scores 79.6%, 1.6 points above both ends at 0.6B, with unchanged query-side cost. Note that the full list of the 72 tasks is not public, so the scores cannot be independently reproduced.

1. Why late interaction, why distill

Retrievers usually trade off between single-vector ANN (fast, loses detail) and cross-encoders (strong, one pass per candidate, only for reranking). Late interaction sits in between: document token vectors are precomputed; at query time only query vectors are computed, then MaxSim. Storage is the cost, so this work compresses each token vector to 128-d.

The authors' other judgment: small models trained with contrastive learning alone are not strong enough; fitting a large model's token vectors works better. A side effect is that differently sized students distilled from the same teacher are interchangeable.

2. Training

2.1 18B teacher: two-stage contrastive learning

The teacher is Qwen3.5-27B with the last 20 layers dropped (18B) and causal masks removed so every token sees both sides. Training has two stages.

Stage 1 uses query–document pairs from 28 datasets, further split by language and domain into 981 subsets, 186M pairs total (88.3% text–text, 8.3% text–image, 3.4% text–screenshot); sampling weights change the mix to 56.5% / 30.9% / 12.6%. Each batch comes from one subset so in-batch negatives are harder. To hit target mix and even spacing, subsets are sampled with a golden-ratio quasi-random sequence rather than independent draws. Contrastive batch size is 16,384 pairs, LoRA rank 128; MaxSim is a Triton kernel to avoid materializing the token-level similarity matrix.

Stage 2 merges LoRA, adds a new rank-32 adapter, freezes vision, and trains only on text triples: each query with one positive and up to 4 hard negatives. Some hard negatives are synthesized by editing key fields in highly templated documents.

2.2 Students: token-wise fit to teacher vectors

Student loss is direct: for every valid query and document token, Euclidean distance between L2-normalized student and teacher vectors, averaged on the query side and document side then summed. The teacher is frozen.
L=∣Q∣1​(i,t)∈Q∑​∥qitS​−qitT​∥2​+∣D∣1​(i,t)∈D∑​∥ditS​−ditT​∥2​
Because the loss needs no in-batch negatives, a batch can mix subsets and gradients are stabler. The 9B student is based on Qwen3.5-9B; LoRA alone underfit, so the last 8 text layers are fully fine-tuned and the rest use LoRA. The 0.6B student is pruned from Qwen3.5-0.8B by dropping 2 of 3 Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers per block (594M total; 254M embedding, 100M vision; ~240M active on text) and is fully fine-tuned.

3. Experiments

3.1 Text retrieval

This checks whether the two distilled models beat same-size single-vector models on text. The domain suite has 72 public tasks (finance 18, law 20, medical 8, dialogue 5, tech 4, multilingual 17), nDCG@10, equal-weight average over six domains:

9B leads every domain except medical; 0.6B leads every domain among sub-1B models.

Q2D-Web is closer to Perplexity's online setting: ~70K agent-rewritten online search queries over 190M web pages, Recall@1000. Relevance merges three sources: documents the agent actually cited, documents ranked high by the online retriever, and LLM-judged relevant docs. On that merge, 9B and 0.6B score 74.8% and 73.6% versus 69.3% for the strongest baseline nemotron-3-embed-8b. This benchmark comes from Perplexity traffic; other models were not tuned for it.

3.2 Document screenshots and images

On images it is not fully dominant. On ViDoRe-V3, vision-specialized EVIE-8B (66.4%) and EVIE-4.5B (65.9%) are higher, but they store 4,096 and 2,048 dims per token, while pplx-embed-v2-late stores only 128-d. On MIRACL-Vision (Wikipedia screenshots) and PPLX-Q2I (Perplexity online image-search logs: 10K queries, 100K images), gemini-embedding-2 is higher.

3.3 Small-model query + large-model index

This checks whether the shared vector space is usable in deployment. Index documents with 9B; encode queries with 9B or 0.6B. 0.6B query + 9B docs beats both-ends-0.6B in all six domains, averaging 79.6% versus 78.0% (both-ends-9B is 81.3%). Query encoding cost matches pure 0.6B; document index cost is amortized over the index lifetime.

3.4 As the retriever for a search agent

BrowseComp+ lets GPT-OSS-120B act as an agent that repeatedly searches a fixed corpus with the tested retriever and answers complex questions, scored by another LLM. 9B accuracy is 64.0%, 4.9 points above another late-interaction model Reason-ModernColBERT and 8.7 above the best single-vector voyage-4-large; mean search count is also lower than every baseline, and recall is highest.

4. Limitations

No storage or latency numbers are given. Multi-vector indexes store a 128-d vector per token; how much more storage and MaxSim cost that is versus single-vector at web scale is unstated. The domain-task list is private, so scores cannot be reproduced. On image retrieval, specialized vision models and gemini-embedding-2 still win on some benchmarks. The claim that distillation beats pure contrastive learning—especially for small models—has no contrastive numbers in the body.

5. Takeaways

For retrieval teams, the most directly usable piece is "large model indexes, small model queries": document compute is paid once, query latency is 0.6B, and quality beats a pure small model by 1.6 points. The premise is that both ends are distilled from the same teacher; independently trained models cannot be mixed this way. The 0.6B text side has only ~240M active parameters; the authors argue it can run on-device. If you are evaluating multi-vector retrieval, measure storage on your own corpus first—that is the unanswered question in the report.

papers.title: OpenSaC: A Python Library for Search as Code in Deep Research Agents
papers.authors: Qi Liu, Jiaxin Mao, Fengbin Zhu, Tat-Seng Chua, Ji-Rong Wen
papers.summary: OpenSaC lets research agents write programs that combine search, reading, reranking, and local processing, returning selected evidence to the model. On BrowseComp, it cuts model-token use by 37.8%.
papers.key_insight: Process intermediate evidence in code and preserve source links for reuse. The library reduces repeated model reading, but requires an execution environment. WideSearch row F1 falls slightly, so efficiency gains do not guarantee better answers.

papers.title: FALCA: Falsification-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Hierarchical Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Deep Search Agents
papers.authors: Zijun Dou, Kun Luo, Chaofan Li, Shuqi Lu, Zheng Liu
papers.summary: Deep search can reinforce an early mistaken hypothesis. FALCA separates answer proposals from independent counterevidence searches and trains research-state revision with hierarchical credit. Its 4B model reaches 56.0% accuracy on BrowseComp.
papers.key_insight: Give counterevidence checking its own context. A useful falsification report names conflicting evidence and unmet constraints, giving the next search a specific gap to resolve.

papers.title: When Agentic Retrieval Fails Silently: Framework and Production Evidence from a Creative AI Assistant
papers.authors: Yan, Liang, Anuj Agarwal, Aditya Reddy Cheruku
papers.summary: CTR, MRR and behavioral NDCG assume the user sees and acts on ranked results. In an agentic assistant a generation layer consumes retrieval first, so attribution breaks on who saw the results, when the user acted, and what caused the outcome—Adobe calls this the attribution gap. LARA (Layered Agentic Retrieval Assessment) measures retrieval quality, engagement and downstream outcomes by layer; production retrieval rate on assistant prompts is only 0.31%, and chat users reformulate more than gallery users (44.4% vs 33.1%). ==Do not evaluate agent retrieval as if the user clicked a SERP—attribute by layer==.

deep_reading.content_html:
Adobe Express's template gallery search and its AI assistant run on the same retrieval system and serve the same users. Intuition says assistant users don't look at result lists, so they should reformulate queries less. In fact the chat entry point has a reformulation rate of 44.4%, against 33.1% for the gallery, 11 points higher. The reason is that "reformulation" means different things on the two sides. In the gallery, a user reformulates because the results were irrelevant and they try other words. In chat, most reformulations come after the user sees a generated result and wants to tweak it, such as "a bit bluer" or "use a bolder font". More surprising still, the assistant actually called retrieval on only 0.31% of prompts. The three Adobe authors call this the attribution gap: CTR, MRR and behavioral NDCG all assume the user saw a ranked list and acted on it, and in an AI assistant that assumption breaks in three directions at once. The paper's evaluation framework, LARA, uses three independent layers of measurement plus four log fields to give credit back to retrieval, without training any new model.

1. The problem: the agent reads first, the user comes later

The authors argue that the failure comes from three structural changes, none of which tuning can fix.

The first change is who looks at the results. In the gallery, a user searches "birthday invitation", scrolls through 40 templates and clicks one, and that click is a grade for retrieval. In the assistant, the user says they want a birthday invitation, a search sub-agent retrieves templates, and the agent picks one and turns it straight into a design; the user never sees the other 39. There may be no click at all, and what the user does see has already been filtered and reordered by the agent.

The second change is that action takes longer to arrive. The same asset may be retrieved in turn 1 and again in turn 3, and only exported in turn 5 or even in another session. The logs have no identifier linking that export to a particular retrieval, so timing alone cannot tell which retrieval deserves the credit.

The third change is that nobody can say what caused the outcome. When the result is bad, there is no way to tell whether retrieval or generation went wrong. When the result is good, the model may have quietly made up for a failed retrieval.

Without per-component instrumentation, teams can only watch session-level signals such as retries, abandonment and task completion. The authors point out that retries alone go wrong in both directions. They fire when generation fails for reasons that have nothing to do with retrieval, and they stay silent when the model covers for retrieval. That third case is the most dangerous, because in session-level signals it looks exactly like success.

2. Method: measure where a problem is first visible

LARA's principle is to measure each component's failures at the earliest point where they can be seen. So it has three layers; the higher the layer, the closer it is to product outcomes and the more it depends on the lineage fields described later.

Layer 1 asks only about retrieval itself: did the sub-agent return the right assets in the right order? The metrics are null rate, precision@1, precision@K and NDCG@K, computed at the moment retrieval fires from server-side logs with offline relevance labels (human or LLM judge), independent of what the user or agent does afterwards. CTR serves here only as a secondary directional signal. Only this layer can catch a retrieval failure that the model has masked.

Layer 2 asks whether what came back was actually used, and whether there are signs that retrieval was wrong. This layer counts positive evidence and failure evidence separately and reports them by "retrieval role". The retrieval role is written to the log at retrieval time and says what the retrieval was for: finding something directly, finding something to look at, finding something to act on, serving as a reference input for generation, being one step in a larger task, or depending on context. The layer has four metrics:

  • Genuine positive rate (GPR): the share of retrievals where, after the results were shown to the user, the user actively used a returned asset, for example by asking a follow-up about it, or by selecting, editing or exporting it.
  • Agent consumption rate (ACR): the share of retrievals where the agent used a returned asset within the same request, before the user received anything, for example when a user asks in one sentence for a logo with the background removed. This also counts as positive evidence, but it is tracked separately, because it reflects only the agent's judgment; the user's later action is the independent confirmation.
  • Observable retrieval failure rate (ORF): the share of retrievals followed by one of three retrieval-specific signals. The first is the user saying the retrieved object or path is wrong. The second is searching again for the same unresolved need. The third is the agent using something else when the flow should have used the returned asset. When the user keeps the asset and only modifies the edit or the generated result, that is a "downstream correction" and does not count as a retrieval failure. 1−ORF should be reported alongside GPR and ACR, but it must not be treated as satisfaction.
  • Unobserved outcome rate (UOR): the share of retrievals with neither evidence of use nor a failure signal. It is its own category, counted as neither abandonment nor success.

Layer 3 asks whether the user reached their goal. In a creative tool the clearest signals are export, share and download. Task completion is defined per retrieval role, and whether the goal was reached needs an LLM judge or human labels. Only when these success events can be linked back, through the lineage fields, to the retrieval that supplied the asset does this layer become a signal about retrieval; otherwise it only reflects overall product health.

3. Read two layers together, then add four log fields

Reading Layer 1 and Layer 2 side by side tells you which component went wrong:

Layer 1Layer 2Diagnosis
LowHigh ORFRetrieval returned the wrong assets
HighLow ORF, many downstream correctionsAssets were fine; generation failed
HighHigh ORF (agent rejection)The agent bypassed good results (parametric knowledge leaking in)
LowORF near zeroA silent retrieval failure masked by the model

The last row is the most dangerous. Without Layer 1 this failure is completely invisible; with Layer 1 it shows up the moment retrieval fires, with no need to wait for user complaints to pile up.

For Layers 2 and 3 to work, the logs must be able to link actions back to retrievals. Today Adobe's production logs have no field shared by retrieval events and action events, and the authors propose four fields to close the gap. The first is a unique retrieval_id on every retrieval. The second is returned_asset_ids, the full ranked list at the moment retrieval fires, recorded before the generation layer filters or reorders it; this field alone makes Layer 1 computable, so it is the single change with the best payoff.
