The third is a consumed_asset_id on every action event, whether the action comes from the user or from an agent tool call. The fourth is a source_retrieval_id on the same event, pointing to the retrieval that supplied the asset; for an asset already placed in the document, the field is inherited from the placement event.

All four are additions to logging, not predictive models. Because source_retrieval_id points to a retrieval rather than a session, attribution stays clear even when the same asset is retrieved again over several turns or exported in a new session. Together the four fields can also recover the rank of the asset that was actually used within the retrieval results, independent of the order finally shown to the user. That lets RAG evaluation frameworks such as RAGAs and ARES use direct attribution instead of guessing from timing.

One example ties the four fields together. A user says in chat, "Find a birthday invitation template and change the title to Xiaoming's 6th birthday." The retrieval event records retrieval_id=r1 and 20 candidates. The agent picks the fourth one and changes the title; this is an agent event carrying consumed_asset_id and source_retrieval_id=r1, and it counts toward ACR. Two days later the user exports from the editor, and the export event inherits r1, counting as a "retrieval-attributed export" in Layer 3. Without these fields, the export would land in another session and the original chat session would be counted as abandoned.

4. Production data from Adobe Express

The authors analyzed production sessions from August 2026. LARA's lineage fields are not live yet, so every "was it used" number below is inferred from timing. Session, user and query counts are withheld under Adobe's disclosure policy; the paper says only that gallery volume is roughly 8–9 times the assistant's.

The data confirms the points from Section 1 in three ways. The first is that the agent reads first. The assistant's overall CTR is close to zero because 99.7% of interactions never called retrieval at all, so there is not even a denominator. When retrieval does fire, it behaves normally: the null rate is 1.51%, and users click about 1.05 times per returned result grid. Testing directly whether the agent used the results would need ACR, which cannot be computed yet.

The second is delayed action. Assistant sessions average 2.04 prompts, and the chat entry point averages 2.65, with the same asset reappearing in later turns. An export started from chat is logged under a different session_guid once the user leaves the chat interface. Session-level attribution then counts those users as abandoning, so the chat abandonment rate (59.5%) is overstated and engagement is understated.

The third is that retrieval and generation are mixed together. The reformulation inversion from the opening is the example: one behavioral signal mixes retrieval failures with tweaks to generated results, so the aggregate number says nothing. LARA splits it in two: "search reformulation", counted only on retrieval turns, and "downstream correction", counted on the other turns.

With current logs, the team can compute only the null rate and clicks per grid today. Precision@K and NDCG@K also need returned_asset_ids and a labeled sample. GPR, ACR, ORF and UOR need the other three fields plus the retrieval role, and for now can only be obtained by labeling traces by hand. In other words, the team can confirm that retrieval works when it fires, but cannot yet confirm whether the user or the agent actually used what came back.

5. A surprise: retrieval is almost never called

Gallery search is retrieval by definition, while the assistant called retrieval on only 0.31% of prompts; about 82% of assistant activity is generative editing with no corresponding search scenario at all. The authors think the bigger risk may be missed retrieval: the planner routes "help me find a birthday invitation template" to generative editing, no retrieval event is created, and Layer 1 has nothing to score. Table 3 shows 10.7% of chat prompts with retrieval intent; this number is only directional. But if it does reflect intent rather than actual triggering, the gap between it and 0.31% is a first estimate of missed retrieval.

The authors call planner routing Layer 0 and treat it as an extension of LARA rather than a fourth layer. It has two metrics. The misroute rate is the share of retrieval calls whose prompt was not actually in scope for retrieval; those calls should be removed from Layer 1. The missed-retrieval rate is the share of prompts with retrieval intent that did not trigger retrieval, which needs ground-truth intent labels. In a sample of 273 prompts, about 5–7% contained two or more distinct retrieval intents, so routing also has to be able to split multi-intent requests.

6. Limitations and practical value

The limitations the authors list are concrete. All the evidence comes from one deployment, and the 0.31% figure and the reformulation inversion may be specific to a creative assistant dominated by generative editing. None of the lineage fields is live, so every Layer 2 number is inferred from timing, and the retrieval roles were inferred after the fact rather than recorded at retrieval time. The chat abandonment rate is overstated by cross-session exports. The data was not validated for schema or value ranges, and synthetic traffic was removed by hand. Latency and tokens per successful task were not instrumented by stage either. LARA covers only the retrieval component; how the agent understands intent, generates queries and splits multi-intent requests needs separate instrumentation. This is a short industry paper, and the framework has not been validated across multiple deployments or in online experiments.

The authors' three lessons for practitioners are useful. First, do not use the assistant's overall CTR or reformulation rate as retrieval metrics: retrieval metrics should be counted only on turns where retrieval fired, and reformulations should be split into search reformulations and downstream corrections. Second, start by logging the full ranked list when retrieval fires; only this field makes Layer 1 computable. Third, define "the user actively used it" once and publish the definition: in Express chat, the effective action rate ranges from 7.6% to 40.5% depending on which behaviors are counted, so without a shared definition the numbers cannot be compared. For teams embedding search into an agent, the paper's biggest reminder is that when retrieval is called on only 0.31% of prompts, the question is not only whether it ranks well, but whether it gets called at all.

papers.title: Chunk Recomputation under Real Document Revisions: Measuring Update Cost and Retrieval Quality of Fixed, Recursive, and Content-Defined Chunking
papers.authors: Yuning Bian, Lele Xu, Yifan Yuan, Xinyu Yin, Chengyan Zhan
papers.summary: RAG chunking schemes are usually compared on one static corpus, but knowledge bases keep changing. Each chunk is embedded on its own, so when an edit moves a chunk boundary, unchanged text must be re-embedded too. The authors measure this on 120 pairs of adjacent Chinese and English Wikipedia revisions, reusing an old vector only when a chunk's embedding input is byte-identical: non-overlapping fixed-size chunking recomputes 57–68% of the new version's embedding input, paragraph-first recursive chunking 38–56%, and content-defined chunking (CDC, which picks cut points from local text fingerprints) 43–54%, while evidence recall under a 2048-token retrieval budget differs by less than 2 percentage points among the three. When 1% of text is inserted at the start of an article, fixed-size chunking recomputes everything, ==because every window after the insertion point shifts, so no chunk matches the old version==. For knowledge bases that change often, ==a chunker's recompute fraction should be reported alongside its retrieval quality==.

deep_reading.content_html:
Chunking schemes for RAG are almost always compared on one static corpus, yet the documents in a knowledge base keep changing. Each chunk is embedded on its own, so if an edit moves a chunk boundary, the chunks on either side become new embedding inputs even when not a single word in them changed. This 6-page short paper measures that update cost directly: the authors take 120 pairs of adjacent revisions of Chinese and English Wikipedia articles, allow an old vector to be reused only when a chunk's complete embedding input is byte-identical to one in the old version, and compare three chunking methods with a frozen BGE-M3 encoder. On the 116 articles where all three methods succeed, non-overlapping fixed-size chunking recomputes 57–68% of the new version's embedding input, paragraph-first recursive chunking 38–56%, and content-defined chunking (CDC) 43–54%; under a 2048-token retrieval budget, the three differ in evidence recall by less than 2 percentage points within each language. Fixed-size chunking shifts everything after the insertion point, so none of the downstream windows can match the old version, which is why it recomputes the most. Which of recursive chunking and CDC is cheaper flips as the chunk-length parameters change.

1. Why measure update cost

An English article had only 0.13% of its text edited, yet fixed-size chunking recomputed 49% of its embedding input while paragraph-first chunking recomputed only 8%. This example from the paper's dataset shows that the amount edited and the amount recomputed can be far apart, and the gap is determined by the chunking rule.

For a knowledge base that is continually updated, the amount recomputed maps directly to embedding compute and to writes into the vector index. Earlier chunking evaluations only compared retrieval quality, but two schemes with similar retrieval quality can differ a lot in update cost: on the English articles in this paper, fixed-size chunking's mean recompute fraction is 1.5 times that of paragraph-first chunking (57% vs 38%). The authors want to answer three questions: how much each of the three chunking methods must recompute; whether that amount is driven by edit size, edit position or cut-point rules; and whether the scheme that recomputes less also retrieves worse.

2. Measurement

The reuse rule is strict: a chunk's complete embedding input (its text plus the encoder's special tokens) must be byte-identical to the input of some chunk in the old version for the old vector to be reused; a single differing character makes it a new input. The cache holds only the previous version of the same document and does not match across documents. The recompute fraction is defined as:
Rc​=∑x∈Uc​(Dnew​)​T(x)∑x∈Mc​​T(x)​
Here Uc​(Dnew​) is the set of distinct embedding inputs that chunking method c produces on the new version, Mc​ is the part of it not found in the old version's cache, and $T(x)$ is the number of input tokens of chunk x. Rc​=0 means everything is reused and Rc​=1 means everything is recomputed. The authors also run a no-edit control: chunking the same version twice must give Rc​=0, otherwise it counts as a pipeline failure.

All three chunking methods see only the current version and fixed parameters, never how the old version was chunked:

  • Fixed-size chunking: greedily cuts non-overlapping windows of at most 304 tokens.
  • Recursive chunking: splits any span longer than the 400-token target, preferring blank lines, then line breaks, then sentence-ending punctuation, and falls back to fixed windows only when none works; it then greedily packs the small units up to the target length.
  • CDC: uses the Steadlith implementation, which computes Rabin rolling fingerprints over the word sequence and places a cut wherever the fingerprint meets a condition, with chunk lengths limited to 176–352 tokens. The method was originally built for file-system deduplication; cut points depend only on nearby content, so inserting bytes near the front of a file does not move the cut points after it.

The chunk-length parameters of the three methods were tuned in advance so that their median chunk lengths are close (the actual maximum ratio is 1.17).

Retrieval quality is measured as follows: each article has two questions, 240 in total, and annotators mark on each version the character spans that answer the question. At retrieval time a batch of articles is put into one candidate pool, chunks are ranked by dot product, and whole chunks are packed into a 2048-token budget in rank order; recall is 1 if the packed chunks cover one complete evidence set.

3. Experiments

3.1 Main result: fixed-size chunking recomputes the most, recall differs little

This experiment answers how much each method must recompute and whether retrieval quality differs. The authors average the recompute fraction and evidence recall with fixed parameters over the 116 articles where all three methods succeed (paper Table I):

LanguageChunkingRecompute fractionEvidence recallMedian chunk length (tokens)
ChineseFixed-size68.4%97.4%304
ChineseRecursive55.7%98.3%356
ChineseCDC54.0%98.3%314
EnglishFixed-size57.4%96.7%304
EnglishRecursive37.9%96.8%342
EnglishCDC42.8%95.0%291

Paired by article, recursive chunking recomputes 12.7 percentage points less than fixed-size chunking (Chinese, 95% interval −19.7 to −6.2) and 19.6 points less (English); CDC recomputes 14.4 and 14.7 points less than fixed-size chunking. Paired differences in recall range from −1.9 to +0.9 points, with all intervals including or touching 0. The authors state explicitly that these intervals cannot rule out a drop in recall and do not prove equivalence, so they do not rank the methods by recall.

Recursive chunking's advantage is smaller in Chinese than in English because of its cut-point rules: Chinese sentence-ending punctuation is usually not followed by a space, so overly long Chinese paragraphs cannot be cut at sentence boundaries and fall back to fixed windows.

The smaller the edit, the larger the gap. On the 28 English articles with small edits (at most 5% edited), fixed-size chunking recomputes 46% on average, recursive chunking 25% and CDC 27%; on the 23 Chinese small-edit articles the figures are 62%, 45% and 36%. When more than 50% is edited, all three must recompute 60–90%.

3.2 Edit position: why fixed-size chunking recomputes so much

This experiment tests whether "boundary shift" is the main source of recomputation. It changes only one variable: the same 1% insertion is placed at the start, middle or end of the article, with everything else unchanged. Result: fixed-size chunking falls from 100% for an insertion at the start to about 12% for one at the end, because every window after the insertion point moves back by the length of the insertion and no downstream chunk can be reused. Recursive chunking and CDC stay below 30% at all three positions, as paragraph breaks and content-fingerprint cut points realign quickly after the edit.

The authors also run a verbatim check: how much of the recomputed input is text that already exists unchanged in the old version. On English articles, 50% of the tokens fixed-size chunking recomputes are text present verbatim in the old version, 33% for CDC and 12% for recursive chunking (47%, 45% and 37% in Chinese). This text was not changed at all; it was only cut into different chunks, so recomputing it is caused entirely by the cut-point rule.

3.3 Whether recursive chunking or CDC is cheaper depends on parameters

This experiment checks whether the ranking of the two content-aware methods is stable. Without retuning, the authors try 6 target chunk lengths between 256 and 496 tokens for each method and compare paired settings whose median-length ratio is at most 1.15. Result: the CDC-minus-recursive recompute difference ranges from −2.4 to +6.2 points in English and from −0.7 to +5.5 in Chinese, flipping sign in both languages. For example, in English raising recursive chunking's target length from 400 to 448 raises its recompute fraction from 37.9% to 46.2%, while CDC at the same 448 is 43.8%. The reason is that recursive chunking packs several small paragraphs into one chunk; once an edit changes one paragraph's length, the packing of several following paragraphs can change too, and the larger the target length, the farther this chain reaction propagates. Fixed-size chunking recomputes the most in every setting.

The authors checked the cost once more on the arXivEdits paper-revision data: the mean recompute fractions of fixed-size, recursive and CDC chunking are 94.5%, 81.4% and 80.2%, with fixed-size still highest. The text-extraction noise of this dataset is unquantified, so it serves only as side evidence on cost.

3.4 Overlapping windows are not the fix

A common remedy is to let adjacent fixed windows overlap by 32 or 64 tokens. The result is a recompute fraction within 1.3 points of the non-overlapping version, 10–26% more total embedding input, and English recall down by 3.0 and 3.9 points, because the duplicated text uses up the 2048-token retrieval budget.

4. Limitations

The authors list these limitations: Wikipedia is the only source; the annotations of the 240 questions were not independently adjudicated by multiple people, and when the authors spot-checked 60 labels themselves, 57 agreed; the median chunk-length ratio of the three methods is 1.17, above the preset 1.15; only one encoder is used; and the related method KARA was not run. CDC failed on 4 Chinese articles because CDC splits words on spaces, so a long run of Chinese text without spaces is treated as a single unit of 403–550 tokens, exceeding the 352 maximum.

Two further points deserve attention. First, all three methods recovered all the evidence in 105 of the 116 articles, and recall is generally above 95%, close to the ceiling, so this retrieval setup cannot distinguish small quality differences between methods. Second, the recompute fraction measures embedding input and is not converted into latency or cost; if embedding is a small part of the whole update pipeline, for example when index rebuilding or review costs more, a gap of a few tens of percentage points is diluted in the total cost.

5. Practical implications

First, if a knowledge base is edited often and in small amounts, do not use non-overlapping fixed-size chunking. Switching to paragraph-first recursive chunking takes the mean recompute fraction on English articles from 57% to 38%, and from 46% to 25% on small-edit articles, with retrieval recall essentially unchanged. The precondition is to use the byte-identical input as the cache key, so that vectors are reused whenever the text has not changed.

Second, when evaluating chunking schemes, report the recompute fraction together with retrieval quality, and measure both under your own chunk-length parameters. The ranking of recursive chunking and CDC flips with parameters, so no ranking in the paper can be carried over as is. For Chinese corpora, check whether the cut-point rules rely on spaces; otherwise recursive chunking falls back to fixed windows and CDC fails outright.

papers.title: EG-GRPO: Evidence-Guided Step-level Credit Assignment for Deep Search Agents
papers.authors: Sijia Luo, Mengjie Gao, Yuxiao He, Mengshu Sun, Cuiping Li, Hong Chen, Jing Zhang
papers.summary: EG-GRPO rewards the first search step that finds support for a required claim, then compares actions from similar evidence states. The 4B agent reaches 45.9% accuracy on GAIA.
papers.key_insight: Reward newly acquired evidence rather than repeated citations. Conditioning comparisons on what an agent already knows reduces unfair comparisons between early and nearly finished trajectories; fallback grouping handles sparse state matches.

papers.title: Grounded Credit Assignment in Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Search Agents
papers.authors: Qirui Liu, Hao Chen, Yi Wen, Weijie Shi, Yao Zhao, Xianhe Chen, Hao Zhao, Xing Tang, Weihong Luo, Yuyu Luo
papers.summary: A search agent can answer correctly without using retrieved evidence. Grounded Credit Assignment separates credit for finding evidence from credit for answering. On the larger evaluated model, it improves average exact match over Search-R1 by 6.3 percentage points.
papers.key_insight: Reward evidence acquisition separately from answer correctness. Otherwise, a lucky answer from memory credits the entire retrieval trace and can improve accuracy while weakening grounding. The proposed correction uses verifiable sub-outcomes without an extra reward model.

papers.title: Directional Posterior Feedback Fusion for Query Reformulation in Dense Retrieval
papers.authors: Yiteng Tu, Qingyi Pan, Weihang Su, Jiaxin Mao, Yiqun Liu, Qingyao Ai
papers.summary: When rewriting a query vector with first-round retrieved documents or an LLM-written hypothetical answer (HyDE), the usual approach averages feedback vectors and interpolates with the original query. DIFF argues that ==each piece of feedback only supports correcting the query along one direction, so other directions should not be pulled back by it==: it subtracts the component parallel to the original query to get each feedback's rotation direction and magnitude, constrains only the projection of the correction onto that direction, weights by query–feedback similarity and group agreement, and solves a K×K linear system—without training any model. On 14 BEIR subsets, bge-base with HyDE rises from 0.5492 to 0.5717 mean NDCG@10; with retrieved-document feedback, vector averaging falls to 0.5045 while DIFF scores 0.5522.

deep_reading.content_html:
In vector retrieval, short queries often under-specify intent. A common fix is to gather feedback text—top documents from a first-round search, or an LLM-written hypothetical answer (HyDE)—and use it to update the query vector. Most methods average the feedback vectors or linearly interpolate with the original query, treating each feedback as "what the new query should look like" and pulling the query toward it as a whole. Tsinghua's DIFF argues that this causes interference: each piece of feedback usually supports correcting the query along only one direction; other directions carry no information from it, yet are still pulled back. DIFF first extracts the direction each feedback adds beyond the original query, requires the corrected query to agree with the feedback only along that direction, weights constraints by feedback quality, adds a "do not drift too far from the original" term, and has a closed-form solution that needs no training. On 14 BEIR subsets, 3 retrievers, and 4 feedback sources, DIFF's mean NDCG@10 is best or tied for best in 12 of 12 settings, but with first-round retrieved documents as feedback it barely improves over the unfeedbacked query.

1. Treating feedback as target points loses complementary information

Let the original query be q and the correction proposed by feedback i relative to q be ei​=ℓi​ui​, with unit direction ui​ and magnitude ℓi​. Pointwise fitting minimizes ∥δ−ℓi​ui​∥2. The authors split it:
∥δ−ℓi​ui​∥2=(ui⊤​δ−ℓi​)2+∥(I−ui​ui⊤​)δ∥2
The first term asks δ's component along ui​ to equal ℓi​—desired. The second penalizes δ on every other direction, which may be exactly what other feedback supports. Example: query "apple event"; one feedback doc is about a new phone, another about a new laptop; pointwise fitting pulls the query halfway between them and travels only halfway on each direction.

They prove that under the same weights, directional constraints yield a correction magnitude at least as large as pointwise fitting, with equality only when all feedback directions are collinear; when feedback directions are pairwise orthogonal, pointwise fitting dilutes each direction's correction by the other feedbacks' weights.

2. Method: four steps

Step 1: new direction per feedback. All vectors are L2-normalized on the unit sphere. For feedback fi​, compute similarity si​=q⊤fi​, then subtract the component parallel to q to get ri​=fi​−si​q. Direction ui​ is where this feedback wants to rotate the query; length ℓi​ equals the sine of their angle—how much new content it adds.

Step 2: credibility per feedback. Credibility τi​=g⋅ai​ has two layers. Per-item quality ai​: standardize the si​ values under the same query by median and MAD, then pass through a sigmoid, so feedback closer to the query weighs more without depending on absolute similarity scales across models. Group credibility g: mean of all correction vectors μ, then compare ∥μ∥2 to dispersion around that mean; g is high when directions agree and low when they conflict, then multiplied by mean per-item quality.

Step 3: jointly solve for the correction. The objective keeps only each feedback's own-direction constraint plus a penalty on correction size:
δ∗=argδmin​ 2λ​∥δ∥2+21​i∑​τi​(ui⊤​δ−ℓi​)2
It has a closed form: solve a K×K linear system (K feedbacks, 5 in the main experiment), cost O(K2D+K3) for dimension D.

Step 4: map back to the sphere. The final rotation angle is the min of ∥δ∗∥ and "g × max allowed angle", then q′=cosϕq+sinϕδ∗/∥δ∗∥. When the group is untrustworthy, g is small and the query barely moves.

3. Experiments

Setup: 14 BEIR subsets (ArguAna, FEVER, HotpotQA, MSMARCO, NQ, SciFact, TREC-COVID, …), three retrievers bge-base-en-v1.5, e5-base-v2, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B. Feedback is either the top-K first-round documents (PRF) or three Qwen3.8-27B generations (HyDE hypothetical docs, Q2D query expansion, CoT reasoning). All methods share the same encoder, the same feedback, and the same index—only fusion differs. Baselines include vector averaging (VPRF), concatenate-and-reencode (Concat-P/L), orthogonal-component OR-PRF, dimension-weighted DIME and Eclipse, and AnchorQE which needs extra retrieval to estimate weights.

3.1 Main results

This checks whether DIFF beats other fusion methods across retrievers and feedback sources. Mean NDCG@10 over 14 subsets; parentheses are the unfeedbacked query:

Two results stand out. First, with retrieved-document feedback, simple averaging (VPRF) pulls scores below the original query—on BGE from 0.5492 to 0.5045; DIFF in that column merely does not lose: 0.5522 on BGE, 0.5252 on E5, 0.5491 on Qwen, barely changing versus the original. Second, with LLM-generated feedback every method gains; DIFF reaches 0.5717 on BGE with HyDE and 0.5777 on Qwen. It is close to AnchorQE (0.5717 vs 0.5700 on BGE + HyDE) but needs no extra retrieval for weights.

3.2 Ablations

This checks whether directional constraints and credibility weighting are each necessary. On BGE, remove or replace one part at a time:

Switching back to pointwise fitting is among the largest drops, directly supporting the paper's core claim: constraining each feedback only along its own direction beats pulling the query toward feedback as a whole. Dropping per-item quality under HyDE falls from 0.5717 to 0.5481—generated hypothetical docs vary in quality and must be treated differently.

3.3 Feedback count

As K grows from 1 to 20, VPRF drops quickly under retrieved-document feedback because later documents are noisier. DIFF stays stable across K; the authors attribute this to group credibility shrinking the correction when feedback becomes mixed.

4. Limitations

The main-table point: with first-round retrieved documents as feedback, DIFF barely beats the unfeedbacked query and is slightly worse on Qwen (0.5491 vs 0.5492). Its value is mainly "not being dragged down by noise" and "using generated feedback well." Experiments are only on BEIR with retrievers up to 0.6B; production-scale corpora and larger embedding models are untested. Group credibility and max rotation angle have hyperparameters whose sensitivity is not analyzed in the body.

5. Takeaways

If you already use HyDE or query expansion and average the encoded text with the original query, consider DIFF: it depends only on vectors, needs no training and no extra retrieval, and solves one 5×5 linear system per query. If feedback is first-round retrieval, this paper's results say gains are limited—at least confirm that averaging is not already hurting metrics.

papers.title: Let Agents Design How They Search: Automatic Interface Optimization for Agentic Search
papers.authors: Sangjune An, Jaeyoon Jung, Yumin Choi, Jinheon Baek, Junmo Cho, Sung Ju Hwang, Hae Beom Lee
papers.summary: Korea University and KAIST have Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) design retrieval tools for a search agent: it reads each question's execution log and score, jointly edits pre-generated index files, executable search scripts, and usage instructions, and after 10 rounds keeps the best version on the optimization set. With GPT-5.4-nano as the search agent, BrowseComp-Plus accuracy rises from DCI's 71.6% to 78.4%, and mean nDCG@10 on four BRIGHT subsets from 45.7 to 55.0. Prompt-only optimization reaches 75.6% and 52.0, ==so the rest of the gain comes from the generated index files and search scripts==; handing the interface unchanged to Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite still beats DCI (73.9% vs 60.9%).

deep_reading.content_html:
When an LLM agent searches a document corpus, the tools it may use, how the corpus is pre-organized, and how the prompt teaches it to use those tools together form the "search interface." Today's interfaces are hand-designed and shared across corpora—for example DCI gives the agent a shell and lets it grep/cat raw documents. Korea University and KAIST's SearchWeaver has another coding agent (Claude Code + Claude Opus 5.5) design that interface automatically: it reads the search agent's full execution log and per-question scores, finds failure causes, then edits three things at once—pre-generated index files, executable search scripts, and the search agent's usage instructions—reruns, scores, and loops for 10 rounds. With GPT-5.4-nano as the search agent, BrowseComp-Plus accuracy rises from DCI's 71.6% to 78.4%, and mean nDCG@10 on four BRIGHT subsets from 45.7 to 55.0; the optimized interface handed unchanged to Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite also beats DCI.

1. One interface does not fit every corpus

Recent agentic retrieval methods all work on a fixed interface: RAG returns retriever passages; DCI lets the agent shell through raw docs; DR-DCI first vector-retrieves docs into a workspace then browses; RISE bounds a restricted workspace and adds model-generated tables of contents. Paper Table 1 shows relative ranking flips by corpus: DR-DCI beats DCI on BrowseComp-Plus (73.1% vs 71.6%) but loses on BRIGHT (42.1 vs 45.7). The authors conclude the interface should be designed for the specific corpus and model.

2. Method: let a coding agent iteratively edit the interface

2.1 What an interface contains

A candidate interface has three parts:

  • Pre-generated files: one-time processing of the whole corpus before any question arrives—for example a title→path index reused by every question.
  • Executable tools: Python scripts that may call provided BM25 and vector retrieval, restrict search to a subdirectory, or merge the agent's document judgments with retrieval ranks.
  • Usage instructions: instructions for the search agent on when to use which tool and how to verify clues.

Candidates may also replace the search agent's base system prompt and context-management policy. The search agent's model weights stay fixed.

2.2 Optimization loop

The designer is Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5). Each round it inspects the corpus and all prior candidates, writes a new interface; the new interface runs on the optimization questions and returns per-question scores plus full execution logs (commands, tool returns, final answer). Gold document IDs for optimization questions are also given to the designer to separate "not found" from "found but not recognized." Every candidate's outcome is kept for later reference regardless of quality. After 10 rounds, the interface with the best mean optimization-set score is evaluated on held-out test questions that never enter the designer's feedback.

3. Experiments

Setup. BrowseComp-Plus (BCP) answers multi-clue questions over a fixed web corpus, judged by GPT-4.1: 30 optimization / 800 test questions. BRIGHT is reasoning-heavy document retrieval on biology, earth science, economics, and robotics: 213 optimization / 210 test questions, scored by nDCG@10. Each corpus gets its own optimized interface. Retrieval resources for the designer: BM25 + Qwen3-Embedding-4B on BCP; BM25 + ReasonEmbed-Qwen3-8B rankings on BRIGHT.

3.1 Main results

This checks whether corpus-optimized interfaces beat fixed interfaces on both benchmarks and every subset:

Optimized strategies differ by corpus: biology restricts retrieval to a topic directory; earth science calls retrieval only when building the final ranking; economics and robotics fold the agent's document judgments into ranking—via document order for the former and relevance grades for the latter.

3.2 Tool time

Per-question tool time (excluding model inference) also falls versus DCI: BCP from 42.4 s to 32.9 s, BRIGHT from 63.2 s to 36.6 s. From the figure, RISE and DR-DCI use even less tool time; SearchWeaver spends more tool time for higher scores, and the authors place it on the Pareto front among evaluated methods.

3.3 Is prompt-only enough?

This checks whether gains come from generated files and tools, not only better prompts. Two variants: the same loop but only prompts may change (Prompt Optimization); and SearchWeaver's final interface with generated files, tools, and matching instructions removed, without re-optimizing.

Prompt-only also gains clearly and even beats SearchWeaver on the economics subset (41.8 vs 38.3). Overall, adding files and tools is better; removing them falls back near DCI.

3.4 Does it transfer across models?

This checks whether the interface reuses across models. The GPT-5.4-nano-optimized interface is handed unchanged to Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite: BCP accuracy 73.9% (DCI 60.9%), BRIGHT mean nDCG@10 58.8 (DCI 50.7), and BRIGHT per-question tool time from 23.1 s to 15.5 s. It works without re-optimization, so a substantial part of what was optimized belongs to the corpus itself, not only to model-specific tricks.

4. Limitations

Experiments use a static corpus. Whether pre-generated indexes and dependent tools must be refreshed after document adds/deletes, and whether updates can be incremental, is explicitly unstudied. BCP optimizes on only 30 questions; overfitting to those 30 is not analyzed. Each optimization round has the designer (Claude Opus 5.5) read full execution logs and the search agent rerun the optimization set—that cost is unreported.

5. Takeaways

For teams building internal knowledge-base QA agents, this gives an operable loop: take a small set of questions with gold answers and let a coding agent generate index files and retrieval scripts from execution logs, rather than only tuning prompts. The ablation where prompt-only raises BCP from 71.6% to 75.6% is also useful—when resources are limited, start with cheap prompt optimization. If the corpus changes often, design your own index maintenance.

papers.title: ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training
papers.authors: Leo Fan, Hongyang Wang, Wenbo Chen, Jingguo Liu, Xian Li, Xuan Wang, Ruochen Wen, Yiming Yan, Hao Wu, Yichuan Li, Qian Q...
papers.summary: LLM training throughput hinges on the recipe—sharding, memory–compute trade-offs, kernels and overlap—and that recipe changes with every model, accelerator and framework. Fixed-knob tuners only search a preset space and check that a job runs, so they miss levers outside that space and can silently change training semantics. Amazon’s ATTUNE is a coding agent that retunes any working recipe unattended inside a GPU-hour budget. On H100/H200/B200 it lifts throughput 1.7× on average and beats four of NVIDIA AutoModel’s published recipes by 6–17%; on held-out models it improves recipes written for another setting by up to 2.6× (MiniMax-M2). ==Throughput gaps often live outside the fixed knob space—letting a coding agent edit the recipe beats grid search==.

deep_reading.content_html:
Before training a large model, engineers have to settle on a "training recipe": how the model is split across tens or hundreds of GPUs, how much computation to trade for memory when memory runs short, which low-level compute routines to use, and how data transfers between GPUs overlap with computation. Move the same model to a different GPU or framework version, and the recipe that used to be fastest often no longer is. Amazon built a system called ATTUNE that lets an AI agent able to write code and run commands tune recipes: give it a recipe that runs and a budget of GPU-hours, and it tries things, analyses bottlenecks and keeps going on its own, with no one watching. But the real point of the paper lies outside the agent: a "correctness gate" run by fixed code the agent cannot change, which rejects before launch any change that would quietly alter what is being trained. After Amazon's fine-tuning jobs for three in-house models switched to the tuned recipes, training ran on average 1.7 times as fast as before, and up to 3.9 times.

1. The problem: existing auto-tuners either cannot find the answer or "break" the training

A training recipe has many "levers" that can be adjusted. The most important is how the model is split: each layer's matrices can be cut up across several cards, different layers can be given to different cards that pass work along like a pipeline, or the data can be split so that several groups of cards each compute one share. There is more: when memory is short, whether to discard intermediate results and recompute them when needed (trading compute for memory); whether to park some data in CPU memory; which version of the attention routine to use.

Existing auto-tuners fall roughly into three kinds. The first picks from a pre-listed set of options using a formula that estimates performance. The second is "black-box" search, such as Bayesian optimisation: it does not understand how the system works, it just runs trial after trial and decides what to try next from the results, but each trial is expensive. The third is the recent kind of large-model tuner, such as OptiCo, which can read performance analyses but likewise only adjusts a fixed list of knobs.

Two observations by the authors shaped ATTUNE's design.

First, part of the speed a stock recipe leaves on the table is hidden in combinations of levers that only help when changed together, and part in levers that the fixed list does not include at all, such as switching to a different routine for distributing data among cards.

Second, some settings quietly change what is being trained, while training still finishes without errors. Two examples. In "mixture-of-experts" models, each input word is sent to a few "expert" sub-networks. A common speed-up parameter caps how many words each expert handles, and words over the cap are simply dropped and not trained on. Another parameter, judging by its name, only "sends gradients at lower precision", but in fact it also makes gradient accumulation low-precision. A tuner that only checks "does it run" would hand both settings over as "optimisations", and the trained model would differ from the original.

2. Method: the agent searches, fixed code judges

One tuning job is called a "campaign": one fixed model, one cluster, a fixed number of GPUs. Every candidate recipe trains exactly the same thing: model, data, length of each example, examples per step and numeric precision stay the same, and every run even reads the same data in the same order. Each trial runs a fixed number of steps; the first few are warm-up and not scored, and after that the score is the average number of words each GPU processes per second.

Speed measurements are noisy, so first one has to decide "how much faster counts as really faster". The original recipe runs at least 5 times on different machines to get its average speed and its spread. A new candidate must beat the current fastest by more than one spread (at least 3%) to replace it. That way a run that happened to be fast is not mistaken for a real improvement.

The agent uses only ordinary tools: reading and writing files (including the training framework's source code), running commands, and calling the cluster's interface. A written "tuning code of practice" sets it six rules; the three most important are:

  • before every launch, write down a hypothesis: which bottleneck to ease, why it should work, and how much faster it should be;
  • change only one lever at a time, or one set of splitting choices that must change together, so the result can be attributed;
  • before using a parameter, read its implementation in the framework source to see whether it quietly changes other parameters too, and record the code location in the ledger.

When the bottleneck is unclear, the agent runs a performance analysis: a fixed analysis program splits each training step's time into computation, data transfer between GPUs, work on the CPU side, and idle waiting, telling the agent where time is mainly being wasted.

Spending is policed by fixed code. An accounting script counts from the moment the cluster allocates machines until they are released, including failed runs and runs used for checks, and nothing launches if the budget is not enough. Re-running a failed recipe unchanged is also refused, forcing the agent to find the cause before changing it.

The correctness gate has two steps, and it is the heart of the system.

The first step happens before launch: compare all parameters and environment variables that finally take effect in the candidate and in the original recipe. Final values are compared because one parameter may quietly change others. Every change is looked up in a register that the agent cannot edit. Changes that alter what is trained (data, examples per step, optimiser, loss function, routing, numeric precision), or that trigger known software defects, are rejected outright. Changes that alter only "how it is computed" and not "what is computed", such as a different way of placing data on GPUs, are passed outright. Anything not in the register is passed on to the second step and written into the report for a person to review.

The second step happens after launch: compare the loss at the first training step, i.e. how wrong the model is on the first batch of data. At the first step the weights have just been loaded and not yet updated, so the candidate and the original face the same weights and the same batch, and their losses should be almost identical. Legitimate changes only cause tiny differences from a different order of computation, whereas weights that were loaded or split wrongly make the loss change several-fold. So the rule is that the first-step loss must be within 5% of the original's, and no loss in the whole trial may be infinite or invalid.

To make it truly unattended, the authors added several hooks around Claude Code: the agent cannot finish until the budget is spent or it has written down a reason to stop, with evidence; when it wants to ask a person something, it instead "takes the default and records the assumption"; unknown destructive commands are blocked. Every run is written into an append-only ledger, so the system can recover even after a crash. When a campaign ends, the agent writes down lessons, which go into the lesson library for next time after human review.

3. Result one: faster than the strongest public recipes

The authors first reproduced NVIDIA's four official benchmark recipes unchanged on their own cluster; three came within 2% of NVIDIA's published speed, showing that the starting point was fair. From those recipes ATTUNE gained another 7% to 26%, putting it 6% to 17% above NVIDIA's published figures. The authors then took four models not seen during development and tuned them starting from public recipes written by others.

ModelHardwareSpeed-up
Qwen3-30B-A3B8 H100s+9.9%
GPT-OSS-20B8 H100s+17.4%
Llama-3.1-70B64 H100s+26.4%
GLM-4.5128 B200s+33.9%
MiniMax-M264 B200s+164.2%
Llama-3.1-405B128 B200s+6.8%
Mixtral-8x22B128 H100s0% (original kept)

How much speed can be gained depends on how far the original recipe is from the current setting. MiniMax-M2's original recipe was written for reinforcement learning on 128 cards and kept the optimiser's data in CPU memory to save GPU memory; on 64 cards doing ordinary training, that trick slows things down instead. ATTUNE turned it off and changed how the pipeline was split, raising the speed to 2.6 times the original. GLM-4.5's recipe was written for H100s; on B200s the diagnosis found the bottleneck had become transferring data between machines and launching many small compute tasks. ATTUNE therefore kept the data exchange between experts within one machine. Llama-3.1-70B switched to a faster attention routine, and computation came to take 98.5% of each step, with almost no idle waiting. The Mixtral and 405B recipes had already been tuned by the vendor for the same hardware, leaving little to gain; Mixtral's best candidate stayed within the noise, so by the rules the original recipe was kept.

4. Result two: with the same budget, it finds better recipes than other tuners

The authors gave every tuning method the same budget: 30 times the GPU-hours of one trial of the original recipe, with the same gate and the same release rules, and 3 campaigns per model. On GLM-4.5, ATTUNE gained 33.9% on average using only 669 GPU-hours and 6.4 hours; OptiCo gained nothing yet spent 1,407 GPU-hours; random search gained 7.8%; Bayesian optimisation only 1.8%. On MiniMax-M2, ATTUNE gained 164.2%, the best rival 55.5%. This shows ATTUNE not only found faster recipes but also spent less on the tuning itself.

Most interesting is why OptiCo failed. The way of splitting the model that ATTUNE found on GLM-4.5 is actually within the 11 knobs OptiCo can adjust, and comes within 2% of ATTUNE's result, but OptiCo did not find it: it only tried the relevant setting with shallower pipelines, and its data exchange between experts always crossed machines. The answer was inside the black-box search space, but without diagnosis to point the way, most attempts either ran out of memory or were slower than the current best and got discarded. This shows that ATTUNE's advantage comes mainly from "look at the bottleneck before acting", not merely from having more things it can change.

The authors also removed ATTUNE's parts one at a time to see the effect. Without the code of practice and lesson library, the speed-ups on the two test models fell from 88.0% to 66.9% and from 49.4% to 42.9%, and half the trials failed to launch properly. Allowed only OptiCo's 11 knobs, GLM-4.7-Flash got just 18.1%, because its biggest gain came from turning off "keep optimiser data in CPU memory", which is not on that list.

5. Can the gate itself be trusted

The authors tested the gate specifically. All 460 legitimate runs were passed, and every configuration error was rejected before launch. They then deliberately planted 6 kinds of errors in the code: the 2 that change the model's forward computation raised the first-step loss by over 150% and were caught. Errors that only act when weights are updated, such as leaving out part of the gradient summation, cannot be seen at the first step at all. Shifting the labels by one word when computing the loss changed it by only 2%, about the same as the largest legitimate difference. These slipped through.

The gate also proved its worth in real use. On Nemotron-3-Nano, the configuration check blocked 19 pipeline splits with "unequal numbers of layers per stage". One of them happened to be the fastest of all trials, but it loaded other layers' weights into the wrong layers, and its first-step loss was 215% to 768% higher than normal. Without the gate, this "fastest recipe" would have been handed over.

6. Limitations and practical meaning

The authors list three limitations. First, the gate only looks at the configuration and the first step, so errors that act only when weights are updated go unnoticed, and a full training run is still needed for validation before real use. Second, the lesson library comes from past tuning, and GLM-4.5 belongs to the same family as a model used during development, so some of the gain may come from "having seen something similar". Without the lesson library, however, GLM-4.5's result was within the noise of the full system. Third, ATTUNE only tunes configuration the framework exposes; it does not change low-level compute routines or code, and does not cover the part of reinforcement learning where the model generates samples. There is one more lesson: when the authors went back and checked the lesson library, about one fifth of the entries were wrong, some holding only for the job on which they were first measured.

For training-platform teams, the most useful parts to borrow are the gate and the accounting, not the agent itself. Whether tuning is done by a person or an agent, you can first build a set of checks: compare the parameters that finally take effect, look them up in an uneditable register of "changes that alter what is trained", then compare the first-step loss. That keeps parameters which quietly change training, like "drop words over the cap" or "accumulate gradients at low precision", out before launch. Budgets should count from machine allocation to release, failed runs included. If your recipe was carried over from other hardware or another task (such as reinforcement learning), auto-tuning pays off most; if you use a vendor recipe tuned for the same hardware, expect much less, as in the paper such recipes gained only 0% to 26%. The lesson library should be checked against the original records regularly, keeping only entries the model does not already know or that correct its wrong intuitions.

papers.title: RemoteANN: A Native Vector Search Engine for Cloud Object Storage
papers.authors: Yutong Gou, Silu Huang, Yue Wang, Jianjun Chen, Cheng Long
papers.summary: RemoteANN co-designs vector indexing and query execution for cloud object storage. Quantized inverted lists, reordered data, merged range reads and local SSD caching reduce remote I/O. At matched target recall, the authors report up to 5.9× higher throughput than representative baselines.
papers.key_insight: The useful optimization target is remote requests per query. Data locality makes request merging and caching effective; faster distance computation alone cannot remove object-store latency.

papers.title: uGDS: A User-Space Development Kit for High-Performance GPU Direct Storage
papers.authors: Jing Wei, Guanyi Chen, Qi Chen, Chuyu Zhang, Zheng Zhou, Chutian Wang, Jian Zhang
papers.summary: NVIDIA GDS moves NVMe↔GPU over PCIe P2P DMA, but still routes every I/O control path through the kernel, imposes total order on the stream path, and ships a closed user-space engine. uGDS is a user-space kit: on a Samsung 990 PRO it reaches up to 12.12× GDS batch-read and 30.69× write bandwidth, and cuts 4-KiB sync write latency 84.1% with two issuing threads. On one stream GDS keeps only 40.8% of its sync 16-MiB read bandwidth; submission calls can eat 99.6% of wall time. ==GPU Direct Storage bottlenecks are often control-path and ordering semantics, not just DMA bandwidth==.

deep_reading.content_html:
Large-model inference services store the KV cache they have already computed on SSDs, so that the next request with the same opening can read them back instead of recomputing. NVIDIA provides GPU Direct Storage (GDS for short below) for this, letting data go from SSD straight into GPU memory without a stop in host memory. Yet when the authors measured it inside the open-source cache system LMCache, asynchronous reads through GDS on a single task queue reached only 2.36 GiB/s, less than half of synchronous read bandwidth; 99.6% of the time was stuck at the "submit request" step. This paper from Sun Yat-sen University, HKUST (Guangzhou) and others open-sources uGDS, which moves the job of "telling the SSD what to do" out of the operating-system kernel and into an ordinary program. Data still goes straight from SSD to GPU; what changes is who gives the orders. On one A100 GPU plus one Samsung 990 PRO SSD, uGDS's batched reads are up to 12 times as fast as GDS and batched writes up to 30 times; plugged into LMCache, the median time-to-first-token for long prompts (from sending a request to seeing the first output word) fell from 1.9 seconds to 0.7 seconds.

1. The problem: data no longer takes a detour, but commands still do

First, the difference between the "data path" and the "control path". The data path is where the data itself flows from and to; the control path is who tells the hardware, and through which steps, "move this piece of data to that place".

GDS fixed the data path: an SSD can DMA data over PCIe straight into GPU memory, without the CPU copying it. But GDS's control path enters the operating-system kernel every time: a read request passes in turn through the virtual file system, the actual file system, the block-device layer and the kernel's SSD driver, and NVIDIA's kernel module also looks up a GPU address for every 4 KiB page of data. When moving one large block, these fixed costs are spread thin and hardly noticed; but in KV cache reads and writes and vector search, requests tend to be small, frequent and latency-sensitive, and these costs become the main expense.

The authors point to two further problems with GDS.

First, the queueing rules are too rigid. GDS's asynchronous interface inherits the rule of GPU task queues (CUDA streams): within one queue, every request waits for the previous one to finish. But when LMCache reads back a stretch of cache, the small pieces need no particular order; they only have to all arrive before the model's computation begins. To use the full bandwidth, applications have to spread requests over many queues, effectively doing GDS's scheduling for it.

Second, problems are invisible. GDS's kernel part is open source, but the user-space library that handles batched submission, background threads and queue integration is released only as a binary. When things stall you can neither find the cause nor change the policy.

Others had already driven SSDs directly from ordinary programs, showing that this path works, but those prototypes supported only NVIDIA GPUs, assumed a single submitting thread, and did not track "requests still in flight", so a program could free a piece of GPU memory while the SSD was still writing into it.

2. Method: the CPU gives commands, the SSD moves data, the GPU only computes

uGDS separates three things.

At start-up, privileged setup is done once, by a small kernel module: it takes the SSD over from the kernel driver, maps the SSD's control registers and command queues into memory the program can read and write directly, locks the GPU memory to be used, and records its addresses on the bus.

During normal reads and writes the kernel is not involved at all. Following the SSD's protocol (NVMe, the standard command format for solid-state drives), the program itself writes a 64-byte command saying where on the disk to read, how much, and which pages of GPU memory to put it in. It then writes a number into a "doorbell" register on the SSD to signal a new command. After that it checks the completion queue for the SSD's report that it is done. The whole process is ordinary memory reads and writes, with no system calls.

The data itself still moves directly between the SSD and GPU memory, not through host memory.

The cost is that the SSD must be detached from the kernel driver and given to uGDS exclusively, and the program sees "byte number such-and-such on the disk" rather than files. The authors argue this fits cache engines like LMCache and Mooncake, which manage their own storage blocks; if files are needed, a user-space file system can be layered on top.

To make this path both fast and safe, uGDS has four designs.

First, it supports both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. When GPU memory is registered, each vendor's memory addresses are translated into a uniform list of page addresses the SSD understands, so code above does not need to know whose card it is.

Second, command queues are split into two groups. SSDs support several sets of command queues. uGDS sets aside one deep queue just for batched requests, and the rest serve single synchronous requests. That way, when a large batch floods in, single requests are not left waiting behind it. Batched requests also gather many commands and ring the "doorbell" only once, saving repeated notification costs.

Third, it prevents "freeing while writing". This is where driving hardware yourself most easily goes wrong. For each request sent, uGDS notes "transfer in flight" against the GPU memory involved; trying to free that memory while a transfer is in flight is refused outright. Each registration also carries an increasing number, so that an old request cannot hit newly allocated memory that reuses the same address. If a command times out, the disk is marked faulty and isolated, and resources can only be reclaimed after a hardware reset confirms the SSD has stopped.

Fourth, completion notification is selectable. By default the CPU keeps polling the completion queue, which responds fastest but occupies a whole CPU core. Hardware interrupts can be used instead, with the kernel only waking the program and everything else still done in user space.

None of these ideas is new on its own: SPDK, which drives SSDs directly from ordinary programs, has long existed. uGDS's contribution is turning them into a GPU storage library that maps one-to-one onto GDS's interface and can be swapped in for production use: it has synchronous, batched and queue-ordered asynchronous interfaces, both vendors' GPUs share one abstraction, the safety mechanisms are in place, and everything from the kernel module to user space is open source. The most practical point is that a single queue can use the full bandwidth, so applications no longer need to split requests over a dozen queues.

3. Experiments: small requests, batched requests and the first batch

Tests used a server with two Intel Xeon CPUs, one A100 GPU and one Samsung 990 PRO 1TB SSD, compared against NVIDIA's current version of GDS.

uGDS starts faster: median initialisation is 42 milliseconds, against 115 for GDS, which spends almost all of it opening NVIDIA's driver session, loading configuration and probing the bus topology. For elastic services that frequently start and retire worker processes, this saves a fair amount of time.

Single small requests gain the most. With 2 threads writing 4 KiB blocks, uGDS's bandwidth is 6.2 times GDS's and average latency falls from 48 microseconds to 7.7, because each request skips a long chain of kernel steps. With more threads and bigger requests, the bottleneck moves to the SSD and the bus themselves, and the gap narrows to 1.2 to 1.4 times. On an AMD platform, against AMD's equivalent library, it is also about 1.2 times as fast.

Batched requests lead across the board. The authors tested 36 combinations of "request size × requests per batch", and uGDS won all of them: reads 2.1 to 12.1 times GDS, writes 2.3 to 30.7 times. The smaller the requests and the more per batch, the bigger the gap.

Following an anomaly, the authors tracked down a problem in GDS. More requests per batch should mean faster, yet for 128 KiB writes GDS got slower as batches grew. The cause is the first batch: with 128 requests per batch, GDS's first batch takes 91 milliseconds to read and 118 to write, nearly ninety percent of the whole 64 MiB transfer time. This is because GDS defers mapping GPU memory addresses until the first read or write, and the authors suspect it also allocates the internal state needed for batching only at the first submission. uGDS does all this during initialisation, so its first batch is almost as fast as later ones. Even leaving out the first batch and looking only at the steady state, with 4 KiB requests and 128 per batch, uGDS still reads 8.8 times and writes 23.8 times as fast as GDS.

Polling and interrupts each have their uses. For small 4 KiB requests, constant CPU polling cuts latency from 21 microseconds to 9, at the cost of a fully busy core. For large 1 MiB requests, switching to interrupts lowers the CPU use of the requesting thread from 100% to 4%, with only 5.5% more latency. So polling suits latency-sensitive cases, and interrupts are better value for large transfers.

4. Real-world effect: inside LMCache

The authors plugged uGDS into LMCache and ran end-to-end tests with the small Qwen3-0.6B model and the vLLM inference framework. To test the SSD path specifically, they turned off vLLM's own in-memory cache, so every cache hit had to be read back from the SSD.

MetricGDSuGDS
Median time-to-first-token, 32,768-token long prompt1915 ms715 ms
Throughput, 1,024-token short requests, 256 concurrentabout 19,000 tokens/s (tops out at 32 concurrent)50,000 tokens/s
Share of total time spent on "submit request"99.6%1.0%
Single-queue asynchronous read bandwidth2.36 GiB/s5.49 GiB/s

For prompts from 3,840 to 40,704 tokens, uGDS's time-to-first-token is consistently about four tenths of GDS's. The time for the GPU to place the read-back data into vLLM's memory is the same on both sides, which shows that all of the saving comes from the storage path. Another key difference is scaling: GDS tops out at around 32 concurrent requests, while uGDS keeps scaling to 256, with 2.6 times GDS's throughput.

5. Limitations

uGDS must have the whole SSD to itself: once detached from the kernel driver, the disk has no file system and cannot be used as an ordinary disk by other programs. Currently one uGDS instance drives only one local SSD; using several disks together and reaching remote SSDs over a network are still planned. Synchronous requests are assigned to command queues in turn and hold the queue until done, so a large request slows small ones on the same queue; the authors plan a load-aware scheduler. The experiments used only one consumer SSD and one A100, with the IOMMU (the hardware that checks addresses when devices access memory) turned off, and the end-to-end test used only a small 0.6B model. How it performs with data-centre SSDs, and with several GPUs sharing a bus switch chip, remains to be verified.

6. Practical meaning

If you work on tiered KV cache storage (GPU memory, host memory and SSD) or GPU vector search, and the SSD is a dedicated local disk, uGDS is worth trying as a replacement for GDS. Small, frequent reads on a single queue are exactly where GDS suffers most and uGDS gains most.

Before going live, confirm three things: whether the SSD can be dedicated and detached from the kernel driver; whether the layer above already manages its own storage-block allocation, as LMCache and Mooncake do; and whether the server's IOMMU settings allow the SSD and GPU to transfer directly. When deploying, pick the completion method by workload: CPU polling for latency-sensitive inference nodes, interrupts for throughput-oriented or CPU-constrained jobs.

Even without switching libraries, two of the paper's findings about GDS apply directly. First, GDS spends tens of extra milliseconds preparing the first time it reads or writes a piece of GPU memory, so after a service starts it should do one warm-up read or write for each "GPU memory and disk" pair. Second, GDS's single queue gets blocked on submission, so critical reads should be split across several queues in parallel.

papers.title: TokenGate: Adapting LLMs for Fast and Memory-Efficient Prefill with Learned Token Pruning
papers.authors: Liana Patel, Rishabh Ranjan, Ion Stoica, Matei Zaharia, Carlos Guestrin
papers.summary: TokenGate trains an existing model to skip less useful tokens in later layers. Token-gated attention supplies a learning signal for token selection. Across the tested tasks, the authors report up to 11.3× faster time to first token without measured accuracy loss.
papers.key_insight: Token selection can be learned during lightweight adaptation instead of imposed as a fixed heuristic. This targets prefill latency and memory, with an adaptation step required before deployment.

papers.title: E8-QAT: Efficient 2-Bit Quantization-Aware Training with Implicit Lattice Codebooks
papers.authors: Xinyu Lei, Hong Huang, Jiebin Zhang, Hongyu Li, Jinlong Song, Decheng Wu, Guanghua Yu, Jianchen Zhu, Sujian Li
papers.summary: Grouped weight quantization avoids an explicit codebook search by projecting onto a structured lattice. At each format’s largest feasible batch, decoding reaches 1.97 times BF16 throughput. This comparison includes the batch-size benefit of lower memory use.
papers.key_insight: Treat storage format and feasible batch size as coupled decisions. Arithmetic lattice projection reduces codebook search overhead, while memory savings create additional serving capacity.

papers.title: Large Flow Language Models
papers.authors: Arnav Chavan, Chanhyuk Lee, Udbhav Bamba, Jaehoon Yoo, Seunghoon Hong
papers.summary: Lafa adapts pretrained autoregressive models into blockwise continuous-flow language models. A single model proposes flow-based drafts and verifies them autoregressively, reaching 2.54 times autoregressive throughput at comparable quality.
papers.key_insight: Drafting and verification can share a model. Retaining autoregressive capability creates a verification path for parallel flow proposals without a separately maintained drafter.

papers.title: Is 2:4 Sparsity Still Worth It? Semi-Structured Sparsity versus Quantization in LLM Inference
papers.authors: Xiuyi Qin
papers.summary: An independent researcher compares "add 2:4 sparsity" versus "drop one precision tier" on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B under matched storage bits (including sparse indices) and matched nominal compute tiers, with measurements on L40S, H100, and RTX PRO 6000. ==As long as a lower precision is still available, adding 2:4 is both less accurate and slower==: 2:4 + INT8 costs the same storage as INT5. At the FP8 floor, a retrained 2:4 model served by vLLM on H100 raises prefill throughput 27% over dense FP8 with matched GSM8K; but ==during retraining perplexity recovers first while reasoning accuracy recovers much more slowly==.

deep_reading.content_html:
From Ampere onward, NVIDIA GPUs support 2:4 sparsity: in a matmul, one operand keeps 2 nonzeros per 4 elements along the accumulate axis, and tensor cores can nominally run twice as fast. It stacks with quantization, so the practical deployment question is: at the current precision, is the next step to add 2:4, or to drop one precision tier? This independent researcher's paper compares, on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B, under "matched storage bits (including sparse position indices)" and "matched nominal compute tiers," all six matmul operand roles in one transformer layer, with speed measured on L40S, H100, and RTX PRO 6000. Conclusion: as long as a lower precision tier is still available, adding 2:4 is both less accurate and slower; only at the hardware's lowest supported precision (FP8 on Ada/Hopper) does 2:4 pay off—on H100, a vLLM-served 2:4 + FP8 model raises prefill throughput 27% over dense FP8 with matched GSM8K, but only after retraining.

1. vLLM already removed 2:4 support—is it still worth using?

On one side every NVIDIA GPU generation keeps sparse tensor cores, and Blackwell adds sparse FP4; on the other, in 2026 vLLM and LLM Compressor removed 2:4 support for lack of users. Prior prune-versus-quantize comparisons mostly use "nominal compression," focus on weights, and do not put "add 2:4" versus "drop one precision" head-to-head on real hardware.

The authors flag four easy-to-miss points:

  • 2:4 stores a position index beside each kept value, so bits per original element exceed half;
  • both claim 2× throughput, but datasheets do not say how much you actually get;
  • at inference most operands (activations, Q, K, V, attention probabilities) are computed on the fly and must be pruned/compressed before every matmul—time invisible if you only time the matmul;
  • hardware dictates which operand may be sparse and along which axis, so tensor-wide statistics (e.g. kurtosis) do not show what 2:4 actually drops.

2. Method: compare at matched cost

2.1 Matched bits

Each format is billed by bits actually stored per original element—values, indices, and scales. Dense INTk uses one FP16 scale per 128 elements: $k+0.125$ bits/element; 2:4 keeps half the elements but adds 1 index bit per original element. So 2:4 + INT8 costs the same as dense INT5; 2:4 + INT4 equals INT3; 2:4 + FP16 costs more than FP8.

At matched storage the real choice is "drop half the elements and store the rest at 2× precision" versus "keep every element and add 1 bit each."

2.2 Matched compute tiers

Pair by datasheet nominal throughput: 2× tier is 2:4 + FP16 versus dense FP8/INT8; 4× tier is 2:4 + FP8 versus dense 4-bit float (Blackwell only).

2.3 How to measure

Accuracy is operator-level relative error versus an FP32 reference, summarized as $R=$ (best 2:4 config error) / (best quantization config error); $R<1$ means 2:4 wins. Each side picks the best among equally effortful methods: 2:4 tries magnitude pruning, Wanda, SparseGPT, etc.; quantization tries round-to-nearest, GPTQ, AWQ; all use C4 calibration. Speed uses cuSPARSELt sparse matmul; on-the-fly operands count online prune or online quantize time on both sides. Over 220K measured configs.

3. Experiments

3.1 Above the lowest precision: dropping a precision tier always wins

This checks whether adding 2:4 can ever be more accurate or faster while a lower precision is still available.

Accuracy. At matched bits, 2:4 loses at every storage budget on both models: at 8 bits the error gap is more than an order of magnitude; the gap shrinks as bits fall but does not vanish; under a 3.1-bit budget the closest comparison (Llama's K versus INT3) still has R slightly above 1. In the 2× tier, 2:4 + FP16 error is 5–16× dense FP8 on every operand.

Speed. Table below is "opponent time / 2:4 time"; >1 means 2:4 is faster (Llama-3.1-8B projection layers, median over 2K–16K tokens):

W = sparse weights, X = sparse activations (including online preprocess). Within each tier, the 2:4 side is slower. The authors' explanation: the energy in the 2 values 2:4 drops per 4 elements (sum of squares) cannot be recovered by giving the kept values more bits, while quantization error halves with each extra bit. On Gaussian data, elementwise 2:4 removes 13.2% of energy.

3.2 At the lowest precision: 2:4 can speed up, but needs retraining

This checks how much 2:4 helps at the FP8 or NVFP4 floor and at what cost. Linear-layer weights are 2:4; attention stays BF16; model is Llama-3.1-8B base.

vLLM end-to-end (single H100), 2:4 model = Sparse-Llama (2:4 Llama retrained on 13B tokens):

2:4 + FP8 beats dense FP8 on both prefill and decode, with no significant GSM8K difference. Serving the same weights with dense kernels removes the speedup, so the gain comes from sparse kernels. Under BF16, vLLM's 2:4 path is not faster than dense.

Retraining cost. One-shot pruning is unusable at every floor. Table: WikiText-2 perplexity / GSM8K accuracy (250 questions):

The authors retrain by distilling from the dense model on 1B FineWeb-Edu tokens: perplexity approaches Sparse-Llama, but GSM8K is only about half. Perplexity overestimates how much retraining has recovered; judging whether retraining is done requires reasoning tasks.

3.3 Blackwell sparse FP4

Blackwell sparse FP4 is not elementwise 2:4; it keeps 2 of 4 adjacent pairs per 8 elements. The kernel is 1.4× dense NVFP4, but removes 20.8% of energy on Gaussian data; one-shot pruning yields perplexity 108.83—five times elementwise 2:4; Sparse-Llama retrained for elementwise 2:4 cannot convert directly. Within the authors' 1B-token retrain budget, GSM8K recovers only to 0.132.

4. Limitations

Only two 8B models; Blackwell 4:8 conclusions are limited to 1B tokens and one untuned retrain recipe—whether longer retraining recovers is untested. The 4-bit integer weight floor (mainly for decode) has no speed numbers because vLLM removed the sparse kernels. Production often adds a Hadamard rotation before low-bit quantization; the authors note that makes 2:4 worse on most operands, so these unrotated results are optimistic for 2:4.

5. Takeaways

If the hardware still supports a lower precision (e.g. H100 BF16→FP8), drop precision first—do not add 2:4. If you already serve FP8, prefill throughput is the bottleneck, and you can get a fully retrained 2:4 model, 2:4 can give real speedups—but vLLM mainline removed support, so you must maintain it yourself. When evaluating a retrained sparse model, do not trust perplexity alone.

papers.title: Cache Engineering for Agents
papers.authors: Tianyu Fu, Ruoxi Wang, Zihan Min, Zhongqi Ren, Zhihao Li, Tengxuan Liu, Shengxu Mu, Hanling Zhang, Yu Wang
papers.summary: On long agent trajectories KV-cache I/O and storage dominate cost, and editing the prefix invalidates later cache and forces re-prefill. This paper shifts from rewriting history text to engineering cache lifetime and eviction. Versus threshold-triggered summarization, a simple tool-response drop policy cuts average cost 27.7% and lifts benchmark scores 1.7 points; with AKV it reaches ~1.2× output throughput and ~1.5× better P95 latency; an RSI policy saves another 7.1% on held-out tasks. KV reads can be 82.4% of API cost. ==Agent cost often turns on not invalidating cache, not only on shorter summaries==.

deep_reading.content_html:
An agent working on a hard task often goes back and forth with tools such as search, web pages and code execution for hundreds of turns. On every turn the model re-reads the KV cache of everything that came before. The paper measures that reading this old cache accounts for 82.4% of total inference cost, far more than generating new tokens. The usual way to save money is to delete or summarize old messages, but any edit to earlier text invalidates all the cache after it, so everything from the edit point onward has to be recomputed. A Tsinghua team proposes working at a different layer: leave the text history untouched and drop only selected entries from the cache, while the remaining entries are reused as they are. They built an inference serving system for this, called AKV. Across three models and four agent benchmarks, a simple policy of "keep the cache of only the 12 most recent tool outputs" beats the common "summarize when the length limit is reached" approach, with a 1.7-point higher average score and 27.7% lower average cost.

1. The problem: recomputation is expensive, and cutting everything at once loses information

The longer an agent's conversation gets, the more trouble the cache causes. The first problem is cost: the cache keeps growing and is read on every turn, so storing and reading it is expensive. The second is accuracy: a model can only handle so much context reliably, and once the content taking part in computation goes past that range, quality drops noticeably.

The standard fix today is to edit the text, also called "context engineering": delete old messages or replace them with summaries. But an LLM's cache is computed in order, and each token's cache depends on everything before it. The earlier the edit, the longer the stretch that must be recomputed. So common agent frameworks wait until the length hits some limit and then summarize most of the history in one go, keeping only the last few turns, which keeps the number of recomputations low. Cutting everything at once like this easily throws away useful information from the middle turns too.

The authors start with a comparison. They run GPT-OSS-120B on the first 100 questions of BrowseComp-Plus (a QA benchmark that needs many rounds of search to answer), 4 attempts per question with at most 100 turns. Keeping only the 12 most recent tool outputs by deleting text every turn costs 1.85 times as much as doing nothing, because of repeated recomputation. Summarizing once at 48K tokens cuts cost by only about 7% and drops accuracy by 5 points. Dropping old tool outputs directly from the cache improves accuracy and cost at the same time.

2. Method: three operations on the cache

The authors first separate two lengths. One is how long the conversation is as text. The other is how much cache actually takes part in later computation, which the paper calls the "active cache". Text editing changes the first; cache editing changes only the second.

In this framing, the paper defines three operations:

  • Append: the normal case. Read in new tokens, attach their cache at the end, and increment the position index.
  • Drop: exclude specified cache entries from all later computation. The remaining entries stay exactly as they are, the text history is unchanged, and new tokens keep counting positions upward as usual.
  • Reposition: renumber the retained entries 0, 1, 2… in their original order, and number the next new token after them.

Why is the third operation needed? Dropping does not make the position indices smaller. The cache shrinks, but the index keeps climbing and will eventually exceed the largest position the model can handle. Repositioning pulls the indices back down. For models that use RoPE this step is cheap: to move an entry from position p to position q, rotate its key by the angle for q−p; the value stays the same and nothing is recomputed.

What gets dropped? The authors looked at the model's attention distribution and found two patterns: older content receives less attention, and at similar distances tool outputs receive less attention than the model's own reasoning. So the main policy is rolling drop of old tool outputs: keep all reasoning content and the 12 most recent tool outputs, and drop the cache of earlier tool outputs step by step.

3. The difficulty: the same text can have different caches

In a normal inference server, the same text prefix means the same cache, so caches can be reused by matching prefixes. Cache editing breaks this: the same text, reached through a different order of operations, yields a different cache.

Take the example in the figure. All three paths end with only B and C kept. But in ①, C was computed while A was still visible, so it carries A's influence. In ②, A had already been dropped when C was computed. In ③, there was no A before B even when B itself was computed. So C's cache differs across the three paths. The paper therefore describes a cache state by "the full sequence of operations applied since an empty cache": for a given model, that sequence uniquely determines the current cache. The inference server has to remember both the text history and the operation history to reuse cache correctly.

4. AKV: turning this into an inference service

AKV's interface is almost identical to a standard chat API. The client sends the full message list as usual, with one extra optional field that says "after message N, drop these entries and reposition here". The client does not need to know which caches the server still holds; each turn it just appends messages and operations as usual.

Inside the server there are three mechanisms.

The first is reuse. Inference servers usually do prefix caching with a radix tree, so requests with the same prefix share a segment of cache. AKV adds "drop" and "reposition" nodes to the tree and matches on both text and operations during lookup. That is why ① and ② in the figure can share the A–B segment, while each keeps its own copy of C because A was dropped at different times.
